domains.title: Mountains, Ski, and the Bow
domains.subtitle: The domain of Skaði
domains.lead:
Skaði is the giantess who walked into Ásgarðr armed and walked out with a settlement. Daughter of the giant Þjazi of Þrymheimr, she came in helmet and byrnie to claim compensation for her father's death, and the gods met her terms: a husband chosen by his feet alone, a laugh no one thought she had in her, and her father's eyes set in the sky as stars.

Her dominion is the high country. Grímnismál remembers her dwelling in her father's ancient home, and Snorri calls her ǫndurgoð and ǫndurdís — the ski-deity who travels the drifts on her ǫndurr and shoots game with the bow. The sea she married into never held her; the mountains took her back.

cards.name: Þrymheimr
cards.desc: Her father's storm-hall in the high peaks; when the sea failed her she went home to its wolves and wind.

cards.name: The Bow and the Ski
cards.desc: Snorri names her ǫndurgoð and ǫndurdís — the ski-deity who fares over winter drifts and shoots her game.

cards.name: The Eyes of Þjazi
cards.desc: Óðinn cast the slain giant's eyes into the sky as two stars — part of the weregild his daughter exacted.

cards.name: The Venom-Snake
cards.desc: Over the bound Loki she fastened a poison-snake; only Sigyn's basin stands between the drops and his face.

symbols.name: Skis (ǫndurr)
symbols.meaning: The snow-shoes that carry her over the winter peaks, source of her titles ǫndurgoð and ǫndurdís

symbols.name: Bow
symbols.meaning: The huntress's weapon; she fares with bow and ski and shoots game in the mountains

symbols.name: Þrymheimr
symbols.meaning: The storm-home, her father Þjazi's hall and her own final refuge

symbols.name: Wolf
symbols.meaning: The mountain cry she preferred, which Njǫrðr found hateful beside the song of swans

symbols.name: Venom-dripping serpent
symbols.meaning: The instrument of her vengeance, fastened above the bound Loki's face

mythology.lead: Skaði is the giantess of the high fells: daughter of Þjazi, inheritor of Þrymheimr, the 'bright bride of the gods' named in Grímnismál. She enters the mythic record already armed — coming to Ásgarðr not as a supplicant but as a claimant — and she leaves it as vengeance incarnate, fastening the venom-snake above the bound Loki. Between those entrances and exits lies the Edda's strangest marriage: chosen by feet, wrecked by geography. Snorri remembers her above all on skis, bow in hand, and names her ǫndurgoð and ǫndurdís, the ski-deity. Her myths ask what compensation can repair, and what terrain a self will not surrender.

myths.title: The Weregild of Þjazi
myths.text:
The giant Þjazi had abducted Iðunn and her apples of youth; when Loki stole her back, Þjazi pursued in eagle shape, and the Æsir kindled a fire that scorched his wings and brought him down inside their garth, where they slew him. Skaði took her father's death as a cause of war: she put on helmet and byrnie and came to Ásgarðr in full war-gear, and the gods chose settlement over battle.

Her terms were three. She would choose a husband from among the Æsir — but only by the feet, the gods hidden behind a screen. They must make her laugh, which she thought no one could do; Loki tied one end of a rope to a goat's beard and the other to his own testicles, and as each hauled and shrieked he tumbled at last onto her knee, and she laughed. And Óðinn took Þjazi's eyes and hurled them into the heavens, where they shine as two stars — a father's face written into the night his daughter would hunt beneath.

myths.title: The Feet She Chose, the Sea She Left
myths.text:
Behind the screen the gods stood bare to the calves, and Skaði picked the fairest pair of feet, certain they could only belong to Baldr. They belonged to Njǫrðr of Nóatún — the sea-god, rich and even-tempered, and entirely of the wrong element. They agreed to divide their marriage by terrain: nine nights in Þrymheimr, then nine at Nóatún.

The verses Snorri preserves are the marriage's epitaph. Njǫrðr: 'Hateful to me are the mountains; I was there not long, nine nights only — the howling of wolves seemed evil to me beside the song of swans.' Skaði answered: 'I could not sleep on the sea's bed for the screaming of the bird; he wakes me who comes from the wide wave every morning — the gull.' Then she went up into the mountains and dwelt in Þrymheimr, where she travels on skis with her bow and shoots game, and is called ǫndurgoð or ǫndurdís.

myths.title: The Snake above Loki
myths.text:
At Ægir's feast, as Loki's flyting turns vicious, Skaði is among those he cannot charm. She warns him that his tongue runs free only a little longer: on a sharp rock, with the guts of his own frost-cold son, the gods will bind him. Loki answers with cruelty of his own — boasting that he was first and foremost among those who dealt Þjazi his death-blow, and claiming that Skaði once invited him to her bed.

The poem's prose epilogue gives her the last word without words. When Loki lies bound, it is Skaði who takes a venomous snake and fastens it above his face so that the poison drips downward. His wife Sigyn kneels beside him holding a basin against the drops; only when she turns to empty it does the venom strike, and Loki writhes — in Snorri's telling, the cause men call earthquakes. The giantess who once demanded a laugh becomes the keeper of the dripping drop.

myths.title: The Son of the Mountain
myths.text:
The Eddas never show Skaði with any husband but Njǫrðr, yet a genealogical tract knew better. Hversu Noregr byggðist ('How Norway Was Settled') names Sæmingr, son of Óðinn and Skaði, as the ancestor from whom the jarls of Hlaðir — Viking-Age Norway's ruling house — claimed descent; Snorri, in Ynglinga saga (ch. 11), knows Sæmingr as Óðinn's son and forefather of Jarl Hákon the Great, but names no mother. The clues to the union were always there: Óðinn hurled Þjazi's eyes into the sky 'as a compensation to Skaði' (Skáldskaparmál), and Loki boasted in Lokasenna that the mountain goddess once invited him to her bed — the Edda remembered the scandal even where it forgot the marriage.

Dynastic myth closes the circle the poems left open: the giantess who walked into Ásgarðr with a claim left Norway with a crown.

skadi.syncretism: Skaði's clearest structural parallels stand inside the Norse corpus itself: Gerðr, the giant's daughter who marries Freyr — Skaði's own stepson by Njǫrðr — so that two giant-brides enter the Vanir household a generation apart; and Ullr, named in the same chapter of Gylfaginning as an archer and snow-shoe runner, who functions almost as her male doublet, his cult the better attested of the two in Scandinavian place-names. Etymologists have connected her name with Gothic skadus and Old English sceadu, 'shadow', and the first element of Scandinavia (Pliny's Scadinavia) has been derived from a related root — both proposals remain conjectural and debated. Beyond the Germanic world she invites comparison rather than borrowing: Artemis, the mountain huntress with the bow, is the obvious Greek functional echo. In later Scandinavian folklore she fades from cult but not from landscape — the wild huntress and the mountain-woman of the high fells keep her outline, and the nineteenth-century Norwegian ski revival made her silhouette a national one.
skadi.culturalLegacy: Skaði never reached Wagner's stage — the Ring is built from Vǫlsunga and Nibelung material, and the giantess of Þrymheimr has no part in it — but modernity found her anyway. The sport she was said to practice made her an emblem of Norwegian winter: she is the 'ski-goddess' of modern handbooks, invoked wherever Scandinavian skiing celebrates its mythic roots. In comics, Marvel's Fear Itself (2011) borrowed her name for the hammer-wielding herald of the Serpent; in games, Smite (2016) fields her as a playable huntress with the winter-wolf Kaldr at her side. Astronomers gave her name to Skathi, a moon of Saturn. In contemporary heathenry she is honored as a goddess of winter, self-reliance, and the hunt — the deity who sets her terms, keeps them, and goes home when the ground is wrong.
skadi.extendedMeditation:
Every other figure in her story negotiates; Skaði stipulates. Wronged, she does not raid and she does not weep — she arms herself, walks to the enemy's gates, and dictates compensation. The settlement is exact: a husband, a laugh, two stars. Even her mistake has integrity. Choosing a god by his feet is absurd, and she abides by the result without complaint.

The marriage to Njǫrðr is the Edda's most honest parable of incompatibility. Neither party is wrong: the gull genuinely wakes her, the wolf genuinely unnerves him, and nine nights each way is the full extent of what compromise can do when identity is terrain. Skaði does not diminish herself to keep the peace; she goes home to Þrymheimr and straps on her skis. And it is she — not Þórr, not Óðinn — who hangs the snake over Loki. The Edda gives its last act of private justice to the daughter who never forgot what she was owed.

sources.name: Poetic Edda: Grímnismál (Bellows translation) — Skaði dwelling in Þrymheimr, 'the god's fair bride'
Poetic Edda: Lokasenna (Bellows translation) — her exchange with Loki and the prose account of the venom-snake
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning (Brodeur translation) — the marriage to Njǫrðr, the nine-night verses, the ski-deity titles
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál (Brodeur translation) — the death of Þjazi and Skaði's weregild
Hversu Noregr byggðist (Flateyjarbók) and Snorri, Ynglinga saga ch. 11 — Sæmingr, son of Óðinn and Skaði, forefather of the jarls of Hlaðir
Skáldskaparmál (Old Norse text, Heimskringla.no)

skadi.archaeology: No material image can be securely identified as Skaði: no runestone names her, and no picture-stone figure is demonstrably the giantess of Þrymheimr. Her attestation is textual — the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270) preserves Grímnismál and Lokasenna, and the Prose Edda manuscripts (Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to; Codex Wormianus AM 242 fol.; Codex Upsaliensis DG 11) carry Snorri's account. The material world her titles presuppose is real enough: prehistoric skis such as the Kalvträsk and Hoting finds from Sweden (c. 3200 BC) and the rock carving of a striding skier at Rødøy in Nordland, Norway (roughly four thousand years old), document the snow-travel culture behind the name ǫndurgoð. Place-names preserve the related ski-god Ullr abundantly; place-name evidence for Skaði herself is sparse and disputed.
skadi.originalScriptNote: Old Norse literature reached us in medieval Icelandic manuscripts written in the Latin alphabet; the earlier epigraphic medium was the Younger Futhark. The theonym Skaði is known from the manuscript tradition alone; a hypothetical runic rendering would approximate ᛋᚴᛅᚦᛁ — the futhark marks no vowel length (ᛅ serves both a and á) and writes the voiced dental fricative with the thorn-rune ᚦ, which covers both [θ] and [ð]. The normalized Old Norse form Skaði therefore carries two features the ASCII form loses: á, the long low back vowel [ɑː] marked by the acute, and ð (eth), the soft dental fricative [ð]. The PUNICODEX registrable form preserves both characters as a Tier-1 restoration of the name's Norse phonology, recovering what neither runes nor ASCII could write.

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b], as in English 'bald'; Old Norse initial b is fully voiced.
Short open back unrounded [ɑ], held brief — Old Norse short a, not the long á.
Lateral [l], voiced stop [d], and the syllabic trill [r̩] of the nominative ending; the final r carries its own beat, as in modern Icelandic.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAHL-dur' — a short open 'ah', the l and d run together, and the final r sounded as a light syllabic trill, as in Icelandic Baldur.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Baldr, son of Óðinn and Frigg; also a rare poetic common noun, baldr 'lord, prince'.

kin.label: Old High German
kin.form: Phol, the figure paired with Wodan in the Second Merseburg Charm, widely — though not universally — read as Baldr.

kin.label: Old English
kin.form: Bældæg, son of Woden in the Anglo-Saxon royal genealogies, whose first element is the same word.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Baldur, the name's unbroken living form.

pronunciation.note: Baldr is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The god's fame vastly outruns his name's orthography; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Light, Beauty, Purity
domains.subtitle: The Best and Fairest of the Æsir
domains.lead: Baldr is the shining son of Óðinn and Frigg — the god Snorri calls simply the best: so fair of face and bright that light itself streams from him, so wise and gracious that his judgments cannot be undone. His hall is Breiðablik, the broad-gleaming, where nothing impure may dwell; his death by the mistletoe shaft is the first grief of the gods and the herald of Ragnarǫk.

cards.name: The Mistletoe
cards.desc: The one shoot too young to swear Frigg's oath — slender, fair, and fatal. From it came the dart that felled the god no weapon could wound.

cards.name: Hringhorni
cards.desc: Baldr's ship, greatest of all ships, launched for his pyre by the giantess Hyrrokkin while the Æsir themselves could not shift it.

cards.name: Draupnir
cards.desc: The drip-gold ring Óðinn laid on the pyre beside his son — the treasure the dead god sent back from Hel as proof the errand reached him.

cards.name: Baldrs Brá
cards.desc: 'Baldr's eyelash' — the whitest of all plants, the daisy, so named because the god's brightness was the measure of whiteness itself.

symbols.name: The mistletoe
symbols.meaning: The overlooked thing that undoes the protected god — young, slender, and unsworn

symbols.name: Hringhorni
symbols.meaning: The greatest of ships, built for the voyage he never took and burned as his bier

symbols.name: Draupnir
symbols.meaning: The ring that travels from pyre to Hel and back — love's token across the boundary of death

symbols.name: Breiðablik
symbols.meaning: The broad-gleaming hall where nothing unclean may be — purity made architecture

symbols.name: Baldrs brá (the daisy)
symbols.meaning: The whitest plant in the world, named for his eyelash — brightness as the standard of measure

mythology.lead: Baldr has the thinnest dossier and the heaviest role of any god in the Edda: he acts in almost nothing, and his death sets everything in motion. The sources agree on the shape — the dreams, the oath, the mistletoe, the blind brother's throw, the burning ship, the failed ransom, the promised return — and almost nothing else about him survives at all.

myths.title: The Best and Fairest
myths.text:
Snorri introduces him in the catalogue of the Æsir with a formula the tradition never varies: Baldr the Good, second son of Óðinn, and 'he is the best, and all praise him'. He is so fair of face and bright that a splendour radiates from him, and one plant is so white that it takes its name from his eyelash — baldrs brá, the daisy, whitest of all plants. He is the wisest of the Æsir, the most beautifully spoken, and the most merciful — yet Snorri adds the one shadow across the portrait: none of his judgments holds; nothing he decides can stand.

His dwelling is Breiðablik, the broad-gleaming, and Grímnismál says of that land that the fewest bale-runes lie there — the place in heaven where impurity has least footing. The Edda paints the perfect god first so that everything after reads as loss.

myths.title: The Dreams and the Prophecy
myths.text:
It begins with dreams. Baldr dreams baleful dreams for his life, and the Æsir take counsel. In Baldrs draumar — the whole poem is this one episode — Óðinn himself saddles Sleipnir, rides down the dark road to Niflhel, and raises a dead völva from her grave east of Hel's gate with spells. She answers unwilling: the benches of Hel are strewn and shining, the mead brewed — for Baldr. Höðr will be his slayer; Váli, born to Óðinn, will avenge him one night old, unwashed and uncombed until he brings Baldr's foe to the pyre. And at the end she names the refusal to come: Þökk will weep dry tears for the burning; let Hel hold what she has.

Völuspá gives the same knowledge to its seeress: 'I saw for Baldr, the bleeding victim, Óðinn's child, what was fated.' The mistletoe stood slim and very fair, high-grown — and from that slender shoot came a dangerous dart of sorrow, and Höðr shot it. Baldr's death is the only event in the Edda told as prophecy before it is told as history: the gods know, and it happens anyway.

myths.title: The Oath and the Mistletoe
myths.text:
Frigg takes the foreseen answer and fights it: she travels the world and exacts an oath from all things — fire and water, iron and every metal, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds, poison, serpents — that they will not harm Baldr. Only the mistletoe, growing west of Valhǫll, seemed too young to demand the oath of. When this was done, the gods' pastime at the assembly was to stand and shoot at Baldr, hurl stones, strike him — and nothing hurt him, and all thought it a great glory.

Loki, Snorri says, could not bear it. In a woman's shape he drew from Frigg the single omission, pulled up the mistletoe, and put it in the hand of Höðr, Baldr's blind brother, who stood at the edge of the circle because he could see nothing and had no weapon. 'Do as the others do,' Loki said; 'I will show you where he stands.' Höðr threw, and the shaft went through Baldr, and he fell dead to the earth — 'the most ill-fated deed,' Snorri writes, 'done among gods and men.' The Æsir could not even take vengeance there, in the sanctuary; they could only weep, and when they found their voices, Frigg asked who would ride to Hel to ransom him.

myths.title: Hringhorni and the One Refusal
myths.text:
The Æsir carried Baldr to the sea and brought out Hringhorni, his ship, the greatest of all ships, meaning to give him a pyre at sea — and they could not move it. A giantess named Hyrrokkin was summoned from Jötunheimr, riding a wolf with vipers for reins, and she launched the ship with one shove so that fire flew from the rollers and the lands quaked. On the pyre they laid Baldr, and when Nanna, his wife, daughter of Nepr, saw him, her heart burst with grief and she was laid on the fire beside him. Óðinn laid the ring Draupnir on the pyre; Þórr hallowed it with Mjölnir, and as he did he kicked the dwarf Litr, who ran before his feet, into the flames.

Then comes the errand every Norse listener knew by heart: Hermóðr rode nine nights to Hel and begged her to let Baldr go, and Hel set the condition — if all things in the world, living and lifeless, weep for him, he shall return. Messengers went through all the world, and all things wept: men and beasts, earth and stones, trees and every metal — 'as you have surely seen these things weep when they come from frost into warmth'. Only one giantess in a cave, who called herself Þökk, Thanks, wept dry tears: 'Let Hel hold what she has.' The Æsir believed Þökk was Loki. Baldr stayed, and the gods' first grief became the first certainty of Ragnarǫk.

myths.title: Balderus and Høtherus
myths.text:
Saxo Grammaticus, writing a generation before Snorri's Edda reached its final form, tells the same death as Danish heroic history. His Balderus is a demigod, son of Odin, whose body no ordinary steel can wound; his rival is not a blind brother but a human prince, Høtherus, and they contend not in a game at the assembly but for the hand of Nanna, whom Høtherus loves and Balderus covets. The supernatural edge of the Edda survives in fragments: Høtherus wins from the wood-satyr Mimingus the sword Mimming and a bracelet; strange forest maidens give him food that steals the gods' strength; and when at last Høtherus wounds Balderus, the demigod lingers three days, dies, and is buried in a barrow. Vengeance follows the old pattern: Bous — Saxo's form of Váli — son of Odin and Rinda, is begotten for the purpose and kills Høtherus, dying himself of his wounds.

Where Snorri's Baldr is innocence murdered by malice, Saxo's is a lover destroyed by rivalry — the euhemerized reading strips the myth of its cosmic grief and keeps its skeleton: the invulnerable man, the one weapon that can harm him, the rival's hand, the begotten avenger. The two accounts are the tradition's own proof that the Baldr story was old, northern, and told in more than one key.

baldr.syncretism: The strongest cross-border witness is the Second Merseburg Charm, preserved in a tenth-century Fulda manuscript and the only pagan theogonic text in Old High German: 'Phol and Wodan rode to the wood; then Balder's foal wrenched its foot' — and Wodan charms it whole, bone to bone and blood to blood. Since Jacob Grimm, Phol has widely been read as Baldr himself, which would make the charm the one continental attestation of the god — though the identification is argued, not proven, and Simek counsels caution. The deeper syncretic debate is modern: nineteenth-century scholars, struck by the innocent god who dies and returns after the world's end, read Baldr as a northern Christ or a Frazerian dying-and-rising vegetation spirit. Current scholarship is cooler — Lindow and Orchard note that Baldr's return is scheduled strictly after Ragnarǫk, and that the myth's true company is not the Gospels but the northern complex of fratricide, failed ransom, and prophesied loss.
baldr.culturalLegacy: Baldr's afterlife is outsized precisely because his dossier is thin: the beautiful dead god became a vessel every age refills. Matthew Arnold's narrative poem 'Balder Dead' (1855) made him the Victorian emblem of vanished perfection; Frazer's 'Balder the Beautiful' volumes of The Golden Bough built a whole theory of dying gods on the mistletoe; and the Norse revival cast him as the North's own god of light. Modern Heathenry keeps him at the centre of its midsummer and funerary rites as the god of the good death and the return. The name never died in the North itself: Icelandic Baldur and Danish-Norwegian Balder remain living given names, and the daisy — baldrs brá — still carries his eyelash in the Old Norse lexicon.
baldr.extendedMeditation: Baldr is the god the Edda built out of an absence. He is given no adventure, no trial, no weapon of his own — only perfection, prophecy, and the one overlooked thing. The myth's engineering is merciless: Frigg's oath is nearly complete, and nearly is the whole story; the gods' game is nearly harmless, and the mistletoe is nearly a plant; the world's weeping is nearly unanimous. Each near-victory is a door closing. What remains is the strangest consolation in the northern corpus — not rescue, but return: after the fire and the flood of Ragnarǫk, Völuspá says, Baldr and Höðr come back together from Hel, the slain and the slayer reconciled, to a green earth. The Edda does not promise that loss can be prevented. It promises that what was best is not lost from the world for good.
baldr.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Baldr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛒᛅᛚᛏᛦ (b-a-l-t-R, the t-rune writing d and ᛦ the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: baldr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Poetic Edda: Völuspá (Baldr's death foreseen, stanzas 31–33; his return with Höðr, stanza 62), Baldrs draumar (Óðinn's waking of the völva), and Grímnismál 12 (Breiðablik)
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 22 (the best and fairest) and 49 (the oath, the mistletoe, the funeral on Hringhorni, Hermóðr's ride, Þökk's refusal); Skáldskaparmál (kennings for Baldr)
Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, Book 3 (Balderus and Høtherus), trans. Peter Fisher, ed. Hilda Ellis Davidson

baldr.archaeology: Baldr is an almost entirely textual god: no runestone invokes him, no votive deposit names him, and the place-name evidence sometimes claimed for him is insecure. The nearest material witnesses are indirect. Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa (c. 983), quoted in Skáldskaparmál, describes the funeral procession — Óðinn, Freyr, Heimdallr, the valkyries, and Hyrrokkin launching the ship — as carved on the panels of Óláfr pái's hall at Hjarðarholt in Iceland, proving the myth's currency in pre-Christian art a generation before conversion. On the continent, the Second Merseburg Charm survives in a tenth-century theological manuscript from Fulda (now Merseburg, Cathedral Library), the only Old High German text that may carry the god's name. The Codex Regius preserves Völuspá and Grímnismál; Baldrs draumar is found only in the fourteenth-century manuscript AM 748 I 4to.

pronunciation.approximation: FRAY-ya — the first syllable is the diphthong ey, close to English 'ay' in 'say' with rounded lips; stress falls on the first syllable, and the -ja sounds like English 'ya'.
pronunciation.note: Old Norse Freyja is the common noun freyja, 'lady', used as a proper name — the feminine counterpart of her brother's name Freyr, 'lord'. Both descend from Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ, and the cognate line runs through Old High German frouwa to the modern German Frau. Freyja is Tier 2 by rule: the normalized Old Norse spelling is plain Latin letters, so the ASCII form loses nothing — there is no diacritic, no thorn, no eth to restore. The temple form differs from the lowercase entry only by capitalization.

domains.title: The Lady of the Vanir
domains.subtitle: Brísingamen, Seiðr, and the Choice of the Slain
domains.lead: Freyja is the preeminent goddess of the Norse pantheon: a Vanir among the Æsir, mistress of seiðr magic, owner of the necklace Brísingamen, rider of a chariot drawn by cats, and chooser of half the slain — for she keeps a hall, Sessrúmnir in the field Fólkvangr, and divides the battle-dead with Óðinn himself.

cards.name: Brísingamen
cards.desc: The necklace of the Brísings, Freyja's great treasure — the jewel Loki steals and Heimdallr wins back, fighting for it in seal-shape.

cards.name: The Cat-Drawn Chariot
cards.desc: Freyja drives a wagon pulled by two cats — the only chariot-team of its kind in the Eddas, and the image her cult made famous.

cards.name: The Falcon Cloak
cards.desc: Her valshamr, the falcon-feather coat that lets the wearer fly between worlds — borrowed twice by Loki, and coveted by the giant Þjazi.

cards.name: Fólkvangr
cards.desc: 'The field of the host', Freyja's domain among the slain: her hall there is Sessrúmnir, 'seat-roomy', and half the battle-dead are hers.

symbols.name: Brísingamen
symbols.meaning: The necklace that is worth any price — beauty, desire, and the things a goddess will not be commanded to trade

symbols.name: The cats
symbols.meaning: Her chariot-team: the household animal elevated to divine harness, love and independence in one pair

symbols.name: The falcon-feather cloak
symbols.meaning: The garment of flight — the power to cross worlds that others must borrow from her

symbols.name: Tears of red gold
symbols.meaning: The weeping for the absent Óðr — the myth the skalds built into the kenning 'Freyja's tears' for gold

symbols.name: Hildisvíni
symbols.meaning: 'Battle-swine', the boar she rides in Hyndluljóðr — the Vanir animal of fertility under a warrior's name

mythology.lead: Freyja is everywhere in the Norse corpus: the Poetic Edda, Snorri's prose, and the opening chapters of Heimskringla all circle her — her hall among the dead, her magic, her necklace, her lost husband, and the flyting in which Loki names her last.

myths.title: Fólkvangr and the Half of the Slain
myths.text: Snorri places Freyja beside Frigg as foremost among the goddesses, and gives her what no other goddess has: a share of the battle-dead. 'Her hall is called Sessrúmnir, and it is large and fair. Whenever she rides to battle, she takes half of the slain, and half belong to Óðinn.' Her field is Fólkvangr, the folk-plain; her hall is 'seat-roomy'. The Grímnismál preserves the same division in verse — Freyja chooses the half of the slain each day, Óðinn the other — so the doctrine is older than Snorri: the Lord of the Slain does not keep them all. The Lady keeps a war-dead of her own.

myths.title: She Taught the Æsir Seiðr
myths.text: Heimskringla's euhemerized history makes Freyja the magic's transmitter: 'Freyja was a blótgyðja, a sacrificial priestess, and she was the first to teach the Æsir seiðr, which had been customary among the Vanir.' Seiðr — the far-reaching, fate-working magic that let its practitioner know the future and shape events — was Vanir craft, and it crossed into the Æsir's world through her; Ynglinga saga adds that Óðinn himself learned it and wielded it beyond anyone. Modern scholarship on seiðr, above all Neil Price's work, treats this notice as the tradition's own memory of a real ritual complex — staffs, seeresses, and performances attested in sagas and graves alike.

myths.title: The Hammer-Ransom
myths.text: When the giant Þrymr steals Mjölnir and names his price — Freyja as his bride — the gods bring her the offer. Her refusal is one of the Poetic Edda's great moments: 'Freyja was enraged, and snorted, so that the whole hall of the Æsir shook beneath her, and the great necklace of the Brísings burst: “You will know me to be most mad for a man, if I drive with you to the realm of the giants.”' No marriage happens. Instead Þórr is dressed in Freyja's bridal linen, with the necklace Brísingamen at his throat and Loki as his handmaid, and goes to Jötunheimr as the false bride — recovering the hammer under the veil. The poem's joke rests on a fixed point: Freyja cannot be given away; she can only be impersonated.

myths.title: Óttarr, Hildisvíni, and the Giantess Hyndla
myths.text: Freyja protects her devotee Óttarr, who has wagered his inheritance on his ancestry, and carries him to the giantess Hyndla to force out the genealogy he needs. She has transformed Óttarr into her boar Hildisvíni, 'battle-swine', and rides him to the giantess's cave; when Hyndla sees through the shape, Freyja answers without flinching and compels the recitation anyway, demanding the memory-ale that will let Óttarr keep the lore through his lawsuit. The poem also preserves, in its catalogue of Óðinn's gifts, the standing notice that Freyja rides to battle and takes her due of the slain — the prose doctrine of Gylfaginning in older verse.

myths.title: Óðr, the Tears of Gold, and the Many Names
myths.text: Skáldskaparmál assembles Freyja's poetic dossier. Her husband is Óðr; their daughters are Hnoss and Gersimi — 'Treasure' and 'Gem' — names so precious that what is costly is still called by them. Óðr went away on long journeys, and Freyja weeps for him, 'and her tears are red gold' — the myth behind the skaldic kenning that calls gold Freyja's tears. Snorri lists her aliases: Vanadís, 'the dís of the Vanir'; Hörn; Gefn; Sýr, 'Sow'; Mardöll — and she is called Valfreyja, 'Lady of the Slain'. The necklace appears too: gold may be called 'Brísingamen' for her, and Húsdrápa remembers that Loki and Heimdallr once fought for the jewel at Singasteinn, each in the shape of a seal.

myths.title: The Flyting
myths.text: In Loki's feast of insults, Freyja speaks against him and receives the flyting's standard charge — that she has been the lover of all in the hall, Æsir and elves alike. Njǫrðr her father answers for her: 'It is no great harm though a woman gets herself a man, a husband or a lover or both.' The exchange is the Edda's shorthand for what the whole corpus shows: Freyja's sexuality is hers, ungoverned by the marriage bargains others try to make of her — and the tradition itself, in Njǫrðr's voice, declines to call it shame.

freyja.syncretism: Freyja's most consequential kinship is internal: her relationship to Frigg. Both are chief goddesses, both own a falcon cloak, both weep for an absent husband (Óðr's name is one consonant from Óðinn's), and scholarship from the nineteenth century onward has debated whether the two were originally one goddess split by the traditions that recorded them — a question the sources leave open and handbooks like Simek and Orchard still mark as unsettled. The interpretatio latina equated her with Venus, and the Germanic week keeps the trace: Friday, dies Veneris, 'the Lady's day' — though whether the day was named for Freyja or for Frigg is itself part of the same debate. Beyond Germania there is no borrowing to claim: the Vanir package — fertility, wealth, magic, and a share of the dead — is the North's own construction, and the goddess who taught seiðr to the Æsir has no exact counterpart anywhere else.
freyja.culturalLegacy: No Norse goddess has a longer afterlife. Wagner fused Freyja with Iðunn into Freia, the goddess of youth whose ransom opens the Ring cycle, and the Victorian mythographies made her the Venus of the North. In the twentieth century she became central to modern Heathenry and Ásatrú, where she is honored as mistress of seiðr and patron of the half of the slain — and to the revival of seiðr practice that scholars and practitioners alike trace to her teaching in Ynglinga saga. Her name never died in Scandinavia: Freyja is a living, and increasingly popular, girls' given name in Iceland and across the North. And the week still speaks her cognate every Friday — the Lady's day, whichever goddess the chronology finally credits.
freyja.extendedMeditation: Freyja holds two things the world keeps trying to separate. She is the goddess of love — desire, gold, the necklace, the weeping for Óðr — and she is a commander of the dead, choosing half the slain before Óðinn takes his half. The Edda refuses the split: the same figure who weeps tears of red gold rides to battle; the same name that means 'lady' heads a war-dead of her own. The restoration Freyja needs no diacritics to make the point — the word itself is the argument. In Old Norse, to say 'the lady' was to say her name. The title and the goddess are one word, and the one word is enough.

sources.name: Poetic Edda (Grímnismál, Þrymskviða, Hyndluljóðr, Lokasenna)

freyja.archaeology: Freyja's attestations are textual — the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda and the Prose Edda's codices (13th-14th c.), with skaldic verse centuries older — but her world has a material record. The theophoric place-names of Sweden and Norway are dense with the Frö-/Frøy- element, though most are assigned to her brother Freyr; a smaller set (Norway's Frøya island among them) is argued either way. The seiðr she taught the Æsir is the best-attested ritual complex in the graves: the 'völva burials' of Viking-Age Scandinavia, with their iron staffs, high-status grave goods, and in some cases mind-altering seeds, are the material context Neil Price's The Viking Way reads as the practice's archaeology. Small silver pendants of standing female figures, once loosely called valkyries, have been reinterpreted in the same frame — the tradition's seeress and its Lady overlap in the metal as they do in the verse.
freyja.originalScriptNote: Old Norse literature was transmitted in medieval Icelandic manuscripts written in the Latin alphabet; the earlier epigraphic medium was the Younger Futhark. The theonym Freyja is known from the manuscript tradition; a hypothetical runic rendering would approximate ᚠᚱᛅᚢᛁᛅ (f-r-au-i-a). Unusually among the restorations, the normalized Old Norse form needs nothing ASCII lacks: Freyja is already the attested spelling, letter for letter — a Tier-2 name whose restoration is complete in plain Latin. The plain-ASCII domain freyja.com is held outside the PuniCodex collection by a third party; the project watches it for release and keeps this temple canonical under the /sites/freyja/ path in the meantime.

Short mid back [o], as in English 'lot'; the Old Norse vowel is short, never the diphthong of English 'low'
Unaspirated velar stop [k] followed by short close front [i]; a light second syllable closed by the vowel, not a consonant

pronunciation.approximation: 'LOH-kee' — two even syllables with the weight on the first; keep the o short and round, and let the second syllable fall away lightly.

pronunciation.note: Loki is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse spelling is Loki, with a short o and no distinctive letter, so the plain ASCII form loses nothing — the restoration and the ASCII form are the same word. The etymology is genuinely uncertain: the most discussed derivation connects the name with the *luk- family — Old Norse lok 'cover, lid, lock', lúka 'to close, end' — whence 'knot', 'lock', or 'the one who closes', a reading that would suit his role at Ragnarök; the nineteenth-century equation with Logi, 'flame', is now abandoned. Attestation and lexicography follow Cleasby & Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary (1874), s.v. Loki; Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (1910), s.v. loki; and de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch (1962), s.v. Loki.

domains.title: Trickery, Chaos, Shape-shifter
domains.subtitle: The domain of Loki
domains.lead: In the Norse tradition, Loki is the trickster of the Æsir — counted among the gods through an oath of blood-brotherhood with Óðinn, yet son of the giant Fárbauti, and the moving cause of their deepest grief. Skáldskaparmál teaches poets to call him the “slanderer of the gods”: the one who cuts Sif’s hair, bargains his own head against dwarfish craft, and finds the loophole in every oath sworn in Ásgarðr.

cards.name: The Flyting at Ægir's Hall
cards.desc: Uninvited, Loki forces his way into the gods' feast and insults every god and goddess in turn, until only Þórr's hammer ends the night.

cards.name: The Mistletoe
cards.desc: The one thing that never swore Frigg's oath; Loki finds it, shapes it, and guides the blind Hǫðr's hand — and Baldr falls.

cards.name: The Wager of the Head
cards.desc: Loki stakes his own head that the dwarf Brokkr's brother cannot out-craft the sons of Ívaldi; he loses, keeps his head on a technicality, and pays with sewn lips.

cards.name: The Bound God
cards.desc: Bound with his own son's entrails beneath a dripping serpent, with Sigyn catching the venom in a bowl — and the world shakes when she turns to empty it.

symbols.name: The sewn lips
symbols.meaning: Brokkr's needle, the price of the lost wager — the trickster's own weapon, speech, bound shut

symbols.name: The mistletoe dart
symbols.meaning: The small, overlooked thing that kills the best of the gods; the loophole made into a weapon

symbols.name: The net of Franangr
symbols.meaning: The first net, which Loki himself devised — and in which the gods catch him when he flees as a salmon

symbols.name: The serpent and the bowl
symbols.meaning: Skadi's venom-dripping snake fixed above his face, and Sigyn's bowl that stands between him and agony

symbols.name: The mare's shape
symbols.meaning: The form he took to lure Svaðilfari from the wall-builder; from that union he bore Sleipnir, Óðinn's eight-legged horse

mythology.lead: Loki stands at the centre of more Eddic narrative than any figure save Þórr and Óðinn — and almost every road through the mythology crosses him at least once. The same wit that recovers Mjǫllnir in Þrymskviða engineers the death of Baldr; the Eddas hold both truths without reconciling them. By the giantess Angrboða he fathers Fenrir, Jǫrmungandr, and Hel; by his wife Sigyn, Nari and Váli, whose fates are spent in his own binding.

myths.title: The Blood-Brother
myths.text:
Deep in the flyting, when Óðinn moves to silence him, Loki invokes the oldest bond in the mythology: 'Do you remember, Óðinn, how in days of old we two blended our blood together? You said you would never taste ale unless it were brought to us both.' The blood-brotherhood oath — attested in the heroic lays as the rite that makes two men one — is the single fact that explains Loki's place among the Æsir: he is not one of them by birth, being the son of the giant Fárbauti, but he cannot be refused a seat while Óðinn's oath stands.

The poem's whole tragedy hangs on that stanza. Every insult Loki hurls is spoken from inside the oath's protection, and every crime he is accused of is a crime against the brothers of his blood. When the Æsir finally bind him, they are not punishing an enemy at the gate but a kinsman at the table — which is why the punishment is not death but endlessness.

myths.title: The Flyting at Ægir's Hall
myths.text:
Ægir the sea-giant brews ale for the gods, and Loki, uninvited, kills Ægir's servant Fimafeng out of sheer irritation at hearing him praised. Driven into the forest, he returns and forces his way back to the bench on the strength of the blood-oath — then works down the hall in order: Bragi, Iðunn, Gefjon, Óðinn, Frigg, Freyja, Njǫrðr, Týr, Freyr, Byggvir, Heimdallr, Skadi, Sif. To each he gives the one wound that will not close: cowardice, secret loves, sold favors, unacknowledged children. No one answers him in kind and wins; the flyting only ends when Þórr strides in from the east and three times vows to strike Loki's head from his shoulders with Mjǫllnir.

The prose epilogue tells what the poetry implies: this is the night the fellowship breaks. Loki flees to the falls of Franangr, and the Æsir's patience, which has survived the theft of Iðunn and the loss of Sif's hair, does not survive the flyting. The Lokasenna is the mythology's hinge — everything before it is mischief, everything after it is the binding and the end.

myths.title: The Bridesmaid
myths.text:
When Þórr wakes to find Mjǫllnir stolen and the giant Þrymr demands Freyja as the price, it is Loki who borrows Freyja's feather-coat and flies to Jǫtunheimr to learn the terms — and Loki who rides beside the disguised thunder-god as his 'maidservant'. At the wedding feast, when the bride devours a whole ox, eight salmon, and three vats of mead, it is Loki's ready tongue that saves the disguise: 'Freyja has eaten nothing for eight nights, so eager was she for Jǫtunheimr.' When Þrymr lifts the veil and flinches from the burning eyes, Loki answers again: 'She has not slept for eight nights, so eager was she.'

The poem shows the companion Loki, the one the gods cannot do without: Þórr supplies the hammer, but the expedition runs on Loki's wits. The Þrymskviða is the strongest evidence that the flyting's hatred was not the whole tradition — the same figure who ends as the Æsir's executioner begins as their most useful passenger.

myths.title: The Wager of the Head
myths.text:
For mischief — 'for love of mischief', Snorri says — Loki cuts off all of Sif's hair. Þórr seizes him and would break every bone in his body, and Loki buys himself free by swearing to get the black-elves to make Sif hair of gold that will grow like other hair. From the sons of Ívaldi come the golden hair, the ship Skíðblaðnir for Freyr, and the spear Gungnir for Óðinn. Then Loki wagers his own head with the dwarf Brokkr that Brokkr's brother Eitri cannot forge three treasures as good.

In the smithy Loki turns himself into a fly and stings Brokkr at the bellows — on the hand, on the neck, at last between the eyes — but the work holds: the boar Gullinbursti for Freyr, the ring Draupnir for Óðinn, and for Þórr the hammer Mjǫllnir, its handle short from the fly's sting yet judged the best of all, the defense of the gods. Loki has lost his head. He concedes the wager — and then observes that the head was Brokkr's but the neck was never in the bargain. The dwarfs, denied the cutting, sew his lips together instead; and when he tears the thong out, the scars remain. Nearly every wonder-weapon of the mythology exists because Loki cheated a craftsman.

myths.title: The Death of Baldr
myths.text:
When Baldr is plagued by dreams of his own death, Frigg takes oaths from all things — fire and water, iron and every metal, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds, poison, serpents — that they will not harm him. Only one shoot was passed over: the mistletoe, which grows west of Valhǫll and seemed too young to swear. Loki, in the shape of a woman, draws the omission out of Frigg; he pulls up the mistletoe, carries it to the assembly where the Æsir amuse themselves by hurling weapons at the invulnerable Baldr, and puts it in the hand of the blind god Hǫðr, offering to guide his aim. The dart goes through Baldr, 'and he fell dead to the earth' — the greatest misfortune ever worked among gods and men.

The aftermath binds the story to Loki twice over. Hermóðr rides to Hel and wins the condition that all things must weep Baldr back; all things weep, except the cave-giantess who calls herself Þǫkk and weeps dry tears: 'let Hel hold what she has.' 'And this,' Snorri says, 'people believe was Loki Laufeyjarson, who has worked most evil among the Æsir.' The loophole he found in the oath is closed forever by his own refusal.

myths.title: The Binding
myths.text:
After the flyting Loki hides on the mountain of Franangr in a house with four doors, and by day takes salmon-shape in the falls below. Brooding on how the Æsir might take him, he devises the net — the first ever made — and burns it as Óðinn, watching from Hliðskjálf, spies out his refuge; the gods understand the ash-pattern, fashion the same net, and drag the falls until Kvasir catches the salmon in mid-leap. The Æsir then turn Loki's own blood against him: his son Váli is changed into a wolf and tears apart his brother Nari — called Narfi in the Lokasenna prose — and with Nari's entrails they bind Loki across three sharp stones. Skadi fastens a venomous serpent above his face.

There Sigyn, his wife, stations herself with a bowl and catches the venom as it drips. But when the bowl is full she must turn to empty it, and in that interval the drops fall on Loki's face; he writhes so hard that the whole earth shudders — 'and those are now called earthquakes.' So he lies, Snorri says, until Ragnarök. The Vǫluspá's sibyl saw the same scene generations before Snorri wrote it: 'There sits Sigyn, not at all glad over her husband.'

myths.title: The Steersman of Naglfar
myths.text:
At Ragnarök the bonds give way. The ship Naglfar — built, Snorri warns, from the nails of the dead, which is why the prudent trim the nails of their corpses — breaks loose on the swelling sea, and Loki himself stands at the steering-oar, bringing the powers of Hel and the hosts of Muspell against the gods. The wolf Fenrir advances with jaws gaping from earth to heaven; Jǫrmungandr blows venom across sea and sky. The kin Loki fathered on Angrboða come home for the reckoning.

In the last melee on the field of Vígríðr, Loki meets Heimdallr — the watchman he once mocked in Ægir's hall, the god who once wrestled him for Freyja's necklace — and the two kill each other. The trickster's career ends not in triumph or pardon but in mutual slaying with the most vigilant of the Æsir: the loophole-closer and the watchman, evenly matched at the world's end. The Vǫluspá gives him his due in a single kenning: 'the kinsman of Býleistr' steers the ship from the east.

loki.syncretism: The oldest comparative frame for Loki is the Greek Promētheús: a benefactor-trickster chained to a rock as punishment, torn daily and writhing — the parallel between the eagle and the dripping serpent was drawn as early as the Romantic mythographers, and Rooth's Loki in Scandinavian Mythology (1961) remains the standard monograph weighing such connections. The comparison illuminates the punishment but not the god: Promētheús suffers for helping mankind, Loki for destroying his own fellowship. The nineteenth century tried to dissolve Loki into a fire-god on the strength of his name's resemblance to Logi, 'flame' — the equation survived in Wagner's Loge — but modern philology rejects it: the o of Loki is short, the two figures are distinct in the texts themselves, and Logi appears in Gylfaginning as the personified wildfire who out-eats Loki at Útgarðr. That episode requires its own honest distinction: Útgarða-Loki, the cunning giant-king whose illusions humiliate Þórr on the eastern journey, is a different being from Loki Laufeyjarson — Snorri never confuses them, and scholarship since de Vries has treated the shared name as a genuine onomastic coincidence, however suggestive the parallel mastery of deception. Within the corpus Loki's clearest double is his byname Loptr, 'the airy one', under which the skalds name him when the poets need him in the sky.
loki.culturalLegacy: Loki has the largest afterlife of any Norse figure after Þórr and Óðinn, and it forked early. The folk record kept a kinder god: the Faroese ballad Lokka táttur makes Lokki the clever helper who, with Óðinn and Þórr, saves a farmer's son from a giant — proof that a benevolent trickster-Loki survived in oral tradition long after the Eddic damnation. Learned Europe first remade him as fire: Wagner's Loge in the Ring cycle, the cynical flame who talks the gods into their bargains, is the nineteenth century's conflation of Loki with Logi rendered as opera. The twentieth century gave him back his malice and his charm at once — Neil Gaiman's 'Low Key Lyesmith' in American Gods hides the bound god in a prison cell — and the twenty-first made him a global franchise: Marvel's Loki, Thor's adopted brother and rival, has carried the name further than the Eddas ever traveled, at the price of thinning the mythology to a family quarrel. Modern heathenry remains honestly divided: many Ásatrú kindreds refuse to hail Loki at blót, reading him as the oath-breaker the Eddas describe, while others honor him as the necessary disturber without whom nothing in Ásgarðr ever changes. The deepest survival is idiomatic: in the Scandinavian languages his name still clings to the trembling air over hot ground and to the spider that ties knots — small, unsettled things that refuse to hold still.
loki.extendedMeditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Loki compresses the most uncomfortable truth the North knew: that the thing which unbinds and the thing which binds are the same. If the uncertain etymology is right — the *luk- root, the knot, the lock, the closing — then his name is his whole story in two syllables: the mind that finds the loophole in every oath, and the god who ends tied in a knot of his own son's entrails while the world shakes with his writhing. The Eddas never resolve him into villain or benefactor, because the tradition's real subject is not morality but contingency: every wonder-weapon the gods own came through his cheating, and so did their death-wound. Unicode restoration has nothing to recover here — the name was never flattened; it arrived whole, which is its own kind of trick — and that too is worth saying plainly: Loki is Tier 2 not because he is lesser, but because this is one name the scribes and the ASCII machines spell exactly alike.

loki.archaeology: One carved stone is the entire candidate corpus for Loki's image: the Snaptun stone (Denmark, c. 1000), a hearth-stone or bellows-shield bearing a bearded face with scarred, sewn-shut lips, commonly identified as Loki from the Brokkr episode — an identification widely repeated but unprovable, since the stone carries no inscription. The Kirkby Stephen stone in Cumbria, showing a bound horned figure, has likewise been read as the bound Loki, though scholars also read it as a bound devil of Christian iconography. His attestation is otherwise textual: the Poetic Edda poems survive chiefly in the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270) and the Hauksbók; Snorri's account is transmitted by the principal Snorra Edda manuscripts (GKS 2367 4to, Codex Wormianus, Codex Upsaliensis). No runic inscription names the god, and no Scandinavian place-name is securely his — a silence that matches his ambiguous cultic standing: the one major god for whom no temple, toponym, or votive deposit is known.
loki.originalScriptNote: The Old Norse form is Loki, attested throughout the manuscript tradition of both Eddas, with a short o and no diacritic; the normalized spelling and the ASCII spelling are identical. In the earlier epigraphic medium, the Younger Futhark, the name would be rendered approximately ᛚᚢᚴᛁ (l-u-k-i) — the Younger Futhark's ᚢ covering the short o among its several vowels — but no runic inscription preserves the theonym itself, so the manuscript form remains the primary witness. Because the restoration preserves no distinctive feature the ASCII form loses, Loki is a Tier-2 name: the plain-ASCII loki.com is the philologically complete form — and it is registered to a third party, held outside the PuniCodex collection, and watched for release. The temple is served at /sites/loki/ in the meantime; no owned domain is claimed for this entry.

phonemes.desc: Voiceless labiodental [f] and trilled [r]; Old Norse keeps the cluster firm at the head of the word, with stress on this single syllable.

Long voiced velar stop [ɡː], the true geminate: the consonant is held and released, as in modern Icelandic Frigg. The old nominative ending has been swallowed into this double-g.

domains.lead: Frigg is the foremost of the ásynjur: daughter of Fjörgynn, wife of Óðinn, mother of Baldr. Her hall is Fensalir, the fen-halls, where she wept for her slain son; her gift is the heaviest in the Edda — she knows all fate, and says none of it.

mythology.lead: Frigg is the foremost of the ásynjur: daughter of Fjörgynn, wife of Óðinn, mother of Baldr. Her hall is Fensalir, the fen-halls, where she wept for her slain son; her gift is the heaviest in the Edda — she knows all fate, and says none of it. Around those two facts, the almost-complete oath and the kept silence, the tradition builds its portrait of the queen who governs the household of the gods.

myths.title: The Oath of All Things
myths.text: When Baldr dreams baleful dreams for his life, Frigg does the one thing foresight permits: she fights the future with an oath. She travels the world and exacts from all things — fire and water, iron and every metal, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds, poison, serpents — the promise that they will not harm Baldr. Only the mistletoe, growing west of Valhöll, seemed too young to demand the oath of. The completeness of the list is the point: Snorri enumerates creation itself, and the myth hangs its whole catastrophe on the one category a mother's thoroughness could not imagine mattering — a plant too young to swear. The oath worked exactly as designed: blades and brands turned aside, and the gods made a sport of hurling weapons at Baldr as he stood laughing and unhurt — the very sport that would give Loki his opening. Frigg's foresight is never faulted in the sources; the myth faults the world for containing even one thing too small to swear.

myths.title: The Tears in Fensalir
myths.text: Loki, in a woman's shape, comes to Fensalir and draws the single omission out of Frigg herself — she tells the stranger that nothing east or west of Valhöll was left unsworn except one young shoot. When the throw falls and Baldr lies dead, it is Frigg who finds the first voice in the silent hall and asks who among the Æsir will ride to Hel and offer ransom — the grief-struck mother still doing strategy. Völuspá gives her the briefest and heaviest line in the poem: 'Then Frigg wept in Fensalir over Valhöll's woe.' And when Hermóðr rides back from the dead, he carries a gift addressed to her: from Nanna, her son's wife who died of grief on the pyre, a linen robe — one bereaved woman remembering another, out of Hel itself.

myths.title: She Knows All Fate, and Says It Not
myths.text: The Poetic Edda's flyting gives Frigg her doctrine. When Loki turns his slander on the queen — taunting her with the allegation that she has taken both of Óðinn's brothers to her bed, the poem's malice contradicted by nothing else in the tradition — Óðinn answers for her, calling Loki a fool and mad; the queen herself does not deign to reply. Then Freyja speaks the line that defines her: 'Frigg knows, I think, all fate, though she does not speak it.' Snorri repeats the same fact as plain prose in Gylfaginning: she knows the fates of men, though she prophesies nothing. In a pantheon where Óðinn hangs nine nights on the tree for knowledge and buys the runes' wisdom with an eye, his wife simply has it — and her power is exactly her refusal to spend it.

myths.title: The Foster-Mother's Wager
myths.text: The prose frame of Grímnismál shows Frigg playing and winning the household's long game. Óðinn and Frigg foster two shipwrecked princes, Agnarr and Geirröðr; Óðinn backs Agnarr, Frigg backs Geirröðr, and Geirröðr takes the throne. When Óðinn boasts of his foster-son's hospitality, Frigg calls it false — Geirröðr starves his guests — and the wager is laid. She then sends Fulla to warn the king that a dangerous wizard is coming, easily known because no dog will leap at him. Óðinn arrives, is seized, and hangs tortured between two fires for eight nights — outmaneuvered by his own wife, until Geirröðr's young son brings him the horn and the whole poem of Grimnir's sayings pours out. It is the one myth where the queen moves the plot against the Allfather, and she wins the move.

myths.title: Frea and the Naming of the Longbeards
myths.text: The goddess's clearest continental appearance is Latin and eighth-century. Paul the Deacon tells how the Winnili, few and threatened by the Vandals, were claimed by Godan (Óðinn) for his enemies' demand of tribute. Frea, Godan's wife — the Langobardic form of Frigg — counselled them: at sunrise the Winnili women were to let down their hair around their faces like beards and stand with their husbands. At dawn Frea turned Godan's bed toward the east and woke him; he looked out, saw the bearded women, and asked, 'Who are these longbeards?' And Frea answered: you have given them a name — now give them the victory. Godan granted both, and the Winnili became the Langobardi. The tale is an origin-legend, but it is also proof that the migration-age mainland knew a goddess Frea at Godan's side, counsellor and kingmaker, centuries before the Icelandic Eddas wrote her as Frigg.

frigg.syncretism: The Roman interpretatio fixed Frigg's identity for all posterity through the calendar: when the Germanic peoples translated the seven-day week, dies Veneris — Venus's day — became Frigg's day, Old English Frīgedæg, Old Norse frjádagr, whence Friday. The equation is Venus-as-consort: the wife of the chief god takes the day of the goddess of love. Greek comparison runs to Hera, the queen and goddess of marriage, but the structural fit is imperfect — Frigg keeps a seeress's knowledge Hera never claims. The deepest syncretic debate is internal: since Grimm, scholars have asked whether Frigg and Freyja were originally one goddess — both ride falcon-cloaks, both are sought by giants, both weep for absent mates — and the handbooks (Simek, Orchard, Lindow) still print the question open. Her one firm continental witness is Langobardic Frea in Paul the Deacon; Saxo, euhemerizing, gives a Frigga who strips gold from Óðinn's statue and disgraces herself — a scandal-story that belongs to Saxo's literary workshop, not to cult.
frigg.culturalLegacy: Frigg's most durable legacy is the fifth weekday: Friday carries her name in every Germanic language, the Germanic answer to the day of Venus. The Victorian revival made her the weeping mother of the North — Matthew Arnold's 'Balder Dead' gives her long grieving speeches the Eddas only imply — and the same century's folklore collectors recorded 'Frigga's distaff' (Friggerock) as the folk name of Orion's belt, from which the romantic image of the cloud-weaving queen descends; the Eddas themselves never give her a loom. Wagner recast her as Fricka, the severe guardian of marriage in the Ring, the operatic portrait most moderns know first. Modern Heathenry honors her as the goddess of hearth, household, and the keeper of frith, and modern fantasy keeps her at Óðinn's side. Her name never needed restoring — it never left the week.
frigg.extendedMeditation: Frigg is the patron of the knowledge that cannot be used. She knows all fate and speaks none of it — not from coldness, but because the Edda understands what foresight costs: she sees the mistletoe coming and still must live the days before it falls. Her one permitted weapon is thoroughness, and she wields it to the limit of the world — fire, water, iron, stone, sickness, serpent, all sworn — and the future enters through the single twig too young to swear. What the tradition leaves her is not failure but a harder thing: the discipline of the one who knows. Every keeper of unwelcome certainty — the parent who sees, the friend who cannot say, the expert whose warning would only spread the panic — works in Fensalir, keeping counsel with a knowledge that has nowhere to go.
frigg.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Frigg — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚠᚱᛁᚴ (f-r-i-k, the k-rune writing the geminate gg, into which the old nominative ending has been assimilated). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: frigg.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

frigg.archaeology: Frigg is an essentially textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and the place-name evidence sometimes claimed for her in Sweden and Denmark is contested by the place-name scholars. Her material footprint is calendrical and linguistic — the weekday itself: the substitution of Frigg for Venus in the Germanic translation of the seven-day week (Old English Frīgedæg, Old Norse frjádagr) is the fossil of the interpretatio romana, preserved in every modern Germanic language. The narrative witnesses are the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda and the Codex Regius and Uppsala manuscripts of Snorri's Edda; her continental attestation, Paul the Deacon's Historia Langobardorum, survives in a rich manuscript tradition descending from the eighth-century original. Scandinavian folk astronomy, recorded by nineteenth-century collectors and noted by Grimm, kept the name Friggerock — 'Frigga's distaff' — for the three stars of Orion's belt, the nearest thing to a living material tradition attached to her.

domains.title: Primordial Giant, Chaos
domains.subtitle: The First Being and the Matter of the World
domains.lead: Ymir is the first living thing in the Norse cosmos — the frost-giant who condensed out of the dripping rime where the heat of Múspell met the ice of Niflheimr in the yawning void of Ginnungagap. He is the ancestor of every jotunn, the cow Auðhumla's nursling, and finally the raw material of creation itself: Óðinn, Vili, and Vé kill him, and from his body build the world — flesh to earth, blood to sea, bones to mountains, skull to sky.

cards.name: Ginnungagap
cards.desc: The yawning void before creation — the charged emptiness between the ice-world of Niflheimr and the fire-world of Múspell where Ymir first took shape.

cards.name: Auðhumla
cards.desc: The primeval cow whose four rivers of milk fed Ymir, and who licked the salty rime-stones until Búri, grandfather of the gods, emerged from the ice.

cards.name: The Dismemberment
cards.desc: Slain by Óðinn, Vili, and Vé, Ymir becomes the world: flesh earth, blood sea, bones mountains, hair trees, skull sky, brains the clouds.

cards.name: Bergelmir's Flood
cards.desc: So much blood poured from Ymir's wound that the whole race of frost-giants drowned — all but Bergelmir and his wife, who rode out the deluge on their lúðr.

symbols.name: Ginnungagap
symbols.meaning: The yawning void at the world's beginning — the unmade space where fire and ice first traded breath

symbols.name: Auðhumla
symbols.meaning: The cow who feeds the giant and frees the gods — plenty and creation flowing from the same rime

symbols.name: The dismembered body
symbols.meaning: The map of the world written in one corpse: every landscape a part of Ymir, the cosmos as anatomy

symbols.name: The blood-flood
symbols.meaning: The deluge from Ymir's wound that drowns the frost-giants — destruction and sea-making in a single act

symbols.name: The four sky-dwarfs
symbols.meaning: Norðri, Suðri, Austri, and Vestri, set by the gods to hold Ymir's skull up at the four corners of heaven

mythology.lead: Ymir has no adventures and no cult: his mythology is cosmogony entire. He exists to be first — first life, first giant, first death — and the corpus treats him less as a character than as a fact of physics: the being out of whom everything had to be made, because before him there was nothing to make it from.

myths.title: Out of the Rime
myths.text:
Before the world there was Ginnungagap, the yawning void, with the frozen rivers of Niflheimr to the north and the sparks of Múspell to the south. Where the heat met the rime, Snorri says, the hoar-frost melted and dripped, and the drops quickened into the shape of a man: Ymir, whom the frost-giants call Aurgelmir. Vafþrúðnismál gives the older verse version — from Élivágar's waves shot poison-drops that froze and grew, until a jotunn arose from them.

He was no god and no friend to gods: Snorri calls him and all his line evil. Yet everything that follows in the cosmos presupposes him — the first living being is the first material, and creation in the Norse telling is not ex nihilo but a reworking of what already is.

myths.title: The Self-Begetting Giant
myths.text:
The scene is the wisdom contest of Vafþrúðnismál: Óðinn, disguised as Gagnráðr, stakes his head on questions the giant Vafþrúðnir cannot answer, and one of them is this — how did Ymir beget children when he knew no giantess? The giant answers with the strangest genealogy in the corpus: from under the primeval giant's arm grew a man and a woman together, and one of his legs begot a six-headed son on the other. The jotnar multiply from the giant's own body — parthenogenesis in sweat and limb, male and female folded into one hermaphroditic mass. Snorri repeats the detail in Gylfaginning 6, and the two versions agree on the essentials.

This is why Ymir is the ancestor of all giants: not through a wife but through himself. Hyndluljóð states the doctrine flatly — all the giants descend from Ymir. The jotnar are not a rival tribe to the gods; they are the older generation of the same world-substance, and the self-begetting giant who needs no partner is the myth's image of a cosmos that has not yet learned to divide.

myths.title: Auðhumla and Búri
myths.text:
Ymir did not starve. From the same dripping rime came the cow Auðhumla, and four rivers of milk ran from her udder to feed him. She herself licked the salty rime-stones, and as she licked, a man's shape emerged from the ice — hair the first day, head the second, the whole man the third: Búri, strong and fair, who begot Borr, and Borr married Bestla the giant's daughter, and their sons were Óðinn, Vili, and Vé.

The detail is the myth's quiet hinge: gods and giants rise from the same frost within days of one another, and the gods' grandmother is herself a giantess. Snorri's genealogy makes the coming killing not a war on strangers but the oldest kind of violence — the young order turning on the body of the old.

myths.title: The Making of the World
myths.text:
Óðinn, Vili, and Vé kill Ymir, and from his body they make the world. Grímnismál gives the catalogue in verse: from Ymir's flesh the earth was shaped, from his blood the sea, from his bones the mountains, from his hair the trees, and from his skull the sky; from his eyelashes the gods made Miðgarðr as a defence against the giants, and from his brains the heavy, wind-driven clouds. Snorri adds the maggots in the flesh, made rational by the gods' decree as the dwarfs, and the four dwarfs — Norðri, Suðri, Austri, Vestri — set to hold up the skull-vault of heaven at its corners.

So much blood ran from the wound that it became a deluge, and the whole race of frost-giants drowned in it — all but one. Bergelmir, Ymir's heir in the verse line, rode out the flood with his wife on his lúðr, and from them the jotnar were born again. Creation's first act is a killing, and its first catastrophe follows immediately: the world is made, and nearly unmade of giants, in a single stroke.

myths.title: 'In Early Days, When Ymir Dwelled'
myths.text:
The völva of Völuspá opens her memory with him: 'It was in early days, when Ymir dwelled; there was no sand nor sea nor cool waves, no earth existed, nor heaven above, a yawning void there was, and grass nowhere.' The giant is the poem's first named being — the datum from which the seeress's whole vision of time unfolds.

Then Burr's sons lift up the earth, and the ordering begins. Völuspá never stages the killing; it simply places Ymir on the far side of a before and an after. That placement is his function everywhere in the corpus: he is the name Norse tradition gives to the raw, unworked world — and the proof that even the raw world had a body.

ymir.syncretism: Ymir stands at the centre of the best-known comparative debate in Germanic mythology: the Indo-European dismemberment cosmogony. The Sanskrit parallel is exact in structure — Rigveda 10.90, the Puruṣasūkta, makes the world from the sacrifice of the primeval man Puruṣa, whose breath became wind, head sky, feet earth — and scholars from the nineteenth century onward have read Ymir as the Norse reflex of the same inherited pattern, most fully in Bruce Lincoln's studies of Indo-European creation myth. The name itself is contested: the strong philological line derives Ymir from the Old Norse verb ymja, 'to scream, roar, resound' — the Roarer — while the alternative connects it to Indo-European *yemo-, 'twin' (Sanskrit Yama, Latin geminus), which would make the hermaphroditic, self-begetting giant the 'Twin'. Simek, de Vries, and Lindow all register the dispute without settling it; this temple records both. Tacitus supplies the Germanic corroboration — Germania chapter 2 has the peoples of Germania sing of Tuisto, 'a god born of the earth', whose name is regularly read as 'twin, two-fold' — as the ancestor of Mannus and all the tribes.
ymir.culturalLegacy: Ymir's afterlife runs wherever Norse myth is retold at scale. Richard Wagner's ring cycle built its world-music on the same dismembered-primordial logic, and the giant survives under his own name across modern popular culture: Robert E. Howard's 'The Frost-Giant's Daughter' (1934) makes its heroine the daughter of Ymir, Marvel Comics has kept Ymir the frost giant in print since 1962 as an antagonist of Thor, and the name recurs across fantasy games from Dungeons & Dragons onward wherever frost-giants are wanted. In scholarship the figure anchors the comparative project — Lincoln's Myth, Cosmos, and Society built its account of Indo-European creation ideology around the Ymir material. Modern Heathenry reads him as the necessary first matter of the cosmos: not a villain to be erased but the body the world is still made of.
ymir.extendedMeditation: Every cosmogony answers the question of what the world is made from; the Norse answer is a body. Before there was matter there was already a being — and so creation is never innocent. The ground is flesh, the weather is a giant's breath, the mountains are bones that once walked. The myth refuses the comfort of an empty beginning: someone had to die for there to be anywhere at all. Yet the Edda does not linger on the killing's guilt; it lingers on the fitting. Flesh to earth, blood to sea, skull to sky — the world is a translation, part for part, of the first body into the lasting one. To live in Miðgarðr, in this telling, is to live inside Ymir: behind a wall of his eyelashes, under a vault of his skull, walking his flesh. The old name for that intimacy is one the modern world is relearning — that the environment is not around us but is what we are made of.

ymir.archaeology: Ymir is an entirely textual being: no runestone invokes him, no votive deposit names him, and no image can be securely identified with him — a silence that fits a cosmogonic abstraction rather than a cult figure. His attestation is the manuscript record. Vafþrúðnismál and Grímnismál survive in the thirteenth-century Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to); Völuspá is preserved both there and in the fourteenth-century Hauksbók; Snorri's creation account rests on the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda and related codices. Skaldic verse keeps the giant alive in kennings — the þulur catalogued in Skáldskaparmál list Aurgelmir, Brimir, and Bláinn among the giant-names — proving the cosmogony's currency in the working vocabulary of pre-Christian and early Christian poets. The comparative witnesses are themselves texts: Rigveda 10.90 and Tacitus' Germania, copied and recopied in Sanskrit and Latin manuscript traditions far from the North.

pronunciation.approximation: FRAY-ur — the ey is a single falling diphthong (between the 'ay' of 'day' and the 'oy' of 'boy'), and the final -r is the nominative ending, lightly syllabic as in modern Icelandic Freyr.
pronunciation.note: Old Norse Freyr descends from Proto-Germanic *frawjaz 'lord' — the same word as Gothic frauja and Old English frēa — and is the masculine counterpart of Freyja, from *frawjōn 'lady'. The ey is the Old Norse diphthong born from an earlier au, which is why a normalized Viking-Age carving reads ᚠᚱᛅᚢᛦ, frauR: the runes keep the older shape of the word. The normalized Old Norse form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no thorn or eth — so the name is Tier-2 by the mechanical rule: nothing distinctive is lost in transit, a statement about orthography, never about the god.

domains.title: The Lord (from *frawjaz) of the Peace-Years
domains.subtitle: Fertility, Sunshine, Rain
domains.lead: Freyr is the Vanir god the Æsir received in the hostage-exchange and never gave back: son of Njǫrðr, brother of Freyja, lord of Álfheimr, the ruler of rain and sunshine and the fruit of the earth — the god Snorri says it is good to call on for harvest and peace, and who governs the wealth of men.
