pronunciation.note: Cernunnos is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the attested Gaulish form is already plain Latin letters — ERNVNNOS in the capitals of the Paris inscription — with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for ASCII to lose. The restoration differs from the lowercase entry only by the capital. The etymology 'the horned one' is the standard reading (Delamarre, Matasović), though the details of the suffix formation remain debated and the connection with Conall Cernach is conjecture, not consensus.

domains.title: Wilderness, Animals, Fertility
domains.subtitle: The Antlered Lord Between the Wild and the Otherworld
domains.lead: Cernunnos is the horned god of Gaul: named once in stone at Paris, pictured across the Celtic world as the cross-legged, antlered lord who holds the torc of rank in one hand and the ram-horned serpent of the underworld in the other, with the beasts of the wild gathered at his back.

cards.name: The Antlers
cards.desc: The stag's crown the single inscription illustrates: the name means 'the horned one', and the Paris stone shows exactly that.

cards.name: The Torc
cards.desc: The gold neck-ring of rank — held in the god's hand on the Gundestrup plate, hung from the antlers on the Paris pillar.

cards.name: The Ram-Horned Serpent
cards.desc: The hybrid creature of Gaulish art — serpent's body, ram's horns — coiled in the god's left hand on the cauldron plate.

cards.name: The Cross-Legged Seat
cards.desc: The seated posture of the Gundestrup figure, echoed at Reims and Saintes: the stillness of the lord of animals.

symbols.name: The antlers
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty over the wild, written into the name itself — the horn made godhead

symbols.name: The torc
symbols.meaning: Rank and offering at once: the wealth the lord of beasts holds, wears, and dispenses

symbols.name: The ram-horned serpent
symbols.meaning: The underworld's animal, held bare-handed — the chthonic power no other Gaulish figure touches so calmly

symbols.name: The gathered beasts
symbols.meaning: Stag, boar, and the beasts of the deep wood: the retinue that answers to him and to no one else

mythology.lead: Cernunnos has no mythology in the literary sense — no tale, no genealogy, no surviving word of his deeds. Gaul wrote no epics down. What survives is a dossier of stone, silver, and bronze: one inscription that names him and a gallery of images that show him, and the whole tradition must be read from those.

myths.title: The Name on Stone
myths.text: Under the choir of Notre-Dame, in 1711, workmen uncovered the monument the boatmen's guild of the Parisii — the nautae Parisiaci — had raised to Jupiter in the reign of Tiberius, early in the first century CE. Among its carved gods, one block shows a balding, bearded head wearing antlers, with a torc hanging from each antler, and above the figure runs the inscription [C]ERNVNNOS. The first letter is lost and restored by convention, but the reading has held for three centuries of scholarship: this is the only text in the world that names the horned god. Everything else called Cernunnos is an identification argued from this single stone. The same monument shows the bull-god Tarvos Trigaranos and the woodcutter-god Esus: Cernunnos keeps company with a whole pantheon of Gaulish powers, all carved beneath a dedication to Jupiter — Rome's frame around native gods.

myths.title: The Cross-Legged Lord
myths.text: In 1891 a peat-cutter's spade struck silver in the Rævemosen bog at Gundestrup in Jutland: a great gilded vessel of thirteen plates, the masterpiece of Celtic metalwork, now in the National Museum of Denmark. On one interior plate sits the figure the whole world now pictures when it hears the name — cross-legged, antlered, a torc gripped in the right hand and a ram-horned serpent in the left, while a stag with matching antlers stands beside him and the animals of the wild close round: boar, bull, and a wolfish beast padding toward him. No inscription names him, and honest scholarship marks the identification as inference — but the face, the horns, the torc, and the serpent are the Paris pillar's figure seated in full. The vessel's other plates — the wheel-god, the antlered lord before a cauldron of warriors, elephants and griffins of exotic tribute — place the horned figure inside a complete cosmology of sacrifice and plenty.

myths.title: The Antlered Lords of Gaul
myths.text: The figure recurs across the Roman Gaulish world without ever being named again. At Reims an altar shows an antlered, cross-legged god seated between Apollo and Mercury, emptying a sack of grain or coin over a bull and a stag — the horned one as the source of abundance. At Saintes a relief gives the cross-legged figure his serpents again. In the rock carvings of Val Camonica in northern Italy a standing antlered figure with torcs on his arms was cut perhaps four centuries before the Paris pillar — the oldest of all the horned images, and the proof that the type long predates the name's one surviving attestation. At every site the figure keeps his two attributes — horns and stillness — while everything Roman around him changes: the god outlasts his interpreters.

myths.title: Conall Cernach and the Insular Echo
myths.text: Insular Celtic literature preserves no Cernunnos — but it preserves a name that has tempted scholars since the nineteenth century. Conall Cernach, the Ulster Cycle hero who stands beside [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]] as the second champion of Ulster, bears the epithet cernach, and the possibility that his name continues the same horn-root as the Gaulish god has been argued from Vendryes to Mac Cana. The honest verdict is suspension: the philology permits the connection, the sources never confirm it, and Mac Cana himself counsels caution. The horned god of Gaul may have an Irish cousin in the hero-lists — or the resemblance may be the oldest false friend in Celtic studies. Either way the debate itself is instructive: it shows how much weight Celtic philology places on a single shared root, and how rarely the texts cooperate.

cernunnos.syncretism: Rome met the horned god the way Rome met every god: by pairing him with her own. The Reims altar seats the antlered figure between Apollo and Mercury — a Roman frame built round a native centre — and the Pillar of the Boatmen itself is dedicated to Jupiter, with the Gaulish gods carved in attendance. The deepest Roman comparison is inferential: Caesar reports (De Bello Gallico 6.18) that all the Gauls claim descent from Dis Pater, father of the underworld, and since the nineteenth century scholars have wondered whether the antlered lord with his serpent and his cross-legged stillness is the god Caesar's informants meant. The identification is suggestive, never provable, and the best handbooks — Mac Cana, Green, Koch — keep it filed under hypothesis. His closest kin inside the lexicon are the other lords of the Celtic otherworld: [[arawn|Arawn]] of [[annwn|Annwn]], who hunts with white red-eared hounds, and [[dagda|the Dagda]], the good god whose cauldron never empties.
cernunnos.culturalLegacy: Cernunnos has the strangest afterlife in the lexicon: a god named once in antiquity who became, two millennia later, the most famous horned figure in modern religion. Margaret Murray's The God of the Witches (1931) made him the prime exhibit of her pan-European witch-cult — a thesis academic history has since dismantled (Ronald Hutton's The Triumph of the Moon is the standard autopsy) — but the image outlived the theory. Gerald Gardner placed the Horned God at the centre of modern Wicca, and 'Cernunnos' became his conventional name in contemporary pagan practice worldwide. The Gundestrup plate did the visual work: that cross-legged, antlered silhouette is now one of the most reproduced images of the ancient world, from album covers to fantasy games. A god with no surviving myth became the emblem of every wild thing that refuses to be tamed.
cernunnos.extendedMeditation: Cernunnos is the god built from evidence alone. No hymn, no saga, no genealogy — one word on a Paris stone, one silver plate from a Danish bog, and a scattered congregation of images that agree with each other across six hundred miles and four hundred years. He asks a different kind of attention than the storied gods: not 'what did he do?' but 'what did they see, that they carved him so carefully and wrote his name so rarely?' The answer the monuments give is always the same: the still one in the middle of the animals, holding rank in one hand and the underworld in the other, entirely at peace. Some gods are known by their stories. This one is known by his posture — and the posture has proved enough.
cernunnos.originalScriptNote: The name is attested exactly once, in Roman capitals on the Pillar of the Boatmen: [C]ERNVNNOS — the initial letter lost and restored by convention, the double NN and final -OS certain. Gaulish was also written in the Greek alphabet elsewhere in Gaul, but this name survives only in the Latin-letter epigraphic tradition; no native Celtic script attests it. The form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — which fixes the name in Tier 2. Because it is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: cernunnos.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

cernunnos.archaeology: Cernunnos is the most materially grounded name in the Celtic lexicon and the most textually impoverished: his entire attestation is archaeological. The Pillar of the Boatmen, raised by the boatmen's guild of the Parisii under Tiberius (14–37 CE) and rediscovered beneath Notre-Dame in 1711, carries the name's only inscription, [C]ERNVNNOS, above the antlered head with torcs; it stands today in the Musée national du Moyen Âge, Paris. The Gundestrup cauldron, cut from the peat at Rævemosen, Jutland, in 1891 and dated to around the first century BCE or CE, shows the cross-legged antlered figure with torc and ram-horned serpent on its most famous interior plate; it is the treasure of the National Museum of Denmark. The supporting gallery is wide: the Reims altar with its antlered figure between Apollo and Mercury, the cross-legged relief from Saintes, the horned figure with serpents from Cirencester in Roman Britain, and the fourth-century BCE antlered carving of Val Camonica — the oldest horned image in the Celtic world.

Long close back [uː] gliding into open [a]; the two vowels of Nuadu fall across a syllable boundary.

pronunciation.note: Nuada is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the attested Old Irish form carries no diacritic and no distinctive letter, so plain ASCII loses nothing. The etymology is honestly uncertain: one proposal reads the name as 'cloud-maker', from a root behind Welsh nudd 'mist'; another, argued by Tolkien for the Gaulish Nodens, connects it to a root meaning 'to catch, acquire' — a fisher or hunter — which would suit the sea-and-hounds imagery of the Lydney temple. Neither is settled, and the temple says so.

domains.title: War, King of Tuatha
domains.subtitle: The Silver-Handed King of the Tuatha Dé Danann
domains.lead: Nuada Airgetlám is the first king of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Ireland — the ruler who lost his arm at the First Battle of Mag Tuired, lost his throne to the law that a blemished man cannot be king, and won both back through the physicians' craft: first the silver arm that named him, then the living arm that restored him. His sword from Findias was one of the Four Treasures of his people, and he died at the Second Battle of Mag Tuired at the hands of Balor of the Evil Eye.

cards.name: The Silver Hand
cards.desc: Dian Cécht's silver arm, made with Credne the brazier, moved in every joint — and gave the king his name, Airgetlám.

cards.name: The Sword from Findias
cards.desc: One of the Four Treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann; once it was drawn from its sheath, no one escaped it.

cards.name: Mag Tuired
cards.desc: The plain of the two battles: against the Fir Bolg, where the arm was lost; against the Fomorians, where the king fell.

cards.name: The Unblemished Throne
cards.desc: Irish kingship law held that no man with a blemish could rule; Nuada's wound cost him Tara, and his healing restored him.

symbols.name: The silver arm
symbols.meaning: Wholeness made by craft when nature failed — the prosthesis that kept a king king in all but law

symbols.name: The sword of Nuada
symbols.meaning: The irresistible weapon from the city Findias, one of the Four Treasures brought to Ireland

symbols.name: Tara (Temair)
symbols.meaning: The seat of the kingship of Ireland, which a blemished man could not lawfully hold

symbols.name: The physician's craft
symbols.meaning: Dian Cécht's silver-work and Miach's flesh-work — healing as the instrument of sovereignty

symbols.name: Dog and fisherman (as Nodens)
symbols.meaning: The hound figurines and sea imagery of the Lydney Park temple, where his Gaulish cognate was worshipped

mythology.lead: Nuada's story is the Irish tradition's great parable of kingship and the body: a ruler can be unmade by a single wound and remade by healing, and the law watches both. The record runs from the Lebor Gabála Érenn through the two battles of Mag Tuired, and his Welsh and Gaulish cognates carry the same silver-handed name across the Celtic world.

myths.title: The First Battle of Mag Tuired
myths.text: When the Tuatha Dé Danann came to Ireland, Nuada had been their king for seven years. They demanded the country from the Fir Bolg, and the two peoples met at Mag Tuired in Connacht. In the battle Nuada fought Sreng, champion of the Fir Bolg, and Sreng struck off his right arm at the shoulder — yet the Tuatha Dé Danann won the field, and the Fir Bolg king Eochaid mac Eirc was driven to his death. The victors then offered the defeated a quarter of Ireland, and the Fir Bolg chose Connacht, which their descendants held. The victory that made the Tuatha Dé Danann masters of Ireland thus cost their king the wholeness the kingship required: one champion's sword-stroke bought a kingdom and unmade its king in the same afternoon.

myths.title: The Silver Hand and the Hand of Flesh
myths.text: Because a blemished man could not hold the kingship, Nuada yielded the throne to Bres. The physician Dian Cécht, with Credne the brazier, made him a full arm of silver that moved in every joint — whence his byname Airgetlám, Silver-hand. But Dian Cécht's own son Miach went further: he set the severed arm to the stump and healed it 'joint to joint and vein to vein' in thrice nine days. Jealous that the son had outdone the father, Dian Cécht struck Miach dead; from the young healer's grave grew three hundred and sixty-five herbs, which his sister Airmed sorted by their virtues — and which Dian Cécht scattered, so that their full knowledge died with him. Healing, in this cycle, is never free of the wound of envy.

myths.title: Bres, the Satire, and the Restoration
myths.text: Bres mac Elatha, half Fomorian by blood, ruled badly: the warriors of Ireland were set to menial labour, hospitality failed, and the poet Cairbre mac Étaíne composed against him what the tradition calls the first satire ever made in Ireland — and Bres's face broke out in blotches. Shamed and deposed, Bres fled to his Fomorian kin and came back at the head of the host that forced the Second Battle. The same law that had unseated Nuada now unseated Bres, for a blemished king could not stand; and with his arm made whole by Miach, Nuada took back the kingship and held it until the war came. The symmetry is exact: one king falls by the body's wound, the other by the wound of the word, and the same unforgiving law of wholeness judges them both.

myths.title: The Second Battle and the King's Death
myths.text: At Tara, on the eve of the war, a stranger came to Nuada's hall claiming every skill at once — harpist, warrior, smith, poet, healer — and Nuada, testing Lugh and finding him unmatched, gave the young god his own seat, the champion's seat, to lead the counsel of war. The Second Battle of Mag Tuired was fought against the Fomorians, and there Nuada Airgetlám and Macha his wife fell together at the hands of Balor of the Evil Eye. Balor's own death followed within the hour, Lugh's sling-stone through the destroying eye, and with the two kings' deaths the war ended and the tribute was lifted forever. The first king of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Ireland died in the victory that secured his people's rule; the sword of Findias passed into memory as the measure of a weapon that cannot be withstood.

nuada.syncretism: Nuada belongs to one of the clearest pan-Celtic name families. In Welsh he is Nudd and, in full form, Lludd Llaw Eraint — 'Lludd of the Silver Hand' — the king of Britain in Lludd a Llefelys, whose byname renders Airgetlám word for word (llaw 'hand', eraint 'silver'). In Gaulish he is Nodens (also Nodons, Nudens), worshipped at the great temple at Lydney Park in Gloucestershire, where Roman dedicants equated him with Mars and where the imagery — hounds, fishermen, the sea — suggests a healer and hunter as much as a warrior. The Romano-British curse tablet of Silvianus, asking 'Lord Nodens' to deny health to the thief of his ring, shows the god working as an enforcer of justice. Scholars (Mac Cana, Koch) reconstruct a Common Celtic *Noudont- or *Noudo- behind all three, though the root's meaning — 'cloud-maker' or 'catcher, fisher' — remains genuinely debated.
nuada.culturalLegacy: Nuada's afterlife runs through scholarship into fantasy. When R. E. M. and T. V. Wheeler published their excavation of the Nodens temple at Lydney Park in 1932, the young philologist J. R. R. Tolkien contributed the appendix 'The Name Nodens', tracing the god's name to a root of catching and acquiring — a fragment of Tolkien's scholarly life that fans of his fiction still chase. In modern Irish the name survives as Nuadha, and Maynooth University's old arms carried Nuada's sword. In popular culture the silver-handed king rides again as Prince Nuada Silverlance in Hellboy II: The Golden Army (2008), and the motif of the magical prosthetic hand — from A Song of Ice and Fire to Japanese fantasy — descends, knowingly or not, from Airgetlám. Modern Celtic pagans honour Nuada as a god of rightful rule, healing, and sovereignty restored.
nuada.extendedMeditation: Nuada is the king of the necessary surrender. The Irish law of the unblemished king looks cruel — a man maimed in his people's victory loses his throne — but the myth refuses both easy readings. It does not mock the law: Bres, who takes the throne, is judged by the same standard and falls to a blemish of the face raised by satire. And it does not abandon the wounded: the whole craft of the physician-gods bends itself to making Nuada whole, first in silver, then in flesh. What the cycle teaches is that sovereignty is not possession but fitness, and fitness can be lost and restored. The silver hand is the emblem of every function that has to be rebuilt after catastrophe: it moves in every joint, it does the work, and it is not the thing it replaces — until Miach's deeper healing shows that even that distinction can be overcome. The king who rules again is not the king who fell. He is the king who was remade.
nuada.originalScriptNote: The attested Old Irish form is Nuadu (later Nuada), written by medieval Irish scribes in the Insular Latin bookhand of the great vellum codices; in the Ogham letter-row the name would have been notched ᚅᚒᚐᚇᚐ (N-U-A-D-A), though no Ogham stone yet found carries it. Because the name is already plain ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: nuada.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

nuada.archaeology: Nuada is textual in Ireland — no inscription names him there — but his Gaulish cognate has one of the best-excavated cult sites in Roman Britain. At Lydney Park, Gloucestershire, overlooking the Severn estuary, a temple complex of the late third and fourth centuries CE was dedicated to Nodens: the Wheelers' excavations (1928–29, published 1932 with Tolkien's philological appendix) uncovered mosaic floors, inscribed slabs reading DEVO NODENTI and D M NODONTI ('to the god Mars Nodens'), bronze dog figurines, a fisherman plaque, and pins and bracelets left as votives — the material of a healing-and-hunting cult. The famous curse tablet of Silvianus, asking Nodens to withhold health from whoever stole his ring until it was returned 'to the temple of Nodens', was found on the site; a gold ring inscribed SENICIANE VIVAS IN DEO, plausibly the very ring, surfaced at Silchester. On the Irish side, the texts are the evidence: the Second Battle of Mag Tuired survives in the sixteenth-century British Library Harley MS 5280, the First Battle in a single late vellum copy edited by Fraser, and the Lebor Gabála in its medieval recensions.

phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar trill [r̥] — the Welsh digraph rh, an r sounded with breath; English has no equivalent, so 'hr' is the usual crutch.
Short close front [i], the light first syllable; Welsh stress has not yet fallen.
Open [a] in the stressed penult — Welsh words stress the next-to-last syllable, so the weight of the name lands here.
Alveolar nasal [n], open-mid [ɔ] (the Welsh o), final [n]; the unstressed ultima closes quietly.

domains.title: The Rider No Horse Can Catch
domains.subtitle: Horses, Sovereignty
domains.lead: Rhiannon is the Great Queen of the Mabinogi: the lady of the Otherworld who rides past Gorsedd Arberth on a pale horse at a slow, even pace that the fastest mounts of Dyfed cannot close — the goddess who chooses her own king, bears a false charge with unbroken dignity, and endures the penance of the horse-collar without bending.

cards.name: Gorsedd Arberth
cards.desc: The mound above Narberth where wonders are seen: whoever sits there receives blows — or sees a marvel. Pwyll saw her ride past.

cards.name: The Uncatchable Pace
cards.desc: She rides a pale horse at a slow, steady walk, and the swiftest riders in Dyfed cannot close the distance — until she is asked to stop.

cards.name: The Birds of Rhiannon
cards.desc: Adar Rhiannon: three birds whose song, though heard far over the sea, is as clear as if they sang beside you — sweeter than any earthly song.

cards.name: The Horse-Block
cards.desc: The marble mounting-block at the gate of Arberth, where she sits out her penance and offers to carry every guest to court on her back.

symbols.name: The pale horse
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty arriving at its own pace — the mount no pursuit can overtake, because the rider alone decides when to stop

symbols.name: The three birds
symbols.meaning: Adar Rhiannon, whose song crosses the boundary between the living and the dead — the Otherworld made audible

symbols.name: The horse-block
symbols.meaning: Dignity under a false sentence: the queen who carries her guests rather than break under the charge she did not earn

symbols.name: The bottomless bag
symbols.meaning: The cleverness that out-plots a forced marriage — Gwawl's undoing, and the game of Badger in the Bag

symbols.name: The collars of asses

mythology.lead: Rhiannon is the strongest female figure in the Four Branches of the Mabinogi, and the tales give her a complete arc: the uncatchable rider who chooses her husband, the accused mother who bears her penance, the captive of the enchantment who comes home still a queen. Every word of her story is medieval Welsh prose, preserved in two great manuscripts.

myths.title: The Rider on the Pale Horse
myths.text: Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, goes up to Gorsedd Arberth, the mound where a man either suffers blows or sees a wonder, and there he sees a lady in shining gold brocade riding past on a great pale horse — at a slow, even pace. He sends his swiftest rider after her; the faster the pursuit, the farther she draws ahead. Day after day it happens, with Pwyll's own horse and Pwyll himself, until at last he calls out: 'Maiden, for the sake of the man you love best, wait for me.' She stops at once: 'I will wait gladly — and it would have been better for the horse had you asked me that long ago.' She is Rhiannon, daughter of Hefaidd Hên, and she has come of her own will: she is being given to a man she does not want, and she has chosen Pwyll instead.

myths.title: The Bag That Would Not Fill
myths.text: At the wedding feast, Pwyll grants a request before he hears it — and the petitioner is Gwawl fab Clud, the suitor Rhiannon refused, who claims her by the promise. Rhiannon is not dismayed; she devises the counter-plot. A year later Pwyll comes to Gwawl's feast disguised as a beggar, asking only that a certain small bag she has given him be filled with food. The bag cannot be filled: it will never be full, she has told him, unless a true lord treads the food down with his feet and declares that enough has been put in. Gwawl rises and treads it down — and Pwyll draws the bag shut over him, blows his horn, and his war-band falls on the hall. Each man strikes the bag and asks what is in it; 'a badger,' comes the answer, and from that night the Welsh played the game called Badger in the Bag. Gwawl buys his release with sureties and a renounced claim, and Rhiannon marries the man she chose.

myths.title: The May-Eve Vanishing and the Penance
myths.text:
After three childless years the nobles of Dyfed press Pwyll to take another wife; he begs one year more, and Rhiannon bears a son. On the night of the birth the six women set to watch all fall asleep, and the child is gone. Terrified of the blame, the women kill the pups of a hound, smear the blood on Rhiannon's face, lay the bones beside her, and swear she has destroyed her own child. Pwyll will not put her away, but a penance is imposed: she is to sit beside the horse-block at the gate of Arberth, tell her story to every traveller who comes, and offer to carry guests and strangers to the court on her back. She accepts the sentence she did not earn, and she bears it without breaking.

The child, meanwhile, has fallen into the strangest rescue in Welsh prose. Teyrnon Twrf Liant, a lord by the sea, loses a foal every May-eve; keeping watch over his mare, he sees a great clawed hand reach through the window to seize the newborn foal, and strikes it off with his sword. Outside the door he finds a baby wrapped in silk brocade. He and his wife rear the boy as Gwri Wallt Euryn, Gwri of the Golden Hair — who grows with uncanny speed and bears, year by year, the very likeness of Pwyll. When Teyrnon hears of Rhiannon's penance, he knows what he must do, and he and his wife bring the boy to Arberth. Rhiannon looks at him and says that if this is true, her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her. From that word the boy is named Pryderi, and the penance ends.

myths.title: The Enchantment of Dyfed and the Collars of Asses
myths.text:
After Pwyll's death, Rhiannon is given in marriage to Manawydan fab Llŷr, and the four of them — Rhiannon and Manawydan, Pryderi and his wife Cigfa — return to Dyfed. There comes a peal of thunder and a fall of mist, and when it lifts, the land is emptied: not a person, not a dwelling, not a beast remains. For two years the four live by hunting; then they try their hand at saddlery, shield-making, and shoemaking in the towns of England, and each time the local craftsmen drive them out for making work too good to allow. Back in empty Dyfed, a shining white boar leads Pryderi and Manawydan to a fortress that was never there before; Pryderi goes in, lays hold of a golden bowl hanging by chains above a marble fountain, and is rooted to the spot, struck dumb. Rhiannon goes in after him, takes hold of the same bowl, and is trapped beside him — and fort, bowl, and both prisoners vanish.

Manawydan undoes the spell by patience. Sowing wheat, he watches three ripe fields stripped bare by mice on successive nights, and on the third he catches one slow, heavy mouse and condemns it to hang as a thief. A clerk, a priest, and a bishop come one after another to beg it off, each offering more than the last, and Manawydan names his price: Pryderi and Rhiannon released, the enchantment lifted from Dyfed, and no vengeance taken. The mouse is the wife of Llwyd fab Cilcoed, transformed with all his household; Llwyd had laid the spell to avenge his friend Gwawl fab Clud. Pryderi comes home with the gate-hammer about his neck, and Rhiannon with the collars of asses about hers — the second humiliation she has worn like a queen, and the second she survives.

myths.title: The Birds of Rhiannon
myths.text: Rhiannon never steps on stage in the Second Branch, but her birds do. When the seven survivors of the Irish war come back over the sea bearing the wounded head of Brân the Blessed, they feast at Harlech for seven years, and there come three birds — the Birds of Rhiannon, Adar Rhiannon — that begin to sing to them. Every other song seems unlovely beside it; and though the birds must be gazed at far out over the sea, their singing is as clear as if they sang in the hall. At Gwales in Penfro the company feasts on for eighty years with the uncorrupted head, in the presence of the birds' song, until the door toward Cornwall is opened and memory and sorrow return. Later Welsh tradition says of the Adar Rhiannon that their song wakes the dead and lulls the living to sleep — the music of a world that does not end.

rhiannon.syncretism: The great comparative debate pairs Rhiannon with Epona, the Gaulish horse-goddess whose dedications — more than two hundred inscriptions from Britain to the Balkans — make her the best-attested Celtic deity of the Roman west. A queenly rider whose whole story is bound to horses, whose name the handbooks reconstruct as 'Great Queen', looks very like an insular reflex of the mare-goddess; Mac Cana and others have argued the parallel, and Koch registers it as the standard comparison — but no inscription names Rhiannon or *Rīgantonā, and the identification remains typological, not epigraphic. The second frame is sovereignty: Mac Cana reads the First Branch against the Irish pattern in which the land's queen chooses and validates the king, so that Pwyll's marriage to Rhiannon is his investiture as much as his wedding. The third is Macha, the Irish sovereignty figure forced to race the king's horses: horse, humiliation, and queenship cluster around both women, and the handbooks have compared them for a century. None of these parallels is an identity; together they map the kind of goddess the Welsh prose is remembering.
rhiannon.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Rhiannon out of the Welsh manuscripts and into the English-speaking world, and the Victorian Celtic revival made her one of the best-known figures of Welsh tradition. Evangeline Walton's twentieth-century retellings of the Four Branches kept her before modern readers, and in 1975 Fleetwood Mac's 'Rhiannon' — written by Stevie Nicks, who found the name in a novel and only afterwards learned it belonged to a Welsh goddess — made the name famous worldwide; the given name Rhiannon, already living in Wales, spread across the English-speaking world in the song's wake. In modern Druid and pagan practice she is honoured as a goddess of horses, sovereignty, and endurance under injustice, and scholars of the Mabinogi rank her among the most fully realized women in medieval European literature — a figure whose dignity the prose never once allows to slip.
rhiannon.extendedMeditation: Rhiannon cannot be caught because she has already decided where she is going. The fastest horses in Dyfed gallop themselves to exhaustion behind a rider who is barely trotting — and the moment she is asked, she stops, because stopping was always hers to give. That is the secret the First Branch teaches about power: the pace of a sovereign is not set by her pursuers. The rest of her story tests the lesson. Falsely accused, she does not rage or plead; she sits down by the horse-block and carries her guests, one by one, until the truth walks home on its own legs. Trapped in the enchantment, she endures the collars of asses and comes out still the Great Queen. Endurance, in her telling, is not passivity — it is the refusal to let an unjust sentence write your name. She waits, she carries, she outlasts; and the land is hers again.
rhiannon.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Rhiannon — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: rhiannon.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/rhiannon/ in the meantime.

rhiannon.archaeology: Rhiannon is a textual figure: no temple, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and the reconstructed *Rīgantonā has no epigraphic attestation anywhere in the Celtic world. Her evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales themselves are dated by debate rather than document, most often to the later eleventh or early twelfth century. The geography of her story is real — Arberth, the court of Dyfed, stands by modern Narberth in Pembrokeshire — but no sanctuary of hers is known. The nearest material horizon is comparative, not hers: the two hundred and more dedications to the Gaulish horse-goddess Epona recovered across the Roman west, against which scholars have long read the rider of Arberth.

domains.title: Magic, Poetry, Trickery
domains.subtitle: Enchanter of Gwynedd — illusion, craft, and the fate of Lleu Llaw Gyffes
domains.lead: In the Welsh tradition, Gwydion fab Dôn is the foremost magician of the Mabinogi: master of illusion, disguise, and the hidden name, whose tricks win a war — and whose craft finally puts a broken world back together.

cards.name: The Enchanted Swine
cards.desc: Disguised as a poet, Gwydion conjured illusory stallions, hounds, and shields to trade for Pryderi's otherworld pigs — the first swine in Wales — and started a war with a vanishing herd.

cards.name: Math's Wand
cards.desc: The wand that transformed Gwydion and Gilfaethwy into deer, boars, and wolves for three years — and that later struck Lleu from eagle back into man.

cards.name: The Flower-Maiden
cards.desc: With Math, Gwydion fashioned Blodeuwedd from the flowers of oak, broom, and meadowsweet — a wife made by craft for the man no earthly wife was allowed.

cards.name: The Eagle on the Oak
cards.desc: When Lleu was struck into eagle-shape, Gwydion followed a sow to the oak, sang three englynion to bring him down, and turned vengeance into restoration.

mythology.lead: Gwydion fab Dôn is the enchanter of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, 'Math fab Mathonwy': nephew of Math the king of Gwynedd, brother of Gilfaethwy, and the foremost magician of medieval Welsh literature. He is poet, trickster, foster-father, and avenger in one figure — the man who makes illusions that pass for wealth, who pays for his crimes in animal skins, and who ends the tale as the careful hand that puts a broken world back into shape.

myths.title: The War for the Swine
myths.text:
King Math of Gwynedd could live only with his feet in the lap of a virgin, except in time of war, and the maiden Goewin held that office. When Gilfaethwy desired her, Gwydion devised the remedy: war. He went to Pryderi of Dyfed in the guise of a poet and asked for the swine — the hobeu, the first pigs ever brought to Wales, a gift from Arawn of Annwfn. Refused, he conjured twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars, and twelve golden shields, and traded the apparitions for the herd. By the time Pryderi's glamour faded, Gwydion was gone, and Pryderi came north with an army.

While Math marched to meet him, Gwydion and Gilfaethwy forced Goewin. At the peace-talks Pryderi demanded single combat, 'for it was because of me that the hosts came'; at Maenor Penard, the tale says, Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour and by magic and enchantment', and Dyfed went home under tribute. The victory is real and so is its cost: Gwydion's finest trick is also his crime, and the Fourth Branch never lets the two be separated.

myths.title: The Punishment of the Brothers
myths.text:
Math's justice is the strangest in the Mabinogi. He struck Gwydion and Gilfaethwy with his magic wand and turned them into a stag and a hind, and sent them into the wild for a year; when they returned with a fawn, he made them a boar and a sow for the second year, and a wolf and a she-wolf for the third. Each year their offspring — Hyddwn, Hychddwn Hir, and Bleiddwn — were sent to the court, baptized, and raised.

After the third year Math struck them back into their own shapes: 'You have had punishment enough, and you have been greatly shamed.' The punishment is exact and even-handed — the brothers suffer in the flesh what they did, and when the debt is paid the king takes them back into honour. It is the Fourth Branch's doctrine of justice in miniature: transformation as sentence, restoration as mercy. And it matters that the wand passes finally into Gwydion's own hand: the man punished by shape-shaping becomes the master of it, and the tale watches to see what he does with the power that once unmade him.

myths.title: The Naming and Arming of Lleu
myths.text:
When Gwydion proposed his sister Arianrhod as Math's new footholder, she stepped over the wand for the virginity test and dropped a yellow-haired boy — Dylan, who made for the sea — and 'something small' that Gwydion hid in a chest at the foot of his bed. From the chest came the boy who would be Lleu. Gwydion fostered him, and Arianrhod, shamed, laid three tynghedau upon him: he should have no name until she named him, no arms until she armed him, and no wife of any race then on earth.

Gwydion undid the destinies by craft. Disguised as a shoemaker with the boy at his side, he came beneath Caer Arianrhod, and when Lleu flung a stone and struck a wren's leg askew, Arianrhod cried that the fair one had struck it with a skilful hand — and so named him Lleu Llaw Gyffes. For the arms, Gwydion conjured a phantom fleet against the castle until Arianrhod herself armed the defenders. The magician wins not by force but by arranging the world so that his opponent speaks the words he needs: the tynged is a lock, and Gwydion's trade is keys.

myths.title: The Flower-Maiden and the Eagle
myths.text:
For the third tynged there was no earthly answer, so Gwydion and Math made one: from the flowers of the oak, the broom, and the meadowsweet they fashioned the fairest woman anyone had seen, and named her Blodeuwedd, 'Flower-face'. She married Lleu — and betrayed him with Gronw Pebr of Penllyn, drawing from her husband the secret of how he could be killed, so that Gronw's spear struck him at the impossible meeting of conditions and Lleu flew off in the shape of an eagle, screaming.

Gwydion searched Gwynedd and Powys until he followed a sow to an oak where rotten flesh fell to her snout, and in the top of the tree sat the eagle. He sang three englynion down the perches of the years until Lleu came to his knee, then struck him with the wand back into human shape — skin and bone, to be nursed with doctors and good care. The vengeance was as crafted as the rescue: Blodeuwedd he would not kill, but turned into an owl, 'the shape hated by all the birds'; and Gronw, standing where Lleu had stood, took Lleu's spear-cast through the slab at Llech Gronw and died. Maker of the woman, finder of the man, instrument of the sentence: Gwydion's whole domain is in this last movement.

myths.title: The Battle of the Trees
myths.text: Outside the Mabinogi, the Book of Taliesin preserves Gwydion's other great fame: Kat Godeu, 'The Battle of the Trees', in which he enchants the trees of the forest to march as an army — the alder in the van, the oak amid the hosts. The poem's speaker, Taliesin, boasts that he was there when Gwydion 'made the sally of the trees'. In the tale-material gathered around the poem, the sons of Dôn fight the forces of Annwfn over a white roebuck, a whelp, and a lapwing, and the battle turns when the hidden name of the enemy's champion is guessed from the alder twigs in his hand — the same magic of the name that the Fourth Branch shows in the wren scene. Whether the poem preserves older myth or later learned fancy is honestly debated, but its Gwydion is unmistakably the Mabinogi's: the magician whose weapons are other things' natures, who wins by knowing what a thing is called and what it can be made to do.

gwydion.syncretism: Gwydion is the Welsh trickster-enchanter, and comparative scholarship has set him beside the other shape-changing cunning figures of Europe: Loki, whose disguises and bargains Gwydion's deceptions recall; Hermês, the poet-thief of the Greek pantheon; and Óðinn in his sorcerer's aspect. Mac Cana treats him as one of the great magician-figures of the Celtic world, and the comparison holds at the level of motif — illusion, disguise, the hidden name, the shape-shifting punishment — not of borrowing. The deeper kinship is insular: Irish tradition is full of druidic shape-shifters, and Gwydion's transformations of and by Math belong to a shared Celtic idiom of magic as metamorphosis. Scholars have also long linked the Fourth Branch's otherworld material — Arawn's swine, the phantom fleet — to the mythology of Manawydan and the First and Third Branches.
gwydion.culturalLegacy: Gwydion's afterlife runs from Welsh tradition into modern letters. Later Welsh usage named the Milky Way Caer Gwydion, 'Gwydion's fortress' — the enchanter's castle written across the night sky — and the antiquarian bards kept his tree-battle in the poetic canon. In the twentieth century he entered world literature twice over: Alan Garner's The Owl Service (1967) rebuilt the Blodeuwedd tragedy as a haunting that repeats itself down the generations of a Welsh valley, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain gave young readers a Prince Gwydion fab Don, heir of Math, drawn directly from the Fourth Branch. Evangeline Walton's retellings of the Mabinogion made his punishment and restoration the moral hinge of her Fourth Branch volume. In scholarship he remains the standard exhibit of the Welsh magician: Ifor Williams's edition, Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi, and Koch's Celtic encyclopedia all treat the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of medieval Welsh prose and Gwydion as its animating intelligence.
gwydion.extendedMeditation: Gwydion is what a culture makes of cleverness when it refuses to call cleverness innocent. His illusions win a war and buy a rape; the tale answers by putting him, for three years, into the bodies of beasts, one year for each shape of the debt. But the same hands that tricked a king out of his swine later coax a dying god out of a tree, one verse at a time, and the same wand that punishes him he is finally trusted to hold. The Fourth Branch's calm is that magic and justice are one craft: to know the true shape of a thing — a name, a name-day, a wound, a woman made of flowers — is to be able to change it, and to be answerable for the change. Gwydion is the enchanter who learns, and teaches, that power over forms is a form of responsibility.
gwydion.originalScriptNote: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Gwydion (the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest), and the ASCII spelling loses nothing — hence Tier 2. The plain-ASCII domain gwydion.com is registered to a third party and held outside the collection; it is watched for release. Until then this temple stands without a domain of its own.

gwydion.archaeology: Gwydion is a textual figure with no pre-Christian material attestation: no inscription, votive object, or image names him. His witnesses are manuscripts — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1400), in which the Fourth Branch survives, and the Book of Taliesin (NLW Peniarth 2, early 14th c.) for Kat Godeu. The tale's geography is walkable real terrain — Gwynedd, Dyfed, Penllyn, the river Cynfael — and a holed stone traditionally pointed out as Llech Ronw, 'Gronw's stone', the slab Lleu's spear pierced, stands in the Cynfael valley; the identification is local tradition rather than proof, but it shows how early and how firmly the story was mapped onto the Welsh landscape.

phonemes.desc: Long close back vowel [oː], the Old Irish ó that opens the name; the later spellings Aengus and Angus record its long drift toward a diphthong and then a plain vowel.
Voiced velar nasal [ŋ], the n drawn back before g — the ng of English 'singer', never a hard en-g split.
Voiced velar stop [g], kept hard after the nasal; the lenition that softens intervocalic g in Irish does not touch this cluster.
Short back [u] with voiceless [s], the unstressed final syllable — the masculine -us ending of the o-stem name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OHN-gus' — one long open 'oh', the ng of 'singer', a hard g, and a short unstressed 'us'. Modern Irish Aonghus and Scottish Aonghas have worn it toward 'AYN-guhs' — the Anglicized Angus.

domains.title: Love, Youth, Poetry
domains.subtitle: The Mac Óc — the Son of the Young, god of Brú na Bóinne
domains.lead: Aengus — Old Irish Óengus, the mac ind Óc, 'son of the young' — is the ever-young god of the Túatha Dé Danann, son of [[dagda|the Dagda]] and Bóand. His power is the strangest in the corpus: not the club or the spear, but the dream, the bargain, and the unaging house. He was born inside a single day, won the greatest mound in Ireland on a grammar quibble, and found his wife in a dream.

cards.name: The Dream
cards.desc: In the Aislinge Óenguso a maiden comes to him in sleep with music; he sickens for love of a woman he has never seen awake, and the dream must be hunted like a quarry.

cards.name: The Swan
cards.desc: Caer Ibormeith lives one year as a girl and one as a swan among thrice fifty swans on Loch Bél Dracon; to win her, Óengus takes the swan-shape himself.

cards.name: Brú na Bóinne
cards.desc: The Brug on the Boyne — síd in Broga, the mound the world calls Newgrange — his Otherworld house, won from the Dagda for 'a day and a night' and kept ever since.

cards.name: The Day and the Night
cards.desc: Asked when he would surrender the mound lent 'for a day and a night', he answered that the whole world is spent in days and nights — and the answer has never been overturned.

symbols.name: Brú na Bóinne
symbols.meaning: The Brug on the Boyne, his unaging house — the síd the tales call síd in Broga and the world calls Newgrange

symbols.name: The swan-shape
symbols.meaning: The form he takes at Samain on Loch Bél Dracon to win Caer Ibormeith — love answered in kind, shape for shape

symbols.name: The dream (aisling)
symbols.meaning: The maiden's nightly visit with her timpán — desire that arrives before its object, and must be pursued into the waking world

symbols.name: The day and the night
symbols.meaning: The quibble that holds the Brug forever — time itself parsed as a loan without a term

symbols.name: The crystal bower
symbols.meaning: The grianán he built at the Brug for Étaín in her fly-shape — shelter given to a hunted woman when no one else could hold her

mythology.lead: Aengus's mythology is a study in winning without fighting. The three great set-pieces — his birth inside a stopped day, his taking of the Brug, and the dream-quest for Caer Ibormeith — are all victories of time: time held still, time parsed, time waited out. The counselor and the host follow: the son whose wit saves his father, and the keeper of the Brug who shelters Étaín when all Ireland has no safer room.

myths.title: The Day the Sun Stood Still
myths.text:
The Dagda desired Bóand, the wife of Elcmar of the Brug, and sent Elcmar away on a day's errand to Bres. To hide what followed, the tale says, the Dagda made the sun stand still: nine months passed, and the world reckoned it a single day — so the child was conceived and born within one day, and Elcmar came home none the wiser. They named the boy Óengus, but the story gave him the name that stuck: mac ind Óc, 'the son of the young', because young was the day that bore him.

The episode fixes the god's signature before he can speak: he is a child of bent time. Bóand, the Boyne itself made goddess, is his mother; the Dagda, the All-Father, his sire; and his first house is the river-bend his father stole a day to give him. The fosterage that followed — with Midir of Brí Léith — placed him among the proudest of the Túatha Dé Danann and set up every tale that came after. A birth concealed inside a stretched day becomes the charter of a god whose entire career will be spent stretching time further.

myths.title: A Day and a Night
myths.text:
When the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of Ireland among the Túatha Dé Danann, Óengus was away fostered with Midir and received nothing. He came home to claim his share, and the Dagda, having no mound left to give, granted him Brú na Bóinne — the Dagda's own house — for a day and a night. When the term was spent and the Dagda asked for his Brug back, Óengus answered that it is in days and nights that the whole world is spent, and so the grant had no end. The All-Father lost the argument, and the greatest mound in Ireland passed to the son who had read the fine print.

The tale is told with a straight face, but its logic is the logic of the síd itself: the Otherworld does not run on mortal clocks. A god born inside a single stretched day is the natural owner of a house held on a day without a term. Irish law prized the exact word; Óengus's first deed makes etymology into real estate, and it never has to be defended with a weapon.

myths.title: The Dream of Óengus
myths.text:
A maiden came to Óengus in sleep, playing a timpán, the sweetest music he had heard; for a year she came, and he could never hold her, and when she ceased to come he wasted with love-sickness. Bóand searched Ireland for a year and found nothing; the Dagda searched a year and found nothing; then Bodb Derg, king of the síd of Munster, searched, and at the year's end found her: Caer Ibormeith, daughter of Ethal Anbuail of síd Uaman in Connacht.

But Caer lived under a rhythm no bargain could break: one year in girl's shape and one as a swan among thrice fifty swans on Loch Bél Dracon, each pair linked by a silver chain and Caer's own of gold, and the change came at Samain. Óengus went to the lake at Samain and called to her, and she answered that she would go with him only if he took the swan-shape beside her. He entered the water, became a swan, and the two flew three times around the lake — and their music put every listener to sleep for three days and three nights — then away to Brú na Bóinne, where the singing of the two swans became part of the mound's music ever after.

myths.title: The Bower of the Purple Fly
myths.text:
When the jealous Fuamnach struck Étaín with a rod of scarlet quicken-tree and made her a pool of water, then a worm, then a purple fly, the fly that was Étaín came at last to Brú na Bóinne, to the hall of Óengus. He knew her — the fly's music and its radiance were hers — and he built her a grianán, a sun-bower of crystal filled with healing herbs and the bloom of every field, and she stayed with him there, and the window of the bower let her pass in and out as she pleased.

It could not last. Fuamnach followed the rumor of the fly's good fortune and raised a magic wind that swept Étaín out of the bower and across Ireland for seven years, until she fell into the cup of Étar's wife at the Bay of Cíú and was drunk, conceived, and born again a thousand and twelve years after her first birth. Óengus's shelter is one of the gentlest episodes in the cycle: the young god keeping one hunted woman safe in the safest house in Ireland, against a malice even his Brug could not finally exclude.

myths.title: The Satirist's Three Gold Coins
myths.text:
Under the tyranny of Bres the Dagda was set to building the usurper's forts, and the satirist Cridenbél taxed him the three best bits of every ration, until the greatest of the gods was failing from hunger — for no one dared refuse a satirist whose curse raised blisters on the face. Óengus came to his father and gave him the counsel that turned the trap: demand of Bres the pick of the cattle of Ireland as wages, and hide three gold coins in the porridge portion meant for the satirist. Cridenbél swallowed greed and gold together and died of it; and when Bres demanded the Dagda's death for the killing, the dead man's own belly gave the verdict — cut open, it held the gold, proof that greed and not the Dagda had killed him.

The episode is the tradition's clearest pairing of father and son: the Dagda's patience carrying the labor, Óengus's wit carrying the case. The young god does not raise a weapon in the whole of Cath Maige Tuired, and does not need to — his contribution to the war that freed the Túatha Dé Danann was a sentence spoken at the right fireside.

aengus.syncretism: The comparison the handbooks prefer for Óengus runs to Gaul and Wales rather than to Rome. The Gaulish Maponos, 'the Divine Son' — known from dedications to Apollo Maponus in the Roman north of Britain and from the Ravenna Cosmography's locus Maponi — is the same figure-type: the ever-young son of a greater divine parent. Mac Cana and Sjoestedt set Maponos beside both Óengus and the Welsh Mabon ap Modron, 'Son son of Mother', the hunter-youth of Culhwch ac Olwen whose name is built on the same Proto-Celtic words *makwos, 'son', and *mātīr, 'mother'. The popular handbooks go further and call Óengus 'the Irish Eros'; the medieval texts give a stranger and more specific figure — a god of dream, youth, and cunning whose love-story is won by patience and shape-changing rather than by arrows. The comparisons are structural and instructive; no inscription identifies him, and the identification of Maponos with Mabon is itself a scholarly argument, not a fact.
aengus.culturalLegacy: No Irish god had a better literary afterlife than the young one. W. B. Yeats made him a byword for longing itself in 'The Song of Wandering Aengus' (1899) — the hazel wand, the fire in the head, the glimmering girl with apple blossom in her hair who called his name and ran — a poem that poured the Aislinge into the bloodstream of modern English verse. James Stephens gave him speaking parts and moods in The Crock of Gold (1912), where Angus Og wanders the Irish countryside being wise and young. In the later Gaelic tradition he never faded: the Fenian tale of Diarmaid and Gráinne keeps him at Brú na Bóinne as Diarmaid's fosterer and protector, and Irish folklore kept the Brug as his house into the modern period. His name took a second, quieter path: worn to Angus, it became one of the most familiar masculine names in Scotland — a theonym hiding in plain sight on every map of Angus and in every roll of Scottish kings. And his address became the most visited prehistoric site in Ireland: Newgrange, where five thousand winters of sun have entered the chamber the tales assigned to the son of the young.
aengus.extendedMeditation:
Aengus is the god of the interval — the stretch of time between wanting and having, and his whole dossier asks what can be done with it. His father held the sun still for nine months to make a day large enough to be born in; the son learned the lesson and spent his career proving that time is a text to be parsed, not a wall to be stormed. A loan of a day and a night is forever, if you read it right. A dream that comes nightly for a year is an address, if you are willing to search every lake in Ireland for it. The name says the same: óen-gus, one vigor, a single strength held undivided — no club, no cauldron, no host, just the one force applied without distraction.

That is why his love-story is the corpus's gentlest. Every other divine wooing in Irish myth is a raid, a riddle, or a revenge; Óengus's is a search. He does not seize Caer Ibormeith; he finds her, asks her, accepts her condition, and meets her in her own shape — a god who becomes a swan because the girl is one. The music the two swans make, which puts the world to sleep for three days, is the dream coming back around: the aisling that began as a haunting ends as a harmony. Youth, in this mythology, is not the season of appetite. It is the season before resignation — the one vigor that has not yet learned to stop looking.
aengus.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Óengus, written in the Insular Latin script of the medieval manuscripts, with a síneadh fada marking the long Ó; the Middle Irish spelling Aengus drops the accent, and the temple follows that unaccented form. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the restored form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: aengus.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

aengus.archaeology: Aengus is a textual god — no ogham stone names him and no votive inscription invokes him — but his mythic address is the single most famous piece of prehistoric architecture in Ireland. Brú na Bóinne, the palace of the Boyne, is a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, and the passage tomb of Newgrange (c. 3200 BCE), older than Stonehenge and the pyramids, has been identified with the tales' síd in Broga, Óengus's Brug, since the medieval topographical tradition. The mound's roof-box, which admits the rising sun into the chamber on the mornings around the winter solstice, was excavated and documented by Michael J. O'Kelly (1962–1975), who observed the phenomenon in 1967 — a real alignment behind the mythology of a god born of a stopped sun. The witnesses to the texts are exact: Tochmarc Étaíne is preserved in the twelfth-century Lebor na hUidre and later manuscripts; Aislinge Óenguso survives in the fifteenth-century British Library MS Egerton 1782, the basis of Shaw's edition. For the comparative figure, the material record is Romano-British: altars dedicated to Apollo Maponus from the military north, including the Corbridge series, with the Ravenna Cosmography's locus Maponi completing the map of the Divine Son's cult — comparative evidence, never identification.

phonemes.desc: Short open back unrounded [ɑ], stressed as the first syllable of every Old Norse word; brief, not the long á.
Alveolar nasal [n] followed by a fully voiced stop [d]; in runic carving the d would be written with the t-rune, which underspecifies voicing.
Voiced labiodental [v] as in English 'very', a second short [ɑ], trilled [r], and a short close [i]; the name is a weak masculine and carries no added nominative -r.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AHND-vah-ri' — three even syllables, stress on the first, the v soft as in 'very', the r trilled, the ending a short 'ih' as in 'bit'.

pronunciation.note: Andvari is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — so the ASCII alphabet loses nothing in copying it. The dwarf's fame rides on his ring, not on his orthography; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Dwarf, Guardian of Gold
domains.subtitle: The Careful One of the Waterfall
domains.lead: Andvari is the dwarf of Andvarafors, the waterfall where he kept his gold in a pike's shape — the careful one whose last ring was taken by force and answered with the curse that ran through Hreiðmarr, Fáfnir, Sigurðr, and the Gjúkungar, and ended in the Rhine.

cards.name: Andvarafors
cards.desc: The waterfall that was his hall — the stream where he swam in a pike's shape and kept his gold, named for him in Reginsmál's prose.

cards.name: Andvaranaut
cards.desc: 'Andvari's jewel' — the last ring of the hoard, hidden in his hand, taken by force, and answered with the curse that every owner would find death in it.

cards.name: Rán's Net
cards.desc: The sea-queen's net that Loki borrowed to drag the waterfall — the tool that turned a fishing into an extortion.

cards.name: The Pike-Shape
cards.desc: The fish-form in which he swept his hoard through the water — the careful one's disguise, netted all the same.

symbols.name: Andvaranaut
symbols.meaning: The ring taken last and cursed first — a treasure that kills every hand it passes through

symbols.name: Andvarafors
symbols.meaning: The waterfall named for its keeper — a hoard-hall that flows and cannot be locked

symbols.name: Rán's net
symbols.meaning: Borrowed catching-power — the gods paying a blood-debt with a fisherman's trick

symbols.name: The pike-shape
symbols.meaning: The disguise of the careful — a form made for guarding, not for fighting

symbols.name: The otter's ransom
symbols.meaning: The wergild that had to cover a dead otter's skin from the inside — gold counted out hair by hair

mythology.lead: Andvari's dossier is a single episode and its long echo: one afternoon's extortion at a waterfall, and a curse that runs through the rest of the Völsung cycle like poison through water. Reginsmál's prose, Snorri's Skáldskaparmál, and Völsunga saga all tell the catching; everything after — Fáfnir's dragon, Sigurðr's sword, the gold sunk in the Rhine — is the curse working itself out.

myths.title: The Otter's Ransom
myths.text:
Óðinn, Loki, and Hœnir were traveling when they came to a waterfall, and there they saw an otter eating a salmon on the bank, its eyes shut. Loki killed it with a stone and boasted of a double catch — otter and fish at one cast. But the otter was Ótr, son of the farmer Hreiðmarr, a shape-shifter who took an otter's form to fish the falls. That night the gods sought lodging at Hreiðmarr's house and showed their catch; Hreiðmarr called his sons Fáfnir and Reginn, and the three seized the gods and bound them. The wergild was set by the skin itself: the otter's hide was to be filled with red gold, and then covered with gold from the outside until not a hair showed. Óðinn sent Loki to get the gold, and Loki went down to the world of the black-elves to find it where it lay — in the keeping of a dwarf at a waterfall.

Snorri tells the same in Skáldskaparmál as the explanation of gold's kennings: this is why poets call gold the otter's ransom, the forced payment of the Æsir. The episode exists in the tradition to gloss poetry — a myth doing the work of a dictionary.

myths.title: The Net of Rán
myths.text:
Völsunga saga gives the fullest account of the catching. Loki went to Rán, the sea-queen who drowns sailors, and borrowed her net, then came to the waterfall called Andvarafors. There lived the dwarf Andvari, who kept a pike's shape in the water and swept his gold about him, guarding everything. Loki cast the net and caught him, and demanded the ransom: all the gold in the waterfall, or Andvari's head.

The dwarf paid over the hoard — but he kept one ring back, a small thing, hidden in his hand. Loki saw it and took that too, despite Andvari's plea that with the ring kept he could breed gold again and would not beggar himself entirely. Loki answered that one coin would be too many to leave him, and went up out of the water with the whole of it. Reginsmál's prose tells the same catching more briefly: Loki got Rán's net, cast it before the pike, and the dwarf paid the otter's ransom from his own keeping.

myths.title: The Curse on the Ring
myths.text:
Stripped of everything, Andvari did the only thing left to a dwarf with nothing: he spoke. Reginsmál's prose preserves the curse as the tradition's own words: the gold that Gustr had owned — Gustr, 'Gust', the other name the prose gives the dwarf — would be the death of two brothers, and would bring strife to eight of the kin-line — eight ættlingar — and no man would ever have joy of his wealth. Völsunga saga gives the same sentence over the ring itself: it would be the death of every man who owned it.

The ring got a name from its first owner's loss: Andvaranaut, 'Andvari's jewel'. Nothing in the corpus says the curse was magic in the modern sense; it needs none. What the careful one laid on the gold was a prophecy any listener could verify, because the gold itself was now worth killing for — and the story spends the rest of its length proving him right, owner by owner.

myths.title: Fáfnir's Bed of Gold
myths.text:
The gods filled the otter-skin and covered it, and the last hair was covered with Andvaranaut itself — Loki had kept the ring back until that final hair, so that even the last coin of the hoard went into the ransom. The gods went free. But Hreiðmarr refused his sons any share, and the curse began its work at once: Fáfnir killed his father sleeping, took all the treasure, and refused Reginn a share in turn. He carried the hoard out to the heath called Gnitaheiðr and brooded on it until he became the worst of serpents — a dragon lying on his gold, wearing the helmet of terror.

Reginn, cheated, went to the court of King Hjálprekr and became foster-father to Sigurðr. He reforged the sword Gram from the shards of Sigmund's blade and egged the young man to the heath. Sigurðr dug a pit in the dragon's path and stabbed up into the belly as Fáfnir crawled over him to drink; warned by the nuthatches that Reginn meant him harm, he cut off his foster-father's head, ate of the dragon's heart, and understood the speech of birds. He loaded the hoard, Andvaranaut and all, on Grani's back. The careful one's gold had its third owner, the greatest hero of the North — and the curse did not care. A curse on gold is not a spell; it is an arithmetic.

myths.title: The Gold in the Rhine
myths.text:
From Sigurðr the treasure passed as blood-price and dowry into the house of the Gjúkungar — Gunnar, Högni, and their sister Guðrún, whom Sigurðr married. When Sigurðr was murdered in his bed over Brynhildr's vengeance, the hoard was the Gjúkungs' alone, and it drew King Atli, Brynhildr's brother, who invited his brothers-in-law to his hall to take it from them. Gunnar and Högni rode knowing the invitation was death, and before they crossed the Rhine they did the last careful thing anyone does with Andvari's gold: they sank the whole hoard in the river, in deep water, where no one would have joy of it — the dwarf's sentence carried out by its victims themselves.

Atli's men cut Högni's heart out and cast Gunnar living into a pit of serpents, where he played the harp with his toes until an adder struck him to the heart; the hoard he died to keep lay at the bottom of the Rhine, ownerless. Atlakviða ends the account with the river itself as the treasure's last keeper: the Rhine shall hold the strife-metal of the Niflungar. Two brothers dead, eight princes at strife, no man the happier — Reginsmál's prophecy closed like a hand. Andvari was avenged on everyone, which is to say on no one in particular, which is exactly what a curse is.

andvari.syncretism: Andvari needs no foreign counterpart to be understood — the cursed-hoard complex is native Germanic and runs through the whole North: treasure extorted is treasure poisoned. The corpus itself supplies the sharpest contrast in another dwarf-ring: Draupnir, forged freely by Brokkr and Sindri for the gods, which drips eight new rings every ninth night — the given ring multiplies, the taken ring kills. Continental heroic tradition keeps the same stratum: the hoard of the Nibelungenlied, sunk in the Rhine and deadly to its holders, is the southern telling of the Andvaranaut complex, and scholars treat the Norse and German versions as one inheritance rather than borrowings. The dwarf caught in fish-shape also has a family resemblance to the water-spirits of later folklore, but the Eddic Andvari is a smith and hoarder first; his pike-form is camouflage, not nature.
andvari.culturalLegacy: Andvari's afterlife is one of the largest in all mythology, under another name. Wagner's Alberich in Das Rheingold — the dwarf of the water's depth who is robbed of his gold, lays a curse on the ring forged from it, and watches it destroy owner after owner through four operas — is built substantially on the Andvari of Reginsmál and Völsunga saga, crossed with the Nibelungenlied's hoard; the curse-motif that drives the entire Ring cycle is the sentence spoken at Andvarafors. William Morris's Sigurd the Volsung (1876) kept the original name before English readers, and the Nibelungenlied's Rhine-gold carried the same hoard into German memory. In Iceland the name itself was revived with no curse attached: Andvari is the title of the learned journal of the Icelandic Literary Society, founded in 1874 — the careful one finally keeping something that multiplies without killing. Modern fantasy's treasury of cursed gold, from dragons' hoards onward, runs downhill from his waterfall.
andvari.extendedMeditation: His name is care itself — andvari, watchfulness, the quality of mind that checks the locks twice. And the myth is merciless to it: the most careful keeper in the corpus is caught in an afternoon, by a borrowed net, in his own water, and stripped to the last hidden ring. Care could not save him, because care guards against theft and what came for him was law — a wergild, a debt, a skin that had to be covered hair by hair. What he had left was speech, and he used it like a dwarf: precisely, vindictively, and with perfect aim. The curse is the one thing he made that nobody could take, because it was already given. Everything after is arithmetic — two brothers, eight princes, no joy — and the myth lets the numbers run for four generations to teach a single lesson the North never tired of: gold that is taken by force does not change owners; it changes victims. Andvari in his waterfall is the small still beginning of the Völsung tragedy, the moment the hook was set. The careful one's revenge on the careless world was simply to tell it the truth about what it had just picked up.
andvari.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Andvari — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛅᚾᛏᚢᛅᚱᛁ (a-n-t-u-a-r-i, the t-rune writing d and úr writing v). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: andvari.com is held outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

Poetic Edda: Fáfnismál (Sigurðr and the dying dragon on the hoard) and Atlakviða (the Gjúkungs, the sunken gold, the Rhine as last keeper)
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál (the otter's ransom and the kennings for gold — 'forced payment of the Æsir', 'Fáfnir's bed', 'metal of Gnitaheiðr')
