andvari.archaeology: Andvari himself is a purely literary figure: no runestone, votive deposit, or named image records him. But the cycle his gold sets in motion is the best-attested narrative in Viking-Age art. The Ramsund carving in Södermanland (Sö 101, c. 1030) cuts the whole Fáfnir episode into a rock face — Sigurðr thrusting up through the serpent's body, the slain Reginn with his smith's tools, Grani loaded with the treasure, and the birds whose speech the dragon-heart taught — and the Gök stone (Sö 327) weaves the same scenes through a runic inscription. The Drävle runestone (U 1163) shows Sigurðr stabbing the serpent, and related scenes appear on the Isle of Man and in English stone sculpture as far west as the Halton cross in Lancashire. The manuscript witnesses are thin in the usual way: Reginsmál and its narrative prose stand in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda, Snorri's account in the codices of the Prose Edda, and Völsunga saga in the paper manuscript NKS 1824 b 4to (c. 1400), the saga's only complete medieval copy.

phonemes.desc: Short open [a], stressed on the first syllable as in most Welsh words; the 'a' of 'cat' opened slightly.
Geminate alveolar nasal [nː], written double and held longer than a single English n.
The letter w is here a full vowel: short high back rounded [ʊ], the 'oo' of English 'put' — never a consonant.
Final alveolar nasal [n], closing the second syllable cleanly.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AN-oon' — two syllables, stress on the first; the w is sounded as a short 'oo', so the name rhymes with 'cannon' said with Welsh vowels.

kin.label: Middle Welsh
kin.form: Annwfn, the spelling of the manuscripts — the f is the voiced [v] of lenited final -m, and the word was often understood as an- + dwfn, “the deep, the abyss”

kin.label: Modern Welsh
kin.form: Annwn, the normalized modern spelling used since the modern period for the Otherworld of the Mabinogi

kin.label: Cognate
kin.form: Welsh dwfn “deep” and Irish domun “world” descend from the same Celtic root *dubno- — the deep beneath, read as the world below ours

kin.label: Etymology
kin.form: an- (negative or intensifying prefix) + dwfn “deep” — “the un-deep, the very deep”; the popular reading “not-world” is a later reinterpretation of the same sounds

pronunciation.note: Annwn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the realm's fame in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Otherworld, Underworld
domains.subtitle: The Deep, the Abyss — realm of the feast and the hunt
domains.lead: Annwn is the Welsh Otherworld of the Mabinogi and the oldest Welsh poetry — a realm of plenty where the feast never fails, ruled in the First Branch by [[arawn|Arawn]], and hunted across by Gwyn ap Nudd, whom God set over the demons of Annwn lest they destroy this world. Its cauldron, borne home from its fortresses at terrible cost, is the oldest quest of Arthurian tradition.

cards.name: The Cauldron of the Head of Annwn
cards.desc: Kindled by the breath of nine maidens, rimmed with pearls, it will not boil a coward's food — the prize of Arthur's voyage in Preiddeu Annwfn.

cards.name: The Hounds of Annwn
cards.desc: Arawn's pack — gleaming white with red ears, the colours the Welsh tradition gives every creature from the Otherworld.

cards.name: Prydwen
cards.desc: Arthur's ship on the voyage to the fortresses of Annwn — three full loads went in; except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.

cards.name: The Hunt of Gwyn ap Nudd
cards.desc: The son of Nudd rides with the hunt of Annwn; in Culhwch ac Olwen, God set him over its demons lest they destroy this world.

symbols.name: The cauldron of Pen Annwn
symbols.meaning: Plenty that will not serve the coward — abundance that answers only to courage

symbols.name: White hounds with red ears
symbols.meaning: The colours of the Otherworld made flesh — beauty that marks the boundary crossed

symbols.name: Caer Sidi and the fortresses
symbols.meaning: The revolving castle and its sister fortresses — the Otherworld as architecture that must be won, not visited

symbols.name: Prydwen
symbols.meaning: Arthur's ship — the voyage into the deep from which only seven returned

symbols.name: The year's exchange
symbols.meaning: Arawn and Pwyll trading shapes and kingdoms — the Otherworld close enough to wear a man's face

mythology.lead: Annwn is named in the very first pages of the Mabinogi and in the most difficult poem of early Welsh tradition. Its dossier is small and immense: a king who trades his shape, a cauldron that will not boil a coward's food, a hunt that keeps the world's demons leashed — and, behind all three, the deep itself.

myths.title: The Year in Annwn
myths.text:
Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, is hunting in Glyn Cuch when he drives a strange pack off a stag — hounds gleaming white, with red ears, the colours of the Otherworld — and feeds his own dogs on the kill. Their master rides up: [[arawn|Arawn]], a king of Annwn, and the offense is real. To make amends Pwyll accepts Arawn's bargain: for a year and a day they will exchange shapes and kingdoms, and at the year's end Pwyll must face Arawn's rival Hafgan — a king who can be killed by a single blow only; strike him twice and by the next day he fights as strongly as before.

Pwyll rules Annwn for the year in Arawn's likeness, in a court of unsurpassed plenty — and each night lies beside Arawn's queen without once touching her. At the appointed ford he strikes Hafgan once, refuses the second blow the wounded king begs for, and Annwn is united under Arawn. When the two kings meet again at Glyn Cuch and resume their own shapes, Arawn learns of the year's chastity and the friendship is sealed with gifts of horses, greyhounds, hawks, and gold. From that day Pwyll was called not Pwyll Prince of Dyfed but Pwyll Pen Annwn — Pwyll, Head of Annwn.

myths.title: The Spoils of Annwn
myths.text:
The poem Preiddeu Annwfn, 'The Spoils of Annwfn', preserved in the fourteenth-century Book of Taliesin and spoken in the poet's own voice, is the oldest surviving account of an Arthurian Otherworld raid. Arthur sails in his ship Prydwen against the fortresses of the deep — Caer Sidi, Caer Pedryfan, Caer Wydyr, and the rest — and the refrain tolls after each: 'except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.' Three full loads of Prydwen went into Annwn; seven men came back.

The prize is the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn — kindled by the breath of nine maidens, its rim set about with pearls, and marked by the rule the Welsh tradition fixes on Otherworld vessels: it will not boil the food of a coward. The poem is elliptical, proud, and mournful at once — the poet stands apart from the swordsmen who went in and never came out — but its facts became permanent: the Otherworld has a cauldron, Arthur went to get it, and almost no one returned.

myths.title: Gwyn ap Nudd and the Demons of Annwn
myths.text:
The great hunting catalogue of Culhwch ac Olwen names its most uncanny huntsman: Gwyn ap Nudd, son of Nudd — 'God has set him over the demons of Annwn, lest this world be destroyed.' The hunt of the boar Twrch Trwyth cannot be accomplished without him, and so Gwyn rides out of Annwn at Arthur's muster: the Otherworld's own power, conscripted to keep its worst inhabitants leashed.

The same tale gives Gwyn his famous quarrel. He had carried off Creiddylad, daughter of Lludd, from her father's house, and Gwythyr ap Greidawl raised a host and took her back; Arthur judged between them — the maiden to remain with her father, and the two to fight for her every May Day until the Day of Judgment, when the winner takes her for good. Gwyn's hunt is therefore not seasonal sport but a standing order: Annwn's violence rides out under a king who is himself a covenant.

myths.title: The King on Glastonbury Tor
myths.text:
The Welsh Life of St Collen gives Annwn its most local address. Collen, keeping his hermitage under Glastonbury Tor, hears two men say that Gwyn ap Nudd — king of Annwn and of the Tylwyth Teg, the Fair Folk — holds his court above. Collen answers that the hosts of the air are demons; a summons follows, and on the summit he finds a castle of the utmost splendour, the king on a golden chair, and a banquet of dishes he has never seen the like of.

Collen sprinkles his holy water over the food, and the whole vision dissolves — castle, court, and king gone as if they had never been, leaving the saint standing on the green Tor. The tale is late and Christian, but it keeps the old facts in place: Gwyn is king of Annwn, his hall is a feast beyond earthly measure, and the Otherworld can open on a hillside in Somerset and close again without a trace.

annwn.syncretism: Annwn's clearest kin are Irish: the síd of the Túatha Dé Danann, where the feast likewise never fails — the Dagda's cauldron of Murias, from which no company went away unsatisfied, is the standing comparison for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn, and Mac Cana sets the two vessels side by side as one Celtic figure-type. The Irish Otherworld of the immrama and echtrai — Mag Mell, Emain Ablach, lands 'without grief, without sorrow, without death' — matches Annwn's profile point for point: plenty, beauty, and the suspension of age and sickness. Yet the Brythonic tradition is not a copy of the Gaelic one: no Irish text knows the name Annwn, and the Welsh corpus built its Otherworld on its own geography — the ford at Glyn Cuch, the revolving fortresses of the Taliesin poem, the Tor at Glastonbury. The Christian redactors left the structure intact while re-labelling its inhabitants: by Buchedd Collen, Gwyn ap Nudd's splendid court could be dismissed as a demonic glamour without surrendering one detail of the feast.
annwn.culturalLegacy: Preiddeu Annwfn stands at the head of the Arthurian tradition: the raid on the Otherworld fortresses is older than every romance of the Grail, and scholars from Loomis onward have read the quest for the Head of Annwn's cauldron — a vessel of plenty that tests the worthy — as the Grail story's deepest Welsh root. The name kept working in Welsh: Annwn remains the living word for the Otherworld, and the white red-eared hounds became the Cŵn Annwn of later Welsh folklore, the pack whose crying in the night sky foretells a death. Gwyn ap Nudd rode out of the texts into modern Druidry and pagan practice as the great huntsman and psychopomp of the Welsh tradition, and Glastonbury Tor — crowned now by the stump of St Michael's tower — still carries his court in the popular imagination. Restoring Annwn in Unicode costs nothing and fixes something: the canonical spelling of the deep, held against the drift of anglicized spellings like Annwvyn and Annwyn.
annwn.extendedMeditation:
Annwn is the rare Otherworld whose name tells you where it is: an- + dwfn, the un-deep, the very deep — not a land over the sea or under a hill but the depth beneath the world, the place the surface world is the skin of. The tradition never pretends it is far away. Pwyll stumbles into it on an ordinary hunt by breaking an ordinary courtesy; it lies a year's shape-shift away, close enough for two kings to trade faces and governments across it.

And its gifts all carry a price exacted in courage. The feast is boundless, but the cauldron will not boil a coward's food; the voyage is possible, but except seven none returned; the hunt rides out, but it rides to keep the demons of the deep leashed for the world's sake. Annwn is the Celtic imagination's answer to the question of what lies underneath: plenty without limit, behind a door that only opens once — and a word for it, five plain letters, that still means the deep.
annwn.originalScriptNote: Welsh has been written in the Latin alphabet throughout its manuscript history, and the normalized form Annwn is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. The manuscripts spell the name Annwfn (Middle Welsh f writes the voiced [v]); the modern normalized spelling is Annwn. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: annwn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed (First Branch of the Mabinogi) — the meeting at Glyn Cuch, the year's exchange, the defeat of Hafgan, the title Pen Annwn; ed. Ifor Williams, Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930); trans. Sioned Davies, The Mabinogion (2007)

Preiddeu Annwfn (The Spoils of Annwfn), Book of Taliesin — Arthur's voyage in Prydwen, the fortresses, the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn, 'except seven, none returned'; ed. and trans. Marged Haycock, Legendary Poems from the Book of Taliesin (2007)
Culhwch ac Olwen — Gwyn ap Nudd set over the demons of Annwn; the May Day fight with Gwythyr for Creiddylad; ed. Rachel Bromwich and D. Simon Evans (1992)
Buchedd Collen (The Life of St Collen) — Gwyn ap Nudd's court on Glastonbury Tor and the banquet dispelled by holy water
Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru / A Dictionary of the Welsh Language, s.v. annwfn ('the otherworld, the abyss')

Mac Cana, Celtic Mythology; Koch, Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia, s.v. Annwfn; MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology, s.v. Annwn (lexicon authorities for this entry: Mabinogion, MacKillop)

annwn.archaeology: Annwn is a wholly textual realm: no inscription invokes it, and the Romano-British epigraphy of Wales is silent on the Otherworld by name. Its manuscript witnesses, however, are exact. The Mabinogi survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1400), the two great codices of medieval Welsh prose; Preiddeu Annwfn is preserved uniquely in the Book of Taliesin (National Library of Wales, Peniarth MS 2, early fourteenth century); and Culhwch ac Olwen comes down in a White Book fragment and the full Red Book text. The one site the tradition ties to Annwn is Glastonbury Tor, Gwyn ap Nudd's seat in Buchedd Collen: excavations on the Tor in the 1960s found sub-Roman and early medieval occupation beneath the ruins of St Michael's church — real archaeology on the hill, though none of it speaks to the Otherworld, whose only true location is the text.

phonemes.desc: Unstressed short open [a], the light first syllable; Welsh stress has not yet fallen.
Trilled or tapped [r] followed by the Welsh diphthong aw [aʊ] — the 'ow' of English 'town'; this is the stressed penult that carries the whole weight of the name.
Final alveolar nasal [n], closing the stressed syllable cleanly.

pronunciation.approximation: 'a-ROWN' — the aw sounds like the 'ow' of 'town', and the stress falls on the second syllable, the Welsh penult.

kin.form: Arawn, a rare but living given name.

kin.label: Welsh folklore
kin.form: Master of the Cŵn Annwn, the white red-eared hounds of the Otherworld — a folk elaboration of his Mabinogi pack.

pronunciation.note: Arawn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The lexicon's traditional gloss is 'silver-tongued', but the etymology is genuinely unsettled: scholars have proposed a learned borrowing of the biblical Aaron (a suggestion going back to Ifor Williams) as well as native Celtic derivations, and no derivation commands consensus (Koch; GPC, s.v. Arawn).

domains.title: The King of Annwn
domains.subtitle: Otherworld, Annwn
domains.lead: Arawn is the king of Annwn, the Welsh Otherworld: the lord whose white, red-eared hounds bring down a stag in Pwyll's hunting-ground at Glyn Cuch, and whose answer to the insult is the strangest exchange in the Mabinogi — a year and a day in which two kings trade faces, thrones, and beds, so that honor may be tested where no one is watching.

cards.name: The White Hounds
cards.desc: Arawn's pack, shining white with red ears — the colour of the Otherworld, a sight Pwyll had never seen on any hound of his own.

cards.name: The Exchange of Shapes
cards.desc: A year and a day in which Arawn takes Pwyll's form in Dyfed and Pwyll takes Arawn's in Annwn — and neither court suspects.

cards.name: The Ford
cards.desc: The appointed meeting-place where Pwyll must face Hafgan, king of the other realm of Annwn — with one blow and no more.

cards.name: The Untouched Bed
cards.desc: Arawn's queen, the fairest woman Pwyll had ever seen — with whom he shares a bed for a year and never turns his face to her.

symbols.name: The white hounds with red ears
symbols.meaning: The colour of the Otherworld — a hunt that arrives from the far side of the boundary

symbols.name: The exchanged shape
symbols.meaning: Kingship as a trust held for another: the year Arawn's face ruled two realms

symbols.name: The single blow
symbols.meaning: Restraint as the condition of victory — strike once, or not at all

symbols.name: The untouched bed
symbols.meaning: Honor kept in the dark, where no one would ever have known

symbols.name: The ford

symbols.name: The yearly gifts

mythology.lead: Arawn's whole dossier is one story, and it is the opening movement of the Mabinogi: the hunting-debt at Glyn Cuch and the year-long exchange that turns an insult into the strongest friendship in Welsh prose. Every word of it is preserved in the First Branch, Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed.

myths.title: The Wrong at Glyn Cuch
myths.text: Pwyll, lord of Dyfed, goes hunting at Glyn Cuch, and there he sees a sight he has never seen: a pack of hounds shining white with red ears bringing down a stag. He drives them off and sets his own hounds on the kill — and the stranger who rides up is Arawn, king of Annwn, and it was his hunt. Arawn names the discourtesy plainly: he will not take revenge, but a man who feeds his hounds on another's kill has wronged him, and Pwyll offers to buy back his friendship at whatever price. Arawn names it. He has a rival, Hafgan, king of the other realm of Annwn, who wars on him without end; let Pwyll take Arawn's shape and his place for a year and a day, and meet Hafgan at the ford at the year's turning. The insult that opens the Mabinogi is small; the answer to it is a year's borrowed life, and the tale means to show what a king is made of when the test is set by his enemy and graded by his wife.

myths.title: The Exchange of Shapes
myths.text: Each king takes the other's form and goes to the other's court, and neither realm suspects. Arawn rules Dyfed so well that there had never been so good a year in it. Pwyll enters Annwn in Arawn's likeness, and that first night he is led to the bed of Arawn's wife — the fairest and most comely woman he had ever seen. He turns his back to her, and he does so every night of the year: he speaks to her with courtesy by day, and in the bed he never once turns his face toward her. The queen never knows. The whole test of the tale is here, in the dark, where no one could have seen the difference — and that is exactly the point. The First Branch argues that honor is what a man does when the only witness is himself, and it stakes the argument on a bed no court could inspect.

myths.title: The Single Blow at the Ford
myths.text: Arawn's instructions were exact: Hafgan — the name suggests 'summer-white' — can be slain by one blow, and only one; strike him a second time and he will rise as strong as before and fight again the next day. At the appointed time the two kings meet at the ford, and at the first clash Pwyll strikes Hafgan one blow that shears through his shield and his armour to the ground, and Hafgan knows that he is dead. 'For God's sake,' he begs, 'finish me' — and Pwyll refuses: the stroke he gave is all Hafgan will have from him. Hafgan's nobles declare their king lost, and Pwyll takes the submission and hostages of Hafgan's realm, so that the two kingdoms of Annwn are made one under Arawn's crown. Restraint, the tale says, is the last weapon of the strong: the blow withheld did what no blow could, and won a war with half a sword-stroke.

myths.title: The Restoration and the Title
myths.text: The two kings meet again at the ford where they had arranged it, each in his own shape, and embrace and go home. Arawn's queen, rejoicing at his return, remarks that he has not spoken to her so sweetly for a whole year — and Arawn praises God for a friend so true. In Dyfed, Pwyll's court hears the story and tells him he did well to make such a friend. From that time the two realms send each other gifts every year: horses and greyhounds and hawks, and every kind of treasure they think will please. And because Pwyll had ruled Annwn and joined its two kingdoms in one, he was called from then on Pwyll Pen Annwn — Pwyll Head of Annwn — in place of Pwyll lord of Dyfed. The exchange ends where the best contracts end: both parties richer, neither diminished, and the friendship audited annually in horses, hawks, and hounds.

myths.title: The Hounds and the Spoils of Annwn
myths.text: The Mabinogi never brings Arawn back on stage, but his world keeps growing. The poem Preiddeu Annwfn, 'The Spoils of Annwn', preserved in the Book of Taliesin, sends Arthur's men in three ships to raid the Otherworld for the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn — Pen Annwfn, the very title the First Branch gives Pwyll as an honor — and only seven come home. The poem never names Annwn's king, and honest scholarship leaves him unnamed. Later Welsh folklore knows the Cŵn Annwn, the Hounds of Annwn — white with red ears, exactly Arawn's pack — whose baying across the night sky was heard as a death-omen, and folk tradition gave their mastery to Gwyn ap Nudd rather than to Arawn. The hounds outgrew their first master; the year of the exchange did not. Arawn's afterlife is that of a perfect guest: he appears once, conducts the greatest test in Welsh prose, and is thereafter remembered in the hounds, the title, and the ford.

arawn.syncretism: Arawn's comparisons are almost all inward, and the Welsh corpus itself supplies them. His clearest rival for the kingship of the Otherworld is Gwyn ap Nudd, whom Culhwch ac Olwen says God set over the demons of Annwn — a second king of Annwn in a second text, and the folklore gave Gwyn the hounds that the Mabinogi gave Arawn. The structural reading runs deeper: commentators since Mac Cana have read the Annwn adventure as the proving of Pwyll's character before the coming of Rhiannon — the hero tested in honor and restraint in the Otherworld before the Otherworld's queen chooses him in this one. The name itself may be the tale's one foreign guest: Ifor Williams proposed that Arawn is a learned borrowing of the biblical Aaron, carried into Welsh by Latin learning, and the handbooks register the possibility without deciding it. No Gaulish or Irish counterpart of Arawn has ever been convincingly proposed; the exchange-of-kings motif is the Mabinogi's own.
arawn.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Arawn out of the White and Red Books and into English, and the white red-eared hounds entered the stock of Celtic imagery from that day. In the twentieth century the figure found his widest audience inverted: Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain (1964–68) made 'Arawn Death-Lord of Annuvin' the arch-villain of five children's novels, and Disney's The Black Cauldron (1985) kept the dark-lord version on screen — a long way from the most honorable king in Welsh prose, but the reason the name is known worldwide. The Cŵn Annwn meanwhile never left Welsh folklore, still baying as a death-omen in folk memory into the modern period. Modern Druid and pagan practice honours Arawn as lord of the Otherworld and patron of kept faith, and the name survives in Wales as a rare living given name.
arawn.extendedMeditation: Arawn sets the one test that cannot be cheated: he gives a stranger his face, his throne, and his bed, and waits a year to learn what the stranger is. Everything Pwyll does in Annwn is invisible — no one in either kingdom can tell the kings apart, and no one will ever know what passed in the bed unless the doer confesses it. That is exactly the point. Honor, the First Branch argues, is what a man does when the only witness is himself. The tale rewards it without sentimentality: the kept faith becomes an unbroken friendship, an otherworld alliance, the title Pen Annwfn, and a court that tells its lord he chose his friend well. Arawn's kingdom is the far side of the world, but his question is asked everywhere: who are you when no one is watching?
arawn.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Arawn — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: arawn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/arawn/ in the meantime.

arawn.archaeology: Arawn is a textual figure: no inscription, votive deposit, or cult site names him, and the epigraphic record of pre-Christian Wales — Latin and ogham memorial stones of roughly the fifth to seventh centuries — records personal names, not theonyms. His evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales' date of composition is argued rather than documented — Ifor Williams placed them in the later eleventh century, and current scholarship generally holds a range around 1060–1120. The geography of the tale is real: Glyn Cuch, where the insult happens, is identified with the valley of the River Cych on the Pembrokeshire–Carmarthenshire border, inside the Dyfed the story governs. The nearest material echo of the Otherworld hunt is literary: the Book of Taliesin, the manuscript that preserves Preiddeu Annwfn, is a fourteenth-century Welsh codex (NLW Peniarth MS 2).

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b], broad (velarized) before a; as in English 'bay', with the tongue already set for the wide vowel.
Short open [a], the stressed vowel of the single syllable — the 'ah' of 'father' held brief.
Lenited [ð], the voiced dental fricative of English 'this', running into lenited final [β], a soft bilabial v — both consonants melt in speech though the spelling keeps them whole.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAH-dhuv' — one short syllable; let the d soften into the 'th' of 'this' and the final b melt into a light v. Modern Irish badhbh keeps the softening, and English ears often hear the word as something like 'bave'.

domains.title: Battle, Death, Crow
domains.subtitle: The Scald-Crow of the Battlefield
domains.lead: Badb is the Irish war-goddess whose name is her shape: badb, the scald-crow — the grey-and-black hooded crow that walks the battlefield when the spears have done their work. She is one of the three of war whom the Lebor Gabála calls the daughters of Ernmas — Badb, Macha, and Anand, the Morrígan — and the Táin gives her its most terrible sound: the shriek over the marching hosts that kills men with fear before a blow is struck. She never fights; she foretells, she panics, and she gathers what the battle leaves.

cards.name: Badb Catha
cards.desc: 'Crow of battle' — her standing title in the texts: the bird that haunts the field and the goddess who owns it are one word.

cards.name: The Shriek over the Hosts
cards.desc: At Gáirech and Irgáirech, the Táin says, Badb and Bé Néit and Némain shrieked above the armies until a hundred warriors fell dead of fright.

cards.name: The Ford
cards.desc: The boundary water where the war-goddess stands washing — the Morrígan at the ford of the Unius, the washer of the doomed in the later Gaelic tradition.

cards.name: The Daughters of Ernmas
cards.desc: Badb, Macha, and Anand — the triple face of Irish war, three sisters of one mother whom the sources also call by the single name Morrígan.

symbols.name: The scald-crow

symbols.name: The shriek

symbols.name: The ford

symbols.name: The washing of spoils

mythology.lead: Badb's dossier is genealogy, sound, and omen rather than adventure: she is the sister in the list, the voice over the army, the bird on the pillar-stone. The Lebor Gabála fixes her family, the Táin fixes her weapon, and the death-tales fix her posture — and the commentators have spent a century and a half working out where she ends and her sisters begin.

myths.title: The Daughters of Ernmas
myths.text:
The Lebor Gabála Érenn, Ireland's medieval book of invasions, gives the war-goddesses their pedigree: 'Badb and Macha and Anand, of whom are the Paps of Anu in Luachair, were the three daughters of Ernmas the she-farmer.' The verse recension sings the same family in another key — 'Badb and Macha, greatness of wealth, Morrígu, springs of craftiness, sources of bitter fighting, were the three daughters of Ernmas' — so that the tradition itself is of two minds: sometimes the Morrígan is the third sister, sometimes the single name for all three.

The same book marries her into the house of the war-god. Neit son of Indui, the god of battle, had two wives — Badb and Nemain — and the pedigree records the slaying of the three of them at Ailech by the Fomorians. Cormac's Glossary had already fixed the marriage in the language of record: Neith, the god of battle among the pagan Gael, and Nemon his wife. Badb is never an isolated figure; she is a sister and a wife in a family whose whole business is war.

myths.title: The Shriek over the Hosts
myths.text:
When the men of Ireland march under [[medb|Medb]] for the brown bull of Cooley, the Táin marks the nights of the hosting with the sound of the war-goddesses: 'Badb and Bé Néit and Némain shrieked above them that night in Gáirech and Irgáirech, so that a hundred of their warriors fell dead of fright.' It is the battle's true opening — the killing has begun before a single spear is cast, and its instrument is a voice.

The passage tells you everything about her method. She does not wound; she announces. The shriek over the column is prophecy delivered as noise, the knowledge of the field's end injected into the march at its beginning — and the Irish phrase for the whole business of battlefield terror, badb catha, the crow of battle, is simply her name at work as a common noun.

myths.title: The War-Goddess at Mag Tuired
myths.text:
The Second Battle of Mag Tuired, the war the Túatha Dé Danann fight against the Fomorians, runs on the war-goddess's work from its eve to its aftermath. On Samain night [[dagda|the Dagda]] met the Morrígan at the ford of the Unius in Connacht, where she stood washing with one foot on either bank; they lay together at the ford, and she pledged herself to the Túatha Dé Danann's cause, promising to bring the hearts of the Fomorian host and the blood of their king Indech.

After [[lugh|Lugh]]'s sling-stone felled [[balor|Balor]] and the Fomorians broke, it was the Morrígan who proclaimed the battle and the rout to the royal heights of Ireland and its síd-hosts, and who uttered the great prophecy — 'Peace up to heaven, heaven down to earth, earth beneath heaven' — and then its darker twin, the vision of the world's ending. The commentators note that the texts keep the sisters' voices interchangeable: what the manuscript gives to the Morrígan, the tradition hears also in Badb's register, and the Lebor Gabála had already made them one family.

myths.title: The Crow on the Pillar-Stone
myths.text:
Cú Chulainn's death-tale, Brislech Mór Maige Muirthemni, gives the crow-goddesses the last word over the greatest of the Ulster heroes. Mortally wounded at Muirthemne, [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]] lashed himself to a pillar-stone so that he would die on his feet, and for three days his enemies would not close in, uncertain whether he lived. Then the battle-goddess Morrígu came with her sisters in the form of scald-crows and settled on his shoulder — and Erc said, 'That pillar is not wont to be under birds,' and only then did the host dare approach and take the hero's head.

It is the emblematic scene of her whole dossier: the scald-crow is the signature of death itself, the field's first and final reader. The living man keeps her off; the dead man is her perch.

myths.title: The Washer at the Ford
myths.text:
The medieval texts give the war-goddess her washing-place — the Morrígan washing at the ford of the Unius on the eve of Mag Tuired — and the later Gaelic tradition gives the figure her full shape: the washer at the ford, the woman seen at the boundary water rinsing the blood-stained garments and harness of those about to die in battle. In Scottish Gaelic folklore she is the bean nighe, the washerwoman whose sight foretells death, and the commentators, Mac Cana among them, treat her as the folk continuation of the Badb's own figure.

The washing is prophecy, not threat. The doom is already written — the garments in her hands belong to men still alive and armed — and she merely launders the evidence. No Irish figure holds the moment before death so patiently: not the blow, not the battle, but the foreknowledge, rinsed clean in running water.

badb.syncretism: Badb's clearest cross-border witness is Gaulish, and it is exact. An altar from Mieussy in Haute-Savoie dedicates to Cathubodua — *catu-*bodwā, 'battle-crow' — the precise reverse compound of Irish badb catha. Delamarre and Koch treat the two names as one formation across the Celtic languages: the crow of battle named in stone on the continent and in saga in Ireland. The Welsh corpus, by contrast, is silent on her — no figure of the Mabinogi continues the name, and the Brythonic silence is recorded rather than repaired. Typological comparison has set her beside the Norse valkyries, the raven-feeding choosers of the slain; the handbooks note the parallel without claiming descent. Within the lexicon her closest kin are her own sisters, [[morrigan|the Mórrígan]] and [[macha|Macha]], and the war she prophesied binds her to [[dagda|the Dagda]], [[lugh|Lugh]], and [[nuada|Nuadu]].
badb.culturalLegacy: The crow of battle rode the Celtic revival in English dress. W. M. Hennessy's 'The Ancient Irish Goddess of War' (Revue Celtique, 1870) had already gathered the Morrígan material for scholars, and Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried Cath Maige Tuired and its war-goddesses to a wide reading public, crow-form and prophecy complete. Modern fantasy and games have made the war-goddess's crow-shape one of the stock images of the genre, and contemporary pagan practice honors Badb among the three of the Morrígan. In the Irish language the word never needed reviving: badhbh has meant the hooded crow all along, and the grey bird on the battlefield needed no gloss for any Irish hearer. Across the water, the Scottish bean nighe kept her folk shape washing at the ford deep into the era of the great folklore collections.
badb.extendedMeditation:
Badb is the rare theonym that refuses to be a metaphor: the word for the bird and the name of the goddess are one, and the medieval writers never felt the need to choose between them. To name her is already to say what she does. Other gods have attributes; she has a species — the grey scald-crow that comes down to the field when the field is finished, and the texts simply ask us to understand that the bird knew all along.

Her power is the moment before. In no surviving text does she strike a blow: she shrieks over the marching column, washes at the boundary water, settles on the pillar-stone — the goddess of foreknowledge and of aftermath, of everything in a battle except the fighting. That is not a small dossier but a strange and exact one: she is what war feels like to those who already know its end. The name keeps the question open in every grey bird on a fence-post: if you could see the end of the day at its beginning, what would you do with the hours between?
badb.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Badb — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: badb.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

badb.archaeology: Badb is a textual goddess: no ogham stone names her, no votive inscription invokes her, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. Her manuscript witnesses are exact. The Táin Bó Cúailnge survives in its oldest recension in Lebor na hUidre, the Book of the Dun Cow (Royal Irish Academy, c. 1100), and in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster; Lebor Gabála Érenn likewise rests on the Book of Leinster and its sister codices; and Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, the basis of Gray's edition. The nearest epigraphic witness is continental: the altar from Mieussy in Haute-Savoie dedicating to Cathubodua, 'battle-crow', is the standing proof that the crow-of-battle compound is old Celtic and not an Irish literary invention — comparative evidence across the water, never an identification.

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b], broad (velarized) before a; as in English 'bay' but with the back of the tongue raised.
Short open [a], the stressed vowel of the first syllable — the 'ah' of 'father' held brief.
Broad (velarized) lateral [l̪ˠ], the dark Irish l with the tongue toward the teeth and the back raised — never the light l of English 'leaf'.
Short [o] closing on a broad trilled or tapped r [rˠ]; the second syllable unstressed, as in all Old Irish words stressed on the first.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAH-lor' — stress the first syllable hard, keep the l dark and broad, and let the final r stay tapped. Modern Irish 'Balor' keeps essentially the same shape.

domains.title: The King of the Evil Eye
domains.subtitle: The Venomed Gaze, the Fomorian Tribute, the Fortress of Tory, the Grandson's Stone
domains.lead: Balor — Balor Béimnech, 'Balor of the Mighty Blows' — is king of the Fomorians, the sea-borne oppressors of medieval Irish tradition, and owner of the most feared weapon in the whole corpus: a single eye so venomed by the fumes of a druids' brew that no army could stand before its gaze. Grandfather of Lugh and doomed by that very grandson's sling-stone at Mag Tuired, he is the Irish tradition's great figure of destructive sovereignty — power that poisons its possessor and is answered, in the end, by his own blood.

cards.name: The Venomed Eye
cards.desc: One eye, poisoned in boyhood by the fumes of a druids' charm-brew; any army it looked upon was worthless, though it were many thousands strong.

cards.name: The Fomorian Tribute
cards.desc: Under Balor and Indech the Fomorians taxed Ireland from the sea, and set the very gods to serf-work until Mag Tuired broke the yoke.

cards.name: The Tower of Tory
cards.desc: In the Donegal oral tradition, the sea-girt tower where Balor prisoned his daughter Eithne against the prophecy of a grandson's hand.

cards.name: The Grandson's Stone
cards.desc: Lugh's sling-stone at Mag Tuired drove the eye backward through Balor's head, so that its own gaze blasted the Fomorian host.

symbols.name: The venomed eye
symbols.meaning: A weapon the owner cannot aim without an army to raise the lid — power that outgrew its possessor.

symbols.name: The polished lid-lifter
symbols.meaning: Four men with a handle passed through the eyelid — kingship reduced to machinery, a gaze other men must operate.

symbols.name: The tower of Tory
symbols.meaning: The sea-girt prison built against a prophecy — the fortress that made the doom it feared.

symbols.name: The Glas Gaibhnenn
symbols.meaning: The grey-green cow Balor stole from Cian in the oral tradition — the theft that set the grandson's birth in motion.

symbols.name: The sling-stone
symbols.meaning: The small, aimed answer to the vast, unaimed gaze — the grandson's hand the druids foretold.

mythology.lead: Balor's dossier is short and total: he exists in the tradition to be the thing that must be brought down. Cath Maige Tuired gives him the war's most famous single stroke, the Lebor Gabála fixes his lineage and his wife's vengeance, and the Donegal oral tradition supplies the prophecy, the tower, and the stolen cow that the medieval manuscripts only glance at. The sources disagree on the details and never on the architecture: a gaze that can only destroy, contained at terrible cost, and turned home at last by his own blood.

myths.title: Balor Son of Dot, Grandson of Nét
myths.text: The book of invasions fixes Balor's place before it tells his deeds: Balor mac Doit meic Néit, 'Balor son of Dot, grandson of Nét', king of the Fomorians — the sea-going race who had pressed on Ireland since the age of the Nemedians, exacting tribute from the outer islands. His wife was Cethlenn of the crooked teeth, whose spear struck the Dagda at Mag Tuired; the Lebor Gabála records that the All-Father afterwards died of Cethlenn's wound — the settled price of Balor's war, long counted in the tally of the battle. His daughter was Ethniu, and by Cian — in the Lebor Gabála's genealogy the son of the healer Dian Cécht — she bore Lugh, the Samildánach, equally skilled in all the arts. Thus the Fomorian king was the grandfather of the Túatha Dé Danann's deliverer: the genealogy on which the whole tragedy of Mag Tuired turns, and the reason no tower, sea, or tax could keep the grandson away.

myths.title: How the Eye Was Poisoned
myths.text:
Cath Maige Tuired explains the weapon before it uses it. Balor had a destructive eye, never opened except on a battlefield, and four men were needed to raise its lid with a polished handle that passed through it; any army that eye looked upon was made worthless, though it were many thousands strong.

The poison had a childhood. When Balor was a boy, his father's druids were brewing a charm, and the boy looked in on the work; the fumes of the brew rose and struck the eye, and from that day its gaze was venom. The detail is the tradition's whole theory of the figure in one image: power taken in unguarded, as a child takes in smoke, and carried incurably for a lifetime. What entered by accident becomes the foundation of a tyranny — and a tyranny that must hire four men to open its own weapon has already told you how it will end.

myths.title: The Tower and the Prophecy
myths.text:
The manuscripts agree that Ethniu was Balor's daughter and Lugh's mother; how that came to be is told by the oral tradition of the north-west, collected in the nineteenth century on and around Tory Island — Balor's sea-girt fortress off the Donegal coast. A druid foretold that Balor would die by the hand of his own grandson, and the king answered the prophecy with masonry: he locked his daughter Eithne in a tower on the rock, with twelve matrons to keep every man from her sight.

The doom came in by the door the theft opened. Balor coveted the Glas Gaibhnenn, the grey-green cow of Cian, and stole her across the water; Cian crossed to Tory for redress, and with the druidess Biróg's aid won into the tower in woman's dress and to Eithne's side. When the child was born Balor had him cast into the sea — but the sea gave him back, fostered and hidden, until a young stranger came to Nuadu's court at Tara and was asked what art he practiced. The question the Fomorians could not answer had been growing up under their own doom all along.

myths.title: The Sling-Stone at Mag Tuired
myths.text:
At the second battle of Mag Tuired the armies broke each other all day, and then Balor came against the Túatha Dé Danann with the Fomorian host, destroying and slaughtering. He commanded that the lid of his eye be raised, so that he might blast the enemy with its look — and the four men set the polished handle to the lid.

It was then that Lugh cast a sling-stone at him, which carried the eye backward through his head, so that it was his own host that looked into it. Balor fell on top of the Fomorian fighting-men, and twenty-seven of them died beneath his side. The weapon the Fomorians had built their tyranny on spent its last gaze on its owners — and the battle turned with the eye. The Túatha Dé Danann took back the tribute from the defeated host, and the power of the Fomorians over Ireland was broken for good. A gaze made to wither enemies had met the one thing it could not wither: a small stone, aimed.

balor.syncretism: Balor's clearest cross-border witnesses are comparative, not cognate. The Welsh corpus preserves no figure derived from the same name — the Brythonic silence is total, as it is for so many of the Fomorian cycle. The parallels the scholarship actually leans on are typological. First, the Greek Acrisius: the king who prisoned his daughter Danaë because a prophecy named her son his slayer, and died by that grandson Perseus all the same — the Eithne tower is the same tale-shape, and comparatists have set the two side by side since the nineteenth century. Second, the one-eyed monster answered by aimed cunning — the Polyphemus pattern — where the single enormous eye is both the ogre's strength and the one place he can be struck. Third, and nearest home, the Irish and Mediterranean complex of the evil eye itself: the belief that a look can wither cattle, milk, and men, which Sjoestedt and Mac Cana both treat as the living folk-ground of Balor's venomed gaze. O'Rahilly read him further, as a figure of death and the western sea; the handbooks register the reading without making it doctrine.
balor.culturalLegacy: Balor entered the modern world through two doors. The first was scholarship: Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried the sling-stone and the tower into English reading, and O'Rahilly's Early Irish History and Mythology (1946) made him the type-case of the Irish death-king — a scholarly afterlife as large as his medieval dossier is short. The second was the folklore itself: the Donegal oral versions — the tower, the stolen cow, the child cast into the sea — were collected in the nineteenth century and never stopped being retold, and 'Balor of the Evil Eye' remains the standing name of the figure in Irish and in English. In the modern imagination he has become the Celtic dark lord par excellence: the remote tyrant in his island fortress whose one weapon poisons everything it touches, answered not by a greater weapon but by the prophesied grandchild the fortress was built to prevent. Tory Island keeps his address; the Irish language never lost his name.
balor.extendedMeditation:
Every part of Balor's story is about containment failing. The eye is contained — cloaked, lidded, lifted only by machinery — and containment is the whole catastrophe: a gaze so dangerous it must be operated by four other men is no longer a weapon but an occupation, a king reduced to the caretaker of his own poison. The daughter is contained in a tower against a prophecy, and the tower is the prophecy's instrument: no tower, no Cian, no Lugh. Balor is the tradition's purest study of power that can only destroy — he is given no craft, no counsel, no feast, no children worth the having, nothing but the eye and the tax it enforces.

And the answer the tradition gives him is exact. Not a bigger eye, not a stronger king, but a sling-stone: small, aimed, and thrown by the one hand the whole machinery existed to forestall. The venom that could wither an army is turned in a single instant into the Fomorians' own epitaph — it was his own host that looked into it. That is the Irish judgment on the evil eye, and on every power built to wither rather than to make: it ends by looking inward. The grandson does not defeat the weapon. He simply turns it around.
balor.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Balor — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: balor.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired), ed. and trans. Elizabeth A. Gray — the poisoned eye and its boyhood origin; the four lid-lifters; the sling-stone and the fall on the Fomorian host
Lebor Gabála Érenn, ed. and trans. R. A. S. Macalister — Balor mac Doit meic Néit; Cethlenn and the Dagda's death-wound; the Fomorian tribute

The Donegal oral tradition of Balor on Tory Island — the tower of Eithne, the Glas Gaibhnenn, the child cast into the sea (collected versions: O'Donovan's note in the Annals of the Four Masters, 1856; Curtin, Hero-Tales of Ireland, 1894; Larminie, West Irish Folk-Tales and Romances, 1893)

Koch, ed., Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia, s.v. Balor, Cath Maige Tuired, Fomorians
Gregory, Lady Augusta, Gods and Fighting Men (1904) — the revival retelling of the tower and the sling-stone
Dictionary of the Irish Language (eDIL) — the name and its manuscript forms

balor.archaeology: Balor is a textual and oral figure: no ogham stone names him, no votive inscription invokes him, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. His manuscript witnesses are exact — Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, the basis of Gray's edition, while Lebor Gabála Érenn is preserved in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster and its sister codices. His geographical anchor is one of the most dramatic pieces of coastline in Europe: Tory Island (Toraigh), nine miles off the Bloody Foreland of Donegal, whose cliffs and sea-stacks — above all the great rock called Tór Mór — the oral tradition names as Balor's fortress and the site of Eithne's tower. The nineteenth-century collectors who wrote the tower story down were recording a living Donegal tradition anchored to those rocks, and the island's medieval monastic remains and round tower have kept the name in continuous local memory.

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b], fully voiced in Old Norse initial position, as in English 'bow'.
The falling diphthong [ɑu] — open back vowel gliding to rounded u, like the 'ow' of English 'cow'; the Old Norse diphthong that later Icelandic monophthongized.
Voiced velar fricative [ɣ] between vowels — not a hard stop: Old Norse g softens medially to a breathy glide, here palatalized before i toward something close to English 'y'.
Short high front [i], unstressed final syllable, as in the last beat of 'happy'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BOW-yee' — the first syllable rhymes with English 'cow', and the medial g is not a stop but a soft voiced glide between the vowels, so the second syllable lands almost like 'yee'.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Baugi, the jötunn brother of Suttungr, named in Skáldskaparmál and listed among the giants in the þulur.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛒᛅᚢᚴᛁ — the Viking-Age runic rendering, transliterated b-au-k-i; the k-rune writes the g, and no rune marks the medial fricative the manuscripts spell with g.

kin.label: Word-kin
kin.form: baugr, the Old Norse masculine noun 'ring, circlet' — the word to which the name is usually, though not securely, connected; it also stands in baugeiðr, 'ring-oath', the very oath Hávamál accuses Óðinn of breaking in this story.

pronunciation.note: Baugi is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter, nothing for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The tier reports the name's orthography, not the figure's standing; the corpus names him in one story and one list, and both are written in unbroken Latin letters.

domains.title: Giant, Brother of Suttungr
domains.subtitle: The Keeper of the Door at Hnitbjǫrg
domains.lead: Baugi is the giant who holds the one door that matters in the story of the mead of poetry: brother to Suttungr, who hoards the mead inside the mountain Hnitbjǫrg, and master of the nine thralls whose deaths open the way to Óðinn's bargain. He is the hinge of the whole theft — the labour-contractor, the reluctant accomplice, and the would-be cheat whose auger-stroke misses a snake by an inch.

cards.name: Hnitbjǫrg
cards.desc: The mountain — its name plausibly 'the clashing rocks' — inside which Suttungr shut the mead of poetry, with his daughter Gunnlǫð set to guard it. Baugi's auger makes the only door it ever had.

cards.name: Rati
cards.desc: The auger Óðinn puts in Baugi's hands — 'the traveller', from the verb rata. Baugi bores the tunnel with it, and nearly ends the story with one stroke of it.

cards.name: The Whetstone
cards.desc: The sharpening stone Óðinn tosses among Baugi's nine mowing thralls; in scrambling to claim it they cut each other's throats, and Baugi is left with a harvest and no hands.

cards.name: The Mead of Poetry
cards.desc: Kvasir's blood brewed with honey, held in Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són — the drink that makes a poet or a sage of whoever tastes it, and the prize the whole bargain is for.

symbols.name: Hnitbjǫrg
symbols.meaning: The mountain of the mead — hoard and fortress in one, opened by craft rather than force

symbols.name: Rati
symbols.meaning: The auger that gnaws through stone — the tool that makes the door, and nearly the weapon that closes the story

symbols.name: The whetstone
symbols.meaning: Óðinn's thrown bait — the small object whose coveting empties Baugi's fields of nine workers at a stroke

symbols.name: The nine thralls' scythes
symbols.meaning: The harvest-tools honed too well — honest labour's edge turned into mutual death by one act of sharpening

symbols.name: Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són
symbols.meaning: The three vessels of the mead — 'heart-stirrer', 'vessel', and 'reconciliation' — emptied in three draughts

mythology.lead: Baugi's entire mythology is one episode, and it is the most consequential single episode in the mythology of poetry: the mead heist of Skáldskaparmál. He appears only there and in the þulur of giant-names — a figure the tradition needed once, at the one door, and never again. But that once is the door through which all skaldic poetry claims to have come.

myths.title: The Mead Comes to Hnitbjǫrg
myths.text:
The story begins before Baugi enters it. From the peace-making of Æsir and Vanir is made Kvasir, wisest of beings; the dwarfs Fjalar and Galar kill him and brew his blood with honey into a mead that makes a poet or a scholar of whoever drinks it, keeping it in three vessels — Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són. The dwarfs then drown the giant Gilling at sea and kill his wife with a millstone, and Gilling's son Suttungr takes revenge: he sets the dwarfs on a tide-washed skerry, and they buy their lives with the mead. Suttungr carries it home, shuts it inside the mountain Hnitbjǫrg, and sets his daughter Gunnlǫð to guard it.

Only now does Snorri bring Baugi on stage, in a single sentence of genealogy: Suttungr had a brother, and his name was Baugi. The hoard is sealed, the guard is set, and the god who wants the mead does not go to its owner — he goes to the owner's brother.

myths.title: The Whetstone and the Nine Thralls
myths.text:
Óðinn comes walking to Baugi's land calling himself Bǫlverkr, 'Evil-doer' — a name that is not a disguise so much as an announcement. Nine of Baugi's thralls are mowing hay. Bǫlverkr offers to sharpen their scythes, and the whetstone he pulls from his cloak hones so well that all nine want to buy it. He says it will be sold dearly, and throws it up among them; in the scramble to catch it, each thrall swings his scythe at another's neck, and all nine lie dead in the field.

That evening Bǫlverkr lodges with Baugi, and Baugi pours out his troubles: his nine thralls are dead and the hay harvest stands uncut. The god has engineered the vacancy he is about to fill — the labour shortage is the lock, and he made it himself.

myths.title: Nine Men's Work for One Draught
myths.text:
Bǫlverkr makes the offer: he will do the work of nine men through the summer, and his wage is one drink of Suttungr's mead. Baugi is careful here, and Snorri gives him the one honest line in the story: he answers that the mead is not his to give — Suttungr alone has control of it — but he will go with Bǫlverkr and they will try together whether they can get it. The bargain is struck: a summer's labour against a hope, with Baugi as broker.

Bǫlverkr does the work of nine all summer. When winter comes they go to Suttungr and Baugi puts the case — and Suttungr refuses flatly: not one drop of the mead. Baugi's brokerage has failed on its stated terms; what remains is the attempt he half-promised, the trying of stratagems.

myths.title: Rati and the Two Blowings
myths.text:
Bǫlverkr now asks Baugi for other ways in, and produces the auger called Rati. Baugi bores into the mountain, and says the hole is through. Bǫlverkr leans down and blows into the bore — and the stone-chips fly back into his face. He knows then, Snorri says, that Baugi meant to betray him: the hole is blind. Baugi bores again, and this time when Bǫlverkr blows, the chips fly inward and away. The tunnel is through.

Bǫlverkr turns himself into a snake and crawls into the hole — and Baugi strikes after him with the auger, and misses. It is the story's tightest instant: the accomplice becomes the assassin at the threshold, and the mead of all poetry hangs on one failed stroke. Inside waits Gunnlǫð; Óðinn lies with her three nights, wins leave for three draughts, and empties Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són entire. Then he rises as an eagle with all the mead in him, Suttungr in eagle-shape hard behind, and the Æsir set out their vats in Ásgarðr's court — Baugi's door standing open in the mountain behind them all.

myths.title: Óðinn's Own Version
myths.text:
Hávamál lets Óðinn boast of the same theft in his own voice, and the differences are instructive. The god names Rati — 'Rati's mouth I made room for me, and it gnawed the rock' — names Gunnlǫð and the golden seat, names Óðrœrir come up among the Æsir. He names Suttungr defrauded of his mead and Gunnlǫð left weeping, and he names the instrument of it: the baugeiðr, the ring-oath Óðinn swore and broke — 'who can trust him?'

But Hávamál never names Baugi. In the god's own telling, the brother at the door has already vanished — the contract, the auger, the missed stroke, all absorbed into Óðinn's solitary cunning. Snorri's prose preserves what the god's boasting omits: that the door had a keeper, that the keeper had a price, and that the keeper tried, at the last moment, to close it on the snake.

baugi.syncretism: Baugi himself has no cross-border reflex — no Old English or continental cognate figure, no cult, no charm; he is a person the Icelandic tradition made for one narrative. The myth he serves, however, sits in one of the oldest comparative dossiers in Indo-European study: the theft of the divine intoxicant. The standard parallel is Vedic — the śyena, the eagle or falcon who snatches the soma and brings it to the gods (Rigveda 4.26–27) — set beside Óðinn in eagle-shape carrying off the mead in his body. The comparison was drawn in the nineteenth century and is still registered, with due caution, in the modern handbooks: Lindow treats the mead myth as the northern member of a genuine inheritance while warning against flattening its specifically Norse machinery — the labour contract, the auger, the broken oath. Baugi's own role belongs to that northern machinery: the intermediary who can be bought, the door that opens from the inside. His closest structural kin in the corpus are the other giants whose households Óðinn penetrates by guile, above all the world of [[suttungr|Suttungr]] itself and the deep giant-lore of [[ymir|Ymir]]'s kin.
baugi.culturalLegacy: Baugi's afterlife is mostly the afterlife of the drink he failed to keep. Skaldic poetry — the entire court-poetry tradition of the Viking and medieval North — called itself by kennings drawn from this myth: Kvasir's blood, the dwarfs' drink, Suttungr's mead, Óðinn's theft, Óðrœrir's wave. Every one of those names is a character in the heist except its doorkeeper; the corpus never minted a 'Baugi's mead'. He survives instead as the specialists' hinge-figure: every scholarly treatment of the mead myth, from Finnur Jónsson to Lindow, must reckon with his two functions — the labour-broker who makes the theft logistically possible, and the wavering accomplice whose bore-hole and auger-stroke are the story's closest brush with failure. In modern retellings of the myth he appears under his name in the better handbooks and in the illustrated Eddas of the Norse revival, always in the same posture: halfway through the mountain, one hand on the auger. The mead myth itself has become the North's great parable of inspiration as something stolen, hoarded, and re-stolen — and the god of poetry, [[bragi|Bragi]], pours out what Baugi could not guard.
baugi.archaeology: Baugi is an entirely textual figure: no runestone invokes him, no picture stone has been convincingly read as the drilling of Hnitbjǫrg, and no place-name or votive deposit carries his name. His attestation is exactly as wide as his story — Snorri's Skáldskaparmál, preserved principally in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (GKS 2367 4to, early fourteenth century), with the Codex Wormianus and Codex Upsaliensis as the other main witnesses, plus his entry in the þulur of giant-names. The mead myth he serves is materially older than its manuscripts: kennings presupposing it — Kvasir's blood, Suttungr's mead, Óðinn's booty — are already at work in ninth- and tenth-century skaldic verse, which proves the story's currency centuries before Snorri wrote it down. Hávamál's telling survives in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270), the same small codex that carries nearly all the mythological poems. The runic record is silent on the theonym, as on nearly all the jǫtnar.
baugi.extendedMeditation: Baugi is the indispensable man nobody remembers. Strip him out and the myth stops cold: without the thralls' deaths there is no vacancy, without the contract there is no access, without the auger in his hand there is no door, and without the door there is no mead — and without the mead, by the tradition's own accounting, there is no poetry at all. Yet he is not a hero of his one story, nor even its villain; he is something rarer in the giant-world of the Eddas, a middleman. He names the limits of his power honestly — the mead is Suttungr's, not mine — and then sells access to what is not his anyway. He helps bore the hole and then tries to kill what crawls through it. The tradition leaves his motives exactly that tangled, and the tangle is the point: every hoard is opened from the inside, by someone whose loyalty is a price rather than a fact. The auger-stroke misses by the width of a snake, and because it misses, poems exist.
baugi.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Baugi — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛒᛅᚢᚴᛁ (b-au-k-i, the k-rune ᚴ writing the g and no rune marking the medial fricative the manuscript spelling preserves). Because the name is pure ASCII, its .com address was registered in the ordinary way and is held outside the PuniCodex collection: no form of the name is currently owned, the plain-ASCII domain is watched for release, and this temple claims none.

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b] plus short open-mid front [ɛ] — the crisp 'bed' of English, with the stress falling here as Welsh stress nearly always falls on the penult.
Voiced dental stop [d] followed by Welsh w, a full vowel here: short close back [ʊ], the 'oo' of 'book' — never the consonant 'w' of English.
Welsh final-syllable y, the close central vowel [ɨ] (southern dialects relax it toward [ɪ]), closed by a tapped or trilled [r] — the syllable that gives the name its un-English ending.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BED-weer' — stress the first syllable; read the w as the vowel 'oo' and the final y as a vowel between 'i' and 'u', with the r lightly rolled.

kin.label: Middle Welsh
kin.form: Bedwyr fab Bedrawc, 'Bedwyr son of Bedrawc' — the standard spelling of the White Book of Rhydderch and Red Book of Hergest texts

kin.label: Medieval Latin
kin.form: Beduerus — Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latinized form, Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136)

kin.label: Old French / English
kin.form: Bedivers, Bedoier — the romance forms from which Malory's Sir Bedivere descends

kin.label: Proto-Celtic (proposed)
kin.form: *Betwo-rīxs, 'birch-king' — Koch's tentative derivation from Welsh bedw, 'birch trees'; a proposal, not a settled etymology

pronunciation.note: Bedwyr is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: medieval Welsh writes the name in plain Latin letters — w and y are vowel-letters in Welsh, but ordinary characters of the Latin alphabet, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII form to lose. Only the capital distinguishes the temple form from the input. The name's meaning is recorded as unknown; Koch's derivation from bedw, 'birch trees', is the standard proposal and remains debated.

domains.title: Knight, One-handed
domains.subtitle: The One-Handed Spearman of Arthur's War-Band
domains.lead: Bedwyr son of Bedrawc is the great companion-hero of the oldest Welsh Arthurian tradition: the warrior who never shrank from any enterprise on which [[kai|Cei]] was bound, the one-handed spearman whose single thrust made a wound equal to nine, and the one man the triads crown with a battle-diadem above the three they name. Before French romance gave Arthur his Lancelot, the Welsh tradition gave him Bedwyr.

cards.name: The Lance of Nine Wounds
cards.desc: His one strange property in Culhwch ac Olwen: his lance would produce a wound equal to those of nine opposing lances — one arm doing the work of nine.

cards.name: The Battle-Diadem
cards.desc: The triad of the Three Battle-Diademed names Drystan, Hueil, and Cei — then adds that one was battle-diademed above all three: Bedwyr son of Bedrawc.

cards.name: Cavall the Hound
cards.desc: In the hunting of Twrch Trwyth, the greatest boar-hunt in Welsh literature, Bedwyr led Cavall — Arthur's own hound.

cards.name: The Wooden Tweezers
cards.desc: On the summit of Pumlumon he and Cei plucked the beard of Dillus the Bearded alive with wooden tweezers — for dead, the bristles would have been brittle, and no other leash could hold the hound Drudwyn.

symbols.name: The one-handed lance
symbols.meaning: A single arm doing the work of nine — prowess measured by what remains, not what is missing

symbols.name: The battle-diadem
symbols.meaning: The triad's crown above the crowned — the one name set over Drystan, Hueil, and Cei

symbols.name: Cavall, Arthur's hound
symbols.meaning: The king's own dog entrusted to his hand in the Twrch Trwyth hunt — trust made visible

symbols.name: The wooden tweezers
symbols.meaning: The impossible instrument for the impossible task — craft serving the quest on Pumlumon

symbols.name: The sword cast back to the water
symbols.meaning: In the later Malorian tradition, Bedivere is the last knight, who returns Excalibur to the lake — loyalty outliving the kingdom

mythology.lead: Bedwyr belongs to the oldest stratum of Arthurian tradition: the Welsh heroic material that predates Geoffrey of Monmouth and the whole romance edifice. His dossier is compact and precise — a poem's roster, a tale's three great episodes, two triads — and across all of it one fact never varies: where Cei goes, Bedwyr goes, and the one-handed man is never the lesser of the pair.

myths.tag: Pa gŵr? · Black Book of Carmarthen
myths.title: The War-Band Remembered
myths.text:
The poem known from its opening line as Pa gŵr yv y porthaur? — 'What man is the gatekeeper?' — is the oldest Arthurian poem in Welsh: preserved in the thirteenth-century Black Book of Carmarthen, and itself composed perhaps centuries earlier. In it Arthur, halted at a fortress gate by the porter Glewlwyd Gafaelfawr, recites the roll of his companions to win entry, and Bedwyr stands in that roll beside Cei and Arthur's son Llacheu — already, in the earliest witness, one of the names Arthur speaks to prove his company.

The poem is fragmentary — it breaks off mid-recitation — but its testimony matters beyond its length: it shows a Welsh Arthurian war-band whose heroes had their own deeds long before Geoffrey of Monmouth drew Arthur into Latin history, and Bedwyr is fixed in that founding generation.

myths.title: The One-Handed Spearman
myths.text:
Culhwch ac Olwen, the earliest full Arthurian prose tale, gives Bedwyr his formal introduction when Arthur calls the companions for the quest of Olwen: Arthur called Bedwyr, 'who never shrank from any enterprise upon which Kai was bound. None was equal to him in swiftness throughout this Island except Arthur and Drych Ail Kibddar. And although he was one-handed, three warriors could not shed blood faster than he on the field of battle. Another property he had: his lance would produce a wound equal to those of nine opposing lances.'

The great court-list earlier in the tale quietly extends the household: Amren son of Bedwyr stands among Arthur's huntsmen, and Eneuawc daughter of Bedwyr among the golden-chained maidens of the Island — the one-handed spearman with a son and daughter woven into the fabric of the court.

myths.title: The Beard of Dillus the Bearded
myths.text:
No leash in the world could hold Drudwyn, the whelp of Greid son of Eri, save one made from the beard of Dillus Farfawc — and the beard was useless unless plucked from him alive with wooden tweezers, for once dead the bristles would turn brittle. As Cei and Bedwyr sat on a beacon cairn on the summit of Pumlumon, 'in the highest wind that ever was in the world', they spied smoke that did not bend with the wind, and found the greatest robber who ever fled from Arthur scorching a wild boar at his fire.

They let him eat his fill and sleep; they shaped the wooden tweezers while he slept; Cei dug a pit beneath him, struck him into it, and together they plucked the beard clean and slew him. The leash was made and delivered to Arthur at Celli Wic — and Arthur answered with an englyn mocking Cei's deed, at which Cei's wrath was so great that the warriors of the Island could scarcely make peace between them, and Cei never again came to Arthur's aid. The episode that shows Bedwyr and Cei at their closest is the tale's own explanation of their company's end.

myths.title: The Sword of Gwrnach and the Cauldron of Diwrnach
myths.text:
For the sword of Gwrnach the Giant, from whose castle no guest had ever returned alive, Cei went in alone under a false craft — the best burnisher of swords in the world — and won Bedwyr admission by a sign: the head of his lance would leave its shaft, draw blood from the wind, and settle on its shaft again. Inside, Cei polished the giant's sword, talked him out of his scabbard, and struck off his head with his own blade; the company despoiled the castle and bore the sword to Arthur's court by the beginning of the year.

In Ireland, for the cauldron of Diwrnach Wyddel, the embassy's request was refused outright — and then Bedwyr arose and seized the cauldron and set it on the back of Hygwyd, Arthur's cauldron-bearer, while Llenlleawg Wyddel caught up Caledfwlch, and they slew Diwrnach and his company and fought their way back to the ship Prydwen, carrying the cauldron off full of Irish treasure. The two episodes are the pair's whole method: Cei's cunning at the gate, Bedwyr's hand on the prize.

myths.title: The Diadem Above the Three
myths.text:
The Welsh triads keep the tradition's compressed memory, and they name Bedwyr twice — both times beside Cei. The triad of the Three Battle-Diademed of the Island of Britain names Drystan son of Tallwch, Hueil son of Caw, and Cei son of Cynyr — and then adds: and one was battle-diademed above all three of them, and that was Bedwyr son of Bedrawc. In the tradition's own arithmetic, the one-handed man outranks the three crowned warriors it had just named.

The second naming is the triad's own joke at the war-band's expense. In the triad of the Three Powerful Swineherds, Drystan son of Tallwch kept the swine of March son of Meirchyawn while the swineherd carried a message to Essyllt — and Arthur and March and Cei and Bedwyr were there, all four, yet did not succeed in getting so much as one pigling, neither by force, nor by deception, nor by stealth. The greatest names in the Island, together, defeated by one watchful man and a herd of pigs.

myths.title: Beduerus at Soissons
myths.text:
Geoffrey of Monmouth, drawing the Welsh heroes into his Latin history of the kings of Britain (c. 1136), makes Bedwyr into Beduerus: Arthur's cupbearer and constable of Normandy, one of the two companions — with Caius the seneschal — closest to the king. In the war against the Roman emperor Lucius, Beduerus falls in the fighting before Soissons — Geoffrey names his killer the giant Ritho of Mount Aravius, whom Arthur afterwards slew in single combat — and Arthur has him carried to Bayeux in Neustria, a city his own ancestors had built, and buried there with great lamentation.

Geoffrey's account is pseudo-history, not Welsh tradition — but it fixed Bedwyr in the Latin chronicle line that Wace and Layamon would follow, and it is the hinge on which the Welsh Bedwyr turns into the Bedivere of European romance: the companion who dies in Arthur's service, far from home, mourned by the king he served.

bedwyr.syncretism: Bedwyr's transmission is the clearest case in the Arthurian corpus of a Welsh hero passing whole into the continental tradition: Welsh Bedwyr becomes Geoffrey's Latin Beduerus, then the Bedivers and Bedoier of Old French romance, and at last Malory's Sir Bedivere — one continuous name-line from the Black Book of Carmarthen to Caxton's print shop. Within Celtic comparison the one-handed warrior who loses nothing of his worth has tempted scholars toward the Irish parallel of [[nuada|Nuadu]] of the Silver Hand, the king who lost his arm at Mag Tuired and ruled again by means of a silver one; the handbooks treat this as a shared Celtic motif of the maimed-but-undiminished champion, not a derivation of one figure from the other. What the Welsh tradition keeps distinct is the pairing: Cei and Bedwyr are a fixed couple — the tradition names them in that order, never the reverse — as elemental a bond in early Welsh Arthurian lore as any kinship.
bedwyr.culturalLegacy: Bedwyr's afterlife runs under a French name. Wace's Roman de Brut and Layamon's Brut carried Geoffrey's Beduerus into the vernacular chronicles; the French romances made him Bedivere, one of the first and last of the Round Table; and Malory gave him the role the whole world now knows — the last knight alive with Arthur after the day of destiny, commanded to cast Excalibur into the water, twice hiding it for its worth and twice rebuked, until at the third throw an arm clothed in white samite rose from the lake, caught the sword, brandished it thrice, and vanished. Tennyson's Idylls of the King sealed the image: it is to Bedivere that the dying Arthur speaks the great consolation — 'The old order changeth, yielding place to new' — before the barge bears him away. Twentieth-century scholarship brought the Welsh original back into view: Bromwich's edition of the triads restored the battle-diadem to Bedwyr son of Bedrawc, and the standard handbooks now present the romance Bedivere as what he is — a Welsh heroic companion who had served Arthur in Welsh for perhaps three hundred years before French poetry ever heard of him. In Wales itself the name never left: Bedwyr remains a living Welsh given name.
bedwyr.extendedMeditation:
Bedwyr is the tradition's proof that loss is not the measure of a man. The texts hand him to us already one-handed — the wound is never narrated, never mourned, never explained — and then spend every remaining line insisting on the arithmetic of what is left: one arm that sheds blood faster than three warriors, one lance that wounds like nine, one diadem above the three crowned. The silence about the missing hand is the point: the Welsh tradition does not tell a story about a maimed warrior; it tells stories about the swiftest, surest companion Arthur has, who happens to fight with one arm.

And beneath the arithmetic stands the quieter fact: he never shrank from any enterprise on which Cei was bound. The tradition could have made him Arthur's mirror or Cei's rival; it made him Cei's shadow instead — the second name in every pair, the hand on the cauldron while the cunning works the gate. Loyalty, in the oldest Welsh telling, is not obedience to the crown but fidelity to a companion: the willingness to sit in the highest wind in the world, on a cairn on Pumlumon, because that is where the quest requires the two of you to sit.
bedwyr.originalScriptNote: Medieval Welsh was written in the Latin alphabet, and the manuscripts write the name Bedwyr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; Welsh w and y are vowel-letters, but ordinary Latin characters. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: bedwyr.com is held outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.
