kin.form: Efnisien, son of Euroswydd and Penarddun, in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest

kin.label: Modern Welsh
kin.form: Efnisien, the standard modern spelling

kin.label: The named opposite
kin.form: Nisien, his brother — the tale presents the two as one contrast: peace-maker and strife-maker

kin.label: English translations
kin.form: Efnisien (Guest), Efnysien — the same name carried into English prose

pronunciation.note: Efnysien is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Middle Welsh manuscript form is written in plain Latin letters, and normalized Welsh orthography attaches no diacritic to the name — there is nothing for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the figure's weight in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Trouble, Mischief
domains.subtitle: The Strife-Maker of the Second Branch, and the Cauldron He Died Breaking
domains.lead: Efnysien is the destroyer of the Mabinogi: introduced by the Second Branch in a single balanced sentence — his brother Nisien could make peace between two armies at their most embittered; Efnysien could make two brothers quarrel when they loved each other best. One act, the maiming of the Irish king's horses, sets two kingdoms on the road to ruin; his last act, breaking the Cauldron of Rebirth, ends the slaughter.

cards.name: The Maimed Horses
cards.desc: At the wedding feast of Aberffraw, in a rage that no one had asked his consent, he cuts the lips, ears, tails, and eyelids of Matholwch's horses — the insult that compensation could not bury.

cards.name: The Cauldron of Rebirth
cards.desc: Pair Dadeni — the vessel Brân gives in compensation: a slain man thrown in today rises tomorrow a fighting man, but speechless. Efnysien dies stretching it to pieces.

cards.name: The Hundred Bags
cards.desc: In the great house the Irish built for Brân, a hundred armed men hide in flour-bags hung on the pillars. Efnysien walks the row, asks what is in each bag, and crushes a skull through the sacking with his fingers.

cards.name: The Boy in the Fire
cards.desc: At the peace feast his nephew Gwern — Branwen's child, newly made king — goes from lap to lap; at Efnysien's lap he is seized and thrown into the flames. After that there is no peace to be made.

symbols.name: The mutilated horses
symbols.meaning: Pride made visible — an insult so literal that no payment could make the injured king forget it

symbols.name: The Cauldron of Rebirth (Pair Dadeni)
symbols.meaning: War stripped of death's limit — the gift that became a weapon, until the one who broke it broke himself

symbols.name: The flour-bags on the pillars
symbols.meaning: Treachery hidden in hospitality — seen through only by the man whose own mind worked that way

symbols.name: Gwern cast into the flames
symbols.meaning: The murder of the heir at the moment of his investiture — the point past which the tale permits no return

symbols.name: The broken heart
symbols.meaning: His only death-wound: he stretched himself inside the cauldron until it burst into four pieces, and his heart broke with it

mythology.lead: Efnysien belongs to one tale and fills it: the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr. The branch is the story of a compensation that failed, and Efnysien is the reason — twice over the author of the injury, and at the end the author of the only sacrifice that stopped the ruin.

myths.title: The Two Brothers
myths.text: The tale introduces him by contrast. Penarddun ferch Beli, mother of Brân the Blessed, Branwen, and Manawydan by Llŷr, bore two sons to Euroswydd: Nisien and Efnysien. Of Nisien the branch says he was a good man and a gentle youth, who could bring peace between two armies at their most embittered; of Efnysien it says he would set two brothers at strife when they loved each other most. The balance of the phrasing is deliberate — peace between armies set against strife between brothers, the public against the intimate, and the intimate wins. The narrator does not call Efnysien evil; he says only what the man did to love: he could unmake it, at will, and did. The whole Second Branch is the working-out of that one sentence, and it will never once pause to explain how a woman of Beli's line and Llŷr's house came to bear such a son.

myths.title: The Maiming of the Horses
myths.text: When Brân gave his half-sister Branwen to Matholwch, king of Ireland, the wedding feast was held at Aberffraw, and the horses of the Irish king were stabled for the night. Efnysien asked why they were there, and was told they belonged to Matholwch, who had married his sister. 'Is this what they have done with a maiden as fine as her, my own sister — given her away without asking me?' In his rage he went under the horses and cut off their lips to the teeth, their ears to the head, their tails to the rumps, and their eyelids to the bone. Matholwch rose in silence and made for his ships; only Brân's embassy — Manawydan among them — and the offer of honour-price brought him back: a silver staff as tall as himself, a gold plate as broad as his face, fresh horses, and the Cauldron of Rebirth, which Brân had from Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid and Cymidei Cymeinfoll, wanderers who had fled to his court out of Ireland.

myths.title: The Hundred Bags of Flour
myths.text: The compensation did not hold. In Ireland the insult was remembered, Matholwch was shamed by his own nobles, and Branwen was sent to the kitchen with a box on the ear from the butcher every day — until she tamed a starling and sent word across the sea. Brân waded the channel, for no ship could carry him, and lay across the river when the Irish destroyed the bridge: 'He who would be a leader, let him be a bridge.' The Irish sued for terms: the kingship would pass to Gwern, Branwen's son, and they would build Brân a house great enough to hold him — the first house he had ever entered. But in that house they hung a hundred bags, an armed man in each. Efnysien walked the row ahead of the feast, laid his hand on each bag — 'What is in here?' 'Flour.' — and squeezed each head through the sacking until he felt the skull give, a hundred times down the hall.

myths.title: The Boy in the Fire
myths.text: At the feast of reconciliation the boy Gwern was invested as king, and — charming everyone, the branch says — he went from lap to lap among his kinsmen, from Brân to Manawydan to Nisien, until he came to Efnysien's lap. 'Why does my nephew not come to me?' Efnysien asked; and when the boy was put into his arms he seized him by the feet and threw him headlong into the great fire. Branwen would have leapt in after her son, but Brân caught her with one hand and took up his shield with the other, and the hall rose in war. It is the tale's darkest sentence, and its hinge: after Gwern, no negotiation is possible. The branch does not stop to mourn the boy, and it has never once stopped for Efnysien; the child-killer is not given a single word of excuse or grief. That silence is the point — the deed is meant to be looked at straight, and judged.

myths.title: The Breaking of the Cauldron
myths.text: In the battle that followed, the Irish had the advantage that could not be beaten: every night they cast their slain into the Cauldron of Rebirth, and every morning the dead rose as fighting men again — speechless, but unkillable in any final sense. Then Efnysien, seeing the ruin he had made, did the one thing only he could do. He lay down among the Irish dead as if he were a corpse, was thrown into the cauldron with them, and stretched himself out inside it until the vessel burst into four pieces — and his own heart burst with it, and so he died. The branch gives him no speech of repentance and no eulogy: the destroyer ends the war his own hand started, at the price of his life, and the narration passes on. Of the hosts of Britain only seven men came home, bearing Brân's head; Branwen died of a broken heart on the shore of Anglesey and was buried in a four-sided grave on the bank of the Alaw.

efnysien.syncretism: The comparison that follows Efnysien everywhere is with [[loki|Loki]]: the malice inside the house, the sworn kin whose mischief costs the gods their peace, the trickster the tale can neither spare nor save. MacKillop and the handbooks register the parallel as typological rather than genealogical — the Mabinogi's strife-maker is a human prince of the Children of Llŷr, not a god, and his story answers to Welsh concerns: the honour-price, the insult remembered, the compensation that fails. The truer Celtic company is the cauldron-complex: the Cauldron of Rebirth belongs to the same deep stock as the Dagda's cauldron from Murias in the Lebor Gabála Érenn, from which no company went away unsatisfied, and the branch itself gives the vessel an Irish provenance through the fugitive Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid. Within the corpus his closest kin are [[nisien|Nisien]], the brother he was written as the opposite of, and [[matholwch|Matholwch]], the king his pride destroyed; [[manawydan|Manawydan]] and [[taliesin|Taliesin]] are among the seven who carried Brân's head home.
efnysien.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried the Second Branch into the English-speaking world, and Efnysien's maiming of the horses and death in the cauldron became set-pieces of the Victorian Celtic revival. Evangeline Walton retold the branch at full length in The Children of Llyr (1971), the second volume of her Mabinogion tetralogy, and gave him the modern novel's inside view without softening him. His widest-reaching legacy is the cauldron itself: Lloyd Alexander drew the deathless cauldron-born warriors of his Prydain chronicles — The Black Cauldron (1965), filmed by Disney in 1985 — directly from the Welsh matter, where a cauldron that returns the slain to silent service is broken at terrible cost. In Welsh memory the branch left two landmarks: the proverb 'A fo ben, bid bont' — he who would be a leader, let him be a bridge — and Bedd Branwen, the grave by the Alaw where the tradition buried the sister his acts helped kill.
efnysien.extendedMeditation:
Efnysien is what a story looks like when it refuses to flatter anyone — including itself. The Second Branch never explains him. He is not possessed, not wronged first, not mad; the tale simply pairs him with Nisien and lets the contrast stand: what one brother binds, the other unbinds, and the world has both kinds of man in it. His evil is small in scale and total in consequence — a night with a knife in a stable, and two kingdoms bleed for a generation. That is the branch's hardest teaching about trouble: it does not need to be great, only timely, and no compensation is large enough to make an injured king forget.

And then the ending, which the Welsh text declines to call redemption. Efnysien sees what his mischief has cost — the speechless dead rising nightly from the cauldron — and lies down among the corpses of the enemy to be thrown in with them. No one forgives him in the text; no one praises him; the branch records only that the cauldron broke and his heart broke. The destroyer is allowed one act of destruction aimed at destruction itself, and it costs exactly everything he has. The Mabinogi does not promise that the man who sets the fire can put it out. It shows him choosing to burn with it.
efnysien.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as Efnisien — Middle Welsh (Brythonic Celtic), attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), recording material composed centuries earlier. The normalized form writes plain Latin letters with no diacritic, so the restoration Efnysien differs from the ASCII input only in the capital. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: efnysien.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

efnysien.archaeology: Efnysien is an entirely literary figure: no inscription, cult site, or votive deposit names him, and the Welsh theonymic record of the period survives in literature rather than stone. His evidence is manuscript evidence — the Second Branch complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with the tales' composition argued to the later eleventh or early twelfth century. The geography of his story is real and walkable: Aberffraw, the royal court of Gwynedd where the horses were maimed; Harlech, where Brân's court sat; and the shore of Anglesey where the survivors landed. The tradition's one material anchor is Bedd Branwen, a cairn on the bank of the Afon Alaw in Anglesey identified since the Middle Ages with Branwen's 'four-sided grave' — excavated by Frances Lynch in 1969 and found to hold Early Bronze Age cremations, far older than any Mabinogi event: the identification is the folklore, not the archaeology, and it is precisely that honesty the record keeps.

phonemes.desc: The Old Norse diphthong ei, [ɛi]: a glide opening at the short front vowel of 'bed' and closing toward 'ee' — one syllable, never two.
The trilled nominative ending [r], lightly sounded, as in modern Icelandic Eir.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AYR' — one syllable: glide from the e of 'bed' into 'ee', and close with a light trilled r; modern Icelanders say it nearly the same way.

domains.title: Healing, Mercy, Medical Skill
domains.subtitle: The Best Physician of the Ásynjur
domains.lead: Eir is the Norse tradition's one physician: third in Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur, defined by a single superlative — læknir beztr, 'the best of healers' — and named again among the healing maidens of Lyfjaberg in Fjölsvinnsmál. Her name is the common noun for mercy itself.

cards.name: Lyfjaberg
cards.desc: The 'mountain of healing' where Menglöð sits with her maidens — lyf is the Old Norse word for medicinal herbs and remedies.

cards.name: The Nine Maidens
cards.desc: Hlíf, Hlífþursa, Þjóðvarta, Björt, Blíð, Blíðr, Fríð, Eir, and Aurboða — the company Fjölsviðr names at Menglöð's knees.

cards.name: The Holy Place
cards.desc: Fjölsvinnsmál's promise: the maidens protect those who make offering at the sacred stead, and no sickness shall drag them down.

cards.name: The Superlative
cards.desc: Læknir beztr — 'the best physician': the only office Snorri gives her, and the only medical title in the ásynjur catalogue.

symbols.name: Lyfjaberg
symbols.meaning: The mountain of remedies — healing made landscape, the high place where help is found

symbols.name: The nine maidens
symbols.meaning: Protection, brightness, joy, mercy: the named company whose gifts are the inventory of recovery

symbols.name: The altar at the holy place
symbols.meaning: The covenant of Fjölsvinnsmál — sacrifice answered with deliverance from sickness

symbols.name: Menglöð's knee
symbols.meaning: The healing maidens sit at the necklace-glad one's knees — mercy attendant upon splendour

symbols.name: The name itself
symbols.meaning: Eir, 'help, mercy': the remedy and the plea for it in a single word

mythology.lead: Eir has the thinnest dossier of any goddess in the Edda — one superlative in Snorri's catalogue and one stanza-list in the Poetic Edda — and the office both witnesses agree on: she heals. Nothing else about her was ever written down, which is itself a kind of evidence about what the North thought worth recording.

myths.title: The Best Physician
myths.text:
Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur runs like a court roll: Frigg is highest; second is Sága at Søkkvabekkr; and then, without genealogy, marriage, or adventure, the third entry: 'Eir is the third: she is the best physician' — Eir er þriðja: hon er læknir beztr. That is the whole notice. No hall is named, no parentage given, no deed narrated. In a catalogue that finds something to say about every goddess — Fulla's headband, Gefjun's plough, Syn's door-keeping — Eir alone is defined by a profession and a superlative, and the profession is medicine. The detail is precious: the North's pantheon contained, by deliberate placement ahead of figures with far longer stories, an explicit deity of healing.

The absence around the entry is the meaning. Where the catalogue elsewhere dignifies its goddesses with households and histories, Eir needs none: the superlative is the whole theology. To call her the best physician is to say that mercy, in the North, held a rank of its own among the powers — and that whoever made the list knew a pantheon without a physician would be incomplete.

myths.title: The Maidens of Lyfjaberg
myths.text:
The Poetic Edda keeps her second witness in the strangest of its love-quests. Svipdagr, come to win Menglöð, must answer the gate-ward Fjölsviðr riddle for riddle; among his questions is this: what are the maids called who sit at Menglöð's knees in harmony together? Fjölsviðr names nine: Hlíf the protectress, Hlífþursa, Þjóðvarta, Björt the bright, Blíð and Blíðr the blithe, Fríð the fair, Eir, and Aurboða. Then comes the promise that makes the list matter: these maidens will give help if men make offering at the holy place, and no sickness so cruel will seize the sons of men that they cannot free them from it. Menglöð's seat is Lyfjaberg, the mountain of healing — and Eir, 'mercy', stands named in its company.

The scene completes the portrait the catalogue began. Mercy does not work alone: it sits named among protection, brightness, gladness, and peace — the full inventory of what recovery feels like from the inside. And the price of the cure is remarkably modest: an offering at the holy place. The Edda's one medical establishment runs on the honour system.

myths.title: Valkyrie and Kenning
myths.text:
The name has a quieter afterlife in the poets' apparatus. The þulur — the metrical name-lists preserved with the Prose Edda — count an Eir among the valkyrie names, and her name joins the stock of goddess-heiti from which the skalds built their woman-kennings: the handbooks of diction teach that any ásynja-name may stand for 'woman' in the periphrastic style, so that 'Eir of the ale' or 'Eir of the rings' would be, in skaldic currency, simply a woman — any goddess's name being lawful tender in the kenning system. Whether the valkyrie Eir of the þulur and the physician of Gylfaginning are one figure under two aspects or two bearers of a fine name, the sources do not say; Simek registers the double attestation and leaves the door open. What the lists prove is that the name lived in the working memory of the poets — a word for mercy kept ready at the tip of the tongue.

For a goddess defined by a superlative, this is the fitting epilogue: she ends as equipment. A name that means 'help' survives longest not in shrines but in the toolkit of anyone who might need to praise, petition, or remember a woman.

myths.title: The Menglöð Question
myths.text:
Who is the lady of Lyfjaberg whom Eir attends? Menglöð — 'the one gladdened by necklaces' — bears a name that points straight at Freyja, owner of the Brísingamen, and much scholarship has taken Menglöð as a byname or hypostasis of the Vanadís rather than a separate figure; the two poems of Svipdagsmál as a whole have often been read as a fragmentary Freyja-myth. The identification is attractive and unprovable, and the cautious handbooks present it as exactly that. If it holds, then the North's one physician sits in Freyja's own retinue — mercy among the attendants of love, which would make a kind of sense: the Edda elsewhere keeps healing close to the Vanir's domain of life and growth. If it does not, Lyfjaberg keeps its own mistress, and Eir keeps hers.

The question matters less than the asking. A two-sentence goddess has, by the accident of one neighbour's name, drawn a century of philological argument — evidence of how hungrily the tradition's readers have looked for a fuller dossier than Snorri left us.

eir.syncretism: No interpretatio romana ever found Eir a Latin name: the classical authors who mapped the northern gods left her unmentioned, and the medieval Icelandic writers who knew her wrote no equation. Her real company is native. The Germanic world knew healing as a craft guarded by female figures and spoken charms — the Second Merseburg Charm, the one surviving Old High German healing spell with divine names, binds Wodan and the healing of a wrenched foot in a formula that has Norse echoes, and the Edda's own Oddrúnargrátr gives a mortal woman, Oddrún, the role of birth-helper 'come from the southland.' Eir is the divine end of that continuum: the household of healing maidens on Lyfjaberg raised to the rank of ásynja. Modern comparisons with Greek healing deities are analogies of office, not borrowings — the name eir is transparently Norse, the common noun for mercy, and the tradition grew its physician out of its own vocabulary of help.
eir.culturalLegacy: Eir's afterlife is quiet and remarkably alive. The name never died in the North: Eir remains a living Icelandic given name, and its family survives in the everyday verb eira, 'to spare, to show mercy'. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú practice, which keeps few of the lesser ásynjur in regular use, has made room for her precisely because her office is the one every household needs — she is invoked in healing rites as the physician Snorri named. Popular culture reached her through the valkyrie list: an Eir numbered among the valkyries appears in modern games and fiction, usually in the healer's role the þulur and Gylfaginning between them suggest. Her scholarly afterlife is disproportionate to her dossier: the two-sentence goddess of Gylfaginning 35 is the standing proof, cited in every handbook, that the Norse pantheon contained an explicit deity of medicine. A superlative, it turns out, was enough.
eir.extendedMeditation:
Eir is the goddess made of a single word, and the word is mercy. The Edda gives her no story because her name is already the story: eir is what the wounded ask for and what the healer gives — help, clemency, the staying of a hand. Snorri places her third among the goddesses, ahead of figures with far longer dossiers, as if the catalogue itself understood that a pantheon without a physician would be incomplete. Fjölsvinnsmál completes the portrait by giving her a company and a mountain: mercy does not work alone but sits named among protection, brightness, gladness, and peace — the full inventory of what recovery feels like from the inside.

To say her name in Old Norse was already to ask for the one thing medicine and prayer both promise. That the word survived as an ordinary Icelandic verb — eira, to spare — may be the best monument any goddess of the North ever built: not a temple, but a verb that still declines at kitchen tables.
eir.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Eir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛅᛁᚱ (a-i-r, the ᛁ rune writing both e and i, ᚱ the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: eir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 35 (Eir third among the ásynjur, 'the best physician'); Skáldskaparmál þulur (Eir among the valkyrie names)
Poetic Edda: Fjölsvinnsmál, the nine-maidens stanzas (the company at Menglöð's knees; the promise of protection from sickness), in the Svipdagsmál pair
The Second Merseburg Charm (Wodan's healing charm), in Braune-Ebbinghaus, Althochdeutsches Lesebuch
Cleasby-Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. eir ('help, mercy, clemency'); Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, s.v. eir, eira, lyf

eir.archaeology: Eir is an entirely textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit or place-name can be securely claimed for her, and no image is identified as hers. Her witnesses are manuscripts. The Gylfaginning notice survives with the Prose Edda — above all the Codex Regius (GKS 2367 4to, c. 1300) and its sister codices — while Fjölsvinnsmál hangs by a thinner thread: the poem is not in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda at all but is preserved only in seventeenth-century paper manuscripts, and it was nineteenth-century editors who first joined it with Grógaldr as the two halves of Svipdagsmál. The late transmission has made some scholars cautious about the poem's age, but its language and metre are accepted as medieval, and its Lyfjaberg catalogue remains the only narrative context in which the physician of the ásynjur is ever seen at her post.

phonemes.desc: Slender (palatalized) labiodental [fʲ], the Irish f before i — as English 'few' but lighter, the tongue lifted toward the hard palate.
Long close [iː], the stressed vowel — the 'ee' of 'fleece' held long; the digraph io is Irish's ordinary way of writing it before a broad final consonant.
Broad dental nasal [n̪ˠ], the velarized double-n of Irish — the tongue against the upper teeth, heavier than an English n.

pronunciation.approximation: 'FEEN' — one syllable; the f is slender and light, the vowel a long ee, the final nn broad against the teeth. 'Fionn mac Cumhaill' runs roughly 'FEEN mak KOO-il'.

pronunciation.note: Fionn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Irish form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The manuscripts write Find, the modern language writes Fionn, and both are Latin letters; the capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input. The hero's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Hunter, Seer, Leader
domains.subtitle: The Salmon of Knowledge, the Burning of Tara, and the Long Chase of the Fianna
domains.lead: Fionn mac Cumhaill is the great captain of the Fianna, the war-band of young hunters and fighters who held the marches of Ireland between the king's peace and the wild: the boy who burned his thumb on the Salmon of Knowledge and swallowed all wisdom with it, the youth who saved Tara from fire on Samain night, and the aging leader who spent sixteen years pursuing Diarmaid and Gráinne across the country he had sworn to protect.

cards.name: The Salmon of Knowledge
cards.desc: An eo fis — the fish that fed on the nuts of the nine hazels over the well of Segais; whoever ate it would know all things.

cards.name: The Thumb of Knowledge
cards.desc: Burned on the salmon's blister and sucked by reflex — afterward Fionn could chew his thumb and the imbas, the great knowledge, would come.

cards.name: The Magic Spear
cards.desc: The birga Fíacha mac Conga put in his hand at Tara: held with its point to the forehead, its enchantment kept a man awake against Aillén's music.

cards.name: Bran and Sceólang
cards.desc: His two great hounds, born of his own transformed kin — the chase made family, and the Fianna's swiftest trackers.

symbols.name: The salmon of knowledge
symbols.meaning: Wisdom caught in a single instant — meant for another, given by chance, and never returned

symbols.name: The thumb
symbols.meaning: Imbas forosnai, the knowledge that illuminates — knowing held in the body, summoned by the bite

symbols.name: The magic spear
symbols.meaning: The discipline to stay awake when the whole court is lulled — vigilance as a weapon

symbols.name: The hounds Bran and Sceólang
symbols.meaning: The bond of hunter and hunted bound into one kinship — the wild running at the leader's heel

symbols.name: Ben Bulben
symbols.meaning: The boar's mountain in Sligo, where the long pursuit of Diarmaid ended and the water slipped through Fionn's fingers

mythology.lead: Fionn's cycle is the fullest hero-corpus Ireland kept: the Boyhood Deeds that make him wise, the Fenian lays and ballads that make him captain, and the two late romances — the pursuit of Diarmaid and the lay of Oisín — that make him tragic.

myths.title: The Boy in the Wild
myths.text: Fionn's father was Cumhall mac Trénmhóir, captain of the Fianna, who abducted Muirne, daughter of the druid Tadg, when her father refused her. Tadg's appeal brought the king's army, and Cumhall fell at the battle of Cnucha to Goll mac Morna, head of the rival Clann Morna. Muirne bore the child in danger and gave him to two women to rear in secret: Bodbmall the druidess and Liath Luachra the warrior-woman, who raised him in the wild places away from his father's enemies. When the boy grew strong he went openly to his grandfather Tadg and exacted the blood-price for Cumhall — the hill of Allen, Almhain, which would become the Fianna's seat. The women they hid him from gave the world the name by which the manuscripts remember him: the boy they raised was named Demne; the name the world would keep was still swimming in the Boyne.

myths.title: The Salmon of Knowledge
myths.text: Demne came to learn poetry from Finn Éces, Finn the poet, who had waited seven years on the Boyne for the salmon of knowledge — the fish that had fed on the nuts of the nine hazels dropping into the well of Segais, so that all the knowledge of the world was in its flesh. When at last the salmon was caught, the poet set the boy to cook it and forbade him to taste any part of it. A blister rose on the fish's skin; Demne pressed it down with his thumb, burned himself, and thrust the thumb into his mouth — and the knowledge was his. Finn Éces asked the boy his name, heard 'Demne', and told him: Finn is your name now, for it was Finn who was prophesied to eat this salmon. The boy ate what remained, and ever after needed only to chew his thumb to know what was hidden.

myths.title: Aillén and the Burning of Tara
myths.text: Every Samain night for twenty-three years, Aillén of the three tongues came out of síd Finnachaidh and burned Tara: he played his timpán so sweetly that every man in the fortress fell asleep, and then he breathed fire over the hall. Fionn came to Tara on Samain, and Fíacha mac Conga, who had served his father, gave him a magic spear and the instruction: hold its naked point to your forehead, and you will not sleep. So Fionn sat wakeful while the court slept around him, and when Aillén turned back for the síd, Fionn cast the spear through him. For that deed Conn Cétchathach restored to him his father's treasure and made him head of the Fianna — and Goll mac Morna, his father's killer, accepted the peace and became the most loyal of his captains.

myths.title: The Pursuit of Diarmaid and Gráinne
myths.text: In his age Fionn was betrothed to Gráinne, daughter of Cormac mac Airt, but at the feast she gave a sleeping-draught to the company and laid a geis — the bond no Fenian could refuse — on Diarmaid Ó Duibhne to take her away. Diarmaid bore a ball seirce, a love-spot on his forehead that no woman could see without loving him, and Gráinne had seen it. For sixteen years the Fianna hunted the pair the length of Ireland, with Óengus of the Brug shielding Diarmaid where he could, until the tale came to the boar-hunt on Ben Bulben: the beast was Diarmaid's own foster-brother, transformed, and it was fated to be his death. Diarmaid killed the boar and took its venom in the doing. Fionn could heal any wound with water carried in his two cupped hands — he had the gift since the salmon — and twice he brought the water from the well and let it slip through his fingers, remembering Gráinne; when Óscar's reproach sent him back the third time, Diarmaid was dead.

myths.title: Oisín in Tír na nÓg and the Long Memory
myths.text: Fionn's son Oisín was taken across the sea by Niamh of the Golden Hair, daughter of the king of Tír na nÓg, the Land of Youth, riding behind her on a white horse that never touched water. What he counted as three years in that country were three hundred years in Ireland. Homesick, he was lent the horse to visit and warned on no account to set foot on Irish soil; he found the Fianna gone and their names become legend, and as he stooped from the saddle to help men shift a stone, the girth broke. Oisín touched the ground, and three hundred years fell on him at once. The medieval Acallam na Senórach frames the whole Fenian memory on this survival: the old, blind Oisín and Caílte mac Rónáin traveling Christian Ireland with Saint Patrick, naming every hill and ford and telling how they were won — the Fianna kept alive as long as one man could still remember them.

fionn.syncretism: Fionn's deepest kin are onomastic and Insular. His name descends from Proto-Celtic *windos, 'white, fair', and the handbooks have long set him beside the Welsh Gwyn ap Nudd — 'white son of Nudd', the Otherworld huntsman of Welsh tradition — as two regional developments of a Celtic figure built on the same word: the fair one who rides between this world and the wild. The more famous comparison is with the Norse corpus: like Sigurðr, who tasted the blood of Fáfnir's heart and understood the speech of birds, Fionn receives a whole mode of knowledge through a single accidental taste — the parallel is a commonplace of the comparative literature, though the two traditions grew the motif independently. Within Ireland his nearest mirror is [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]], the Ulster Cycle's solitary champion set against Fionn's communal war-band: the two heroes divide the Irish heroic imagination between them.
fionn.culturalLegacy: Fionn became, for a century, the most famous Celt in Europe. James Macpherson's Fragments of Ancient Poetry (1760) and Fingal (1762) presented 'Ossian' — Oisín — as the bard of a northern Homer, with Fingal his mighty father; the poems swept the continent, were carried by Napoleon and quoted by Goethe, and set off a running war over their authenticity in which Samuel Johnson demanded the manuscripts and Macpherson never produced them. The Celtic Revival reclaimed the genuine cycle: Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) brought the Fenian tales into modern English, and Irish scholarship — Meyer's Fianaigecht, Murphy's Duanaire Finn, Dooley and Roe's Acallam translation — rebuilt the cycle from its real witnesses. In Ireland the name never faded: Fianna Éireann named the warrior-band after him, the political tradition borrowed Fianna Fáil, 'the war-band of Ireland', Finn is once again a living given name, and Tír na nÓg remains the Irish idiom for youth that outlasts its bargain.
fionn.extendedMeditation: Fionn is the patron of accidental wisdom — of the knowledge you were not supposed to have, caught while doing someone else's cooking. The salmon was seven years promised to Finn Éces, and it went to the kitchen-boy's burned thumb instead; the tradition does not call this theft, and it does not pretend the boy planned it. It says something harder: that readiness is the only part of fortune you can control. The rest of Fionn's life is the price and use of that gift — the long captaincy, the saved Tara, the sixteen-year pursuit in which knowledge and desire pulled opposite ways and he let the water fall. The Acallam gives him the last word through his son: wisdom is memory kept against time, and it survives only as long as somebody keeps telling it.
fionn.originalScriptNote: The normalized Irish form is Fionn — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of Find or any Fenian name has been read on them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: fionn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

fionn.archaeology: Fionn is a textual hero: no ogham stone names him, and his cycle survives in the great Irish codices — the Acallam in the Book of Lismore and its sister manuscripts, the Boyhood Deeds and the Fenian lays across the Laud and Book of Leinster traditions. His landscape, by contrast, is real and visitable. The salmon of knowledge was caught in the Boyne, the river that bends around Brú na Bóinne — the Newgrange passage-tomb complex (c. 3200 BCE) that the myths make the síd of Óengus, Diarmaid's protector. Tara, the royal seat Aillén burned every Samain, is the hill of Teamhair in County Meath, an Iron Age ceremonial complex of earthworks and standing stones. Ben Bulben, where the boar killed Diarmaid, stands over Sligo as the tales describe it. The Fenian cycle is unusual among Irish corpora for how densely it maps onto ground that can still be walked.

phonemes.desc: Voiceless labiodental [f], short open-mid back [ɔ], trilled [r] — the preposition for, 'before', held brief and stressed, as in every Old Norse word.
Voiceless alveolar fricative [s] and short front [ɛ]; all three vowels of the name are short — Old Norse marks no length here.
Voiceless dental stop [t] and short close front [i]; the final -i is the weak masculine ending, so the name takes no nominative -r.

pronunciation.note: Forseti is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no thorn or eth, nothing for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The name is a law-term before it is a personal name: Old Norse forseti means 'chairman, president', the one who sits before the assembly, and the god is the office made personal. Only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Justice, Mediation
domains.subtitle: The Hall of Glitnir and the Settler of All Suits
domains.lead: Forseti is the son of Baldr and Nanna, and the quietest great office in the northern pantheon: he owns Glitnir, the hall of gold pillars and silver roof, and every quarrel that comes before him ends in peace — Snorri says all who bring their lawsuits to him go away reconciled, and Grímnismál says he dwells there day after day and puts all suits to sleep.

cards.name: Glitnir
cards.desc: 'The shining one': Forseti's hall, propped with gold and roofed with silver — the tenth dwelling in Grímnismál's tally of the homes of the gods.

cards.name: The Dómstaðr
cards.desc: The best court of judgment among gods and men — Snorri's verdict on the seat from which every party departs reconciled.

cards.name: The Spring of Fosetesland
cards.desc: The holy well on Heligoland whose water was drawn only in silence — the Frisian cult of Fosite that Alcuin records around 796.

cards.name: The Title
cards.desc: Forseti, 'he who sits before': the god's name is an office, and the office outlived the god — it is Iceland's word for its president.

symbols.name: Glitnir

symbols.name: The dómstaðr
symbols.meaning: The judgment-seat called the best among gods and men — authority measured in reconciled parties

symbols.name: Sátt, the settlement

symbols.name: The silent spring

symbols.name: The title forseti

mythology.lead: Forseti has the thinnest dossier of any god in the Edda with a hall to his name: one stanza in the Poetic Edda, two sentences in the Prose, and not a single adventure. What those lines build is nonetheless complete — a god whose whole mythology is the thing he does to quarrels.

myths.title: The Tenth Hall
myths.text: Grímnismál counts the dwellings of the gods, and the tenth is his: 'Glitnir is the tenth; it is propped with gold and thatched with silver too, and there Forseti dwells most days and puts all suits to sleep.' The verb is the miracle — svæfir, he lulls: not wins, not crushes, but puts to sleep, the way one settles a restless child. The poem gives him no weapon, no journey, no adversary — only a shining hall and the daily practice of ending strife.

myths.title: The Best Court Among Gods and Men
myths.text: Snorri builds the same hall twice. In the survey of the heavenly places, Glitnir stands with walls, pillars, and posts of red gold and a roof of silver. In the catalogue of the Æsir he names its owner: the son of Baldr and Nanna, daughter of Nep, is called Forseti; he owns that hall in heaven which is called Glitnir, and all who come to him with lawsuits go away reconciled — 'that is the best court of judgment among gods and men, as it is said here' — and Snorri quotes the Grímnismál stanza as his proof. The Prose Edda's whole account of the god is one sentence, and the sentence is enough: the child of the slain best of gods sits in the shining hall, and no quarrel survives him.

myths.title: The Spring on Fosetesland
myths.text: The god's name is older on parchment than the Eddas by four centuries. Around 796, Alcuin tells in his Life of Willibrord how the missionary was driven ashore on a Frisian island 'called Fosetesland after the god Fosite, whom those peoples worship' — Heligoland, the holy land. The island held a sacred spring whose water might be drawn only in silence, and the cattle that grazed there were untouchable. Willibrord baptized three men in the spring and had some of the cattle slaughtered for food; the islanders watched for the trespassers to be struck mad or dead, and when nothing happened they dragged the company before King Radbod, who cast lots daily for three days. The lot never fell on Willibrord; one of his companions was chosen and died for the sacrilege. Whether Frisian Fosite and Norse Forseti are one god remains the standing scholarly question — but the island, the silence, and the sanctity are recorded history of the cult.

myths.title: The Thirteenth Law-Speaker
myths.text: Late medieval Frisian legal texts preserve a foundation legend that Jacob Grimm could not keep away from Fosite. The Frisians, wanting law of their own, were set adrift in a boat; they prayed, and a thirteenth man appeared among the twelve law-speakers, steered them to land, threw a golden axe ashore — and where it struck, a spring burst forth — and there taught them the law. The golden axe, the spring, and the divine lawgiver made the identification irresistible to nineteenth-century scholarship; modern readers generally take the thirteenth for Christ, the usual stranger of medieval legend. The story is kept here for what it genuinely is: proof that the Frisian-speaking world remembered law as a gift that came over the water to found a thing-site by a spring.

myths.title: The Name in the Roll
myths.text: Where narrative fails, the catalogues keep him. The þulur — the mnemonic name-lists of the skaldic tradition — count Forseti in the roll of the Æsir, and Snorri's two Glitnir notices carry the hall independently of its owner. No saga stages him, no skald builds a kenning on him, and yet the name never drops out of the lists. The tradition treats him the way law treats a good judge: no stories, only the record that the court was held.

forseti.syncretism: The standing cross-border question is the equation Forseti = Fosite. Jacob Grimm made it, and the philology keeps it alive: Old Norse forseti is a transparent folk-formation — 'the one who sits before' — while Frisian Fosite cannot be derived from it, which is why Lindow entertains that the Norse god was borrowed from the Frisian cult, the form attested four centuries earlier, and re-etymologized into a law-term on the way north. The Norwegian place-name Forsetlund, 'Forseti's grove', shows the name lived in Scandinavian cult-geography whatever its direction of travel. Within the corpus his true kin is Týr, the pantheon's other god of law: where Týr guarantees the oath with his right hand in the wolf's jaws, Forseti dissolves the quarrel the oath was sworn to settle. And his own house is a study in inheritance: Snorri says of Baldr that none of his judgments can stand, and of Baldr's son that no judgment of his is ever refused — the father's flaw retired in the son's office.
forseti.culturalLegacy: Forseti's afterlife is the word itself. Old Norse forseti was the law-term for the presiding judge — the one who sits before the court — and when Iceland became a republic in 1944 it reached for the same word for its head of state: the President of Iceland is to this day Forseti Íslands, and no other god of the North still signs laws. In scholarship, the god's single sentence in Gylfaginning became one of the most-quoted passages on the Norse legal imagination, the standing citation for the proposition that the North idealized reconciliation over verdict. Modern Heathenry keeps him as the patron of mediation and of disputes ended without feud; and on the Frisian side, Heligoland — the holy land — still carries the memory of the cult in its name. He left no image, no saga, no drama: he left his title to a republic.
forseti.extendedMeditation: Forseti is the patron of the outcome the sagas almost never reach: the quarrel that ends. The heroic literature of the North is a literature of feud — insult answered by wound, wound by killing, killing by lawsuit, lawsuit by ambush — and into that world the Edda sets one shining hall where the arithmetic stops. All who come with their cases go away reconciled: it is the only perfect record in the corpus, and it belongs to the son of the god whose own judgments could not stand. The tradition seems to know what it was asking. Reconciliation is not the absence of justice but its completion — the verdict both parties can live inside — and the god who delivers it is given nothing else: no weapon, no journey, no death, no prophecy. His silence is the teaching. In a mythology that counts its heroes by what they break, Forseti counts by what he puts to sleep.

forseti.archaeology: Forseti is a textual and onomastic god: no runestone invokes him, no image or amulet names him, and no votive deposit can be laid at his hall. The ground evidence is the place-name: Forsetlund, 'Forseti's grove', in Vestfold near the Oslo fjord, attests that the name lived in Scandinavian cult-geography and not only in Icelandic books. The Frisian witness is earlier than any Norse manuscript: Alcuin's Life of Willibrord (c. 796) preserves the island Fosetesland — Heligoland, 'holy land' — with its silent spring and sacred herd, the only near-contemporary description of the cult site of the god-name's continental form. The Norse literary witnesses are the Codex Regius (Grímnismál) and the fourteenth-century codices of the Prose Edda. The Younger Futhark rendering ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ is a normalized reconstruction of how the name would have been carved; no Viking-Age inscription of the theonym is known.

pronunciation.approximation: FULL-ah — a short, rounded u as in 'put', a genuinely long, doubled l, and a short open 'ah'; two even syllables, stress on the first.
pronunciation.note: Old Norse Fulla is a transparent formation on fullr, 'full' — the same word as English 'full' and German 'voll' — so the name means 'Fullness, Plenty', an abstract noun worn as a personal name, like her sister ásynjur Sjǫfn and Lofn. The double l is a true geminate, held twice as long as a single l. The normalized Old Norse form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no thorn or eth — so the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: nothing distinctive is lost in transit, a statement about orthography, never about the goddess.

domains.title: The Keeper of the Casket
domains.subtitle: Abundance, Secrets — the Trusted One of Frigg's Hall
domains.lead: Fulla is Frigg's handmaid and confidante — the virgin goddess who goes with her hair loose and a golden band about her head, who carries the queen's little box, looks after her shoes, and shares her secret counsels. Her name is Fullness itself: plenty made a person, trusted with everything a queen cannot carry alone.

cards.name: The Eski
cards.desc: Frigg's little casket, which Fulla carries — the portable treasury of the queen of the gods, and the clearest badge of her office.

cards.name: The Golden Band
cards.desc: The gold snood Fulla wears about her loose hair — Snorri's one detail of dress, and the mark of wealth her name promises.

cards.name: The Queen's Shoes
cards.desc: Fulla looks after Frigg's footwear — the humblest duty in the catalogue, and the surest sign of a servant admitted to every chamber.

cards.name: The Shared Counsels
cards.desc: She shares Frigg's leyniráðagørðir — the queen's secret deliberations: the duty that outranks every object she carries.

symbols.name: The eski (little casket)
symbols.meaning: Frigg's portable treasure-box, entrusted to the hand that never lets it go — custody as a form of intimacy

symbols.name: The golden hair-band
symbols.meaning: The virgin's loose hair bound with gold — unmarried freedom dressed in plenty

symbols.name: Frigg's shoes
symbols.meaning: The queen's footwear in her keeping — the lowest duty held by the highest confidence

symbols.name: The finger-ring from Hel
symbols.meaning: Nanna's gift carried back by Hermóðr — a token from the dead addressed, of all the ásynjur, to her

mythology.lead: Fulla has no saga of her own: her dossier is four precise notices, and every one of them places her at Frigg's side. What the tradition lost in narrative it kept in definition — no goddess in the Edda is more exactly described in a single sentence.

myths.title: The Keeper of the Casket
myths.text: Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur gives Fulla her entire portrait in one sentence, and the tradition never varies it: 'Fulla is a virgin and goes with her hair loose and a golden band about her head; she carries Frigg's eski, looks after her footwear, and shares her secret counsels with her.' The three duties descend in rank and rise in intimacy — the box is treasure, the shoes are service, the counsels are trust itself. She is named immediately after Gná, Frigg's errand-rider, and the pairing has stuck: where Gná carries the queen's words out through the worlds, Fulla keeps the queen's words that never leave the hall. Scholars since Grimm have read both as hypostases of Frigg — aspects of the queen walking about as attendants — but the Edda keeps them as persons, and Fulla's golden band and loose hair make her the most visually fixed of all the minor ásynjur.

myths.title: The Warning to Geirröðr
myths.text: Fulla's one errand in the Poetic Edda is given in prose, at the head of Grímnismál. Óðinn and Frigg had quarrelled over their foster-sons: Frigg accused King Geirröðr, Óðinn's favourite, of being so stingy he tortured his guests for lack of food, and Óðinn laid a wager on his man and set off disguised to test him. Frigg, knowing the road, sent her handmaid Fulla to Geirröðr ahead of him, to warn the king to beware of a certain sorcerer coming to his land to bewitch him — and gave her the token by which he could be known: no dog, however fierce, would leap at him. The warning is the trap: Geirröðr seized the blue-cloaked stranger, named Grímnir, and tortured him between two fires — and out of that fire the god spoke the whole catalogue of the worlds. Fulla appears only to deliver the message and vanish, but the wager, the torture, and the poem's entire revelation turn on her errand.

myths.title: The Ring from Hel
myths.text: When Hermóðr rode nine nights to ransom Baldr and came home with the tidings, he brought tokens from the dead: Baldr sent back the ring Draupnir to Óðinn, and Nanna — Baldr's wife, who had died of grief on his pyre — sent gifts out of Hel to the two women of Frigg's hall: a linen headdress for Frigg, and a finger-ring for Fulla. It is the smallest bequest in the whole Baldr cycle, and the most telling: when a dead goddess thinks of Ásgarðr's household, she thinks of the queen and of the queen's handmaid by name, and Frigg's hall is remembered as having a second woman in it who mattered. Fulla stands in that sentence exactly where her office puts her — the second woman of the hall, remembered with jewellery from beyond the world.

myths.title: Volla, Friia's Sister
myths.text: The one continental witness comes from a tenth-century Fulda manuscript, the Second Merseburg Charm — the only pagan theogonic text in Old High German. Phol and Wodan rode to the wood, and Balder's foal wrenched its foot; then the goddesses chant over it in sequence: Sinthgunt, Sunna her sister; Friia, Volla her sister; and at last Wodan, who knows how, and the limb is knit bone to bone and blood to blood. Since Jacob Grimm, Volla — Friia's sister — has widely been read as Fulla, Frigg's attendant: the name is the exact Old High German form of the same word, and the charm puts her, precisely as the Edda does, at Friia's right hand. The identification is argued, not proven, and the handbooks counsel the usual caution — but if it holds, Fulla is one of the very few Norse goddesses with a continental footprint older than the Icelandic books.

fulla.syncretism: Fulla's cross-border life runs through one word and one relationship. The word is fullr: Proto-Germanic *fullaz gives English 'full', German 'voll', Gothic fulls, and Old Norse Fulla — a goddess whose name is the ordinary adjective turned abstract noun, 'Fullness'. The relationship is the one the Merseburg Charm preserves: Volla beside Friia, as Fulla beside Frigg — and since Grimm, the identification of the two has been the standing reading, with Simek registering both the fit and the doubt. The deeper syncretic question is what kind of being she is. Gylfaginning's ásynjur catalogue is full of abstract-noun goddesses — Sjǫfn ('affection'), Lofn ('praise, permission'), Vár ('vows') — and scholars have long suspected that Fulla, Gná, and their sisters are facets of Frigg herself, the queen's plenitude and far-ranging given names and errands of their own. Whether she began as an independent goddess of plenty or as an aspect that walked off on its own, the sources keep her a person: she receives a ring, runs an errand, and wears her own gold.
fulla.culturalLegacy: Fulla's afterlife is scholarly and liturgical rather than popular. Grimm devoted a chapter of Teutonic Mythology to her and Volla, and every handbook since — Simek, Orchard, Lindow — keeps her as the standing example of the abstract-noun ásynja, the goddess whose name tells you exactly what she is. Her image — loose hair, golden band, the queen's casket on her arm — became the fixed Victorian and modern picture of the trusted northern handmaid, and she appears in nearly every retelling of the Baldr cycle by virtue of one finger-ring. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú practice keeps her at Frigg's side as a goddess of plenty, household trust, and well-kept secrets, invoked where abundance must be held in confidence. She never became a Marvel character or a video-game boss; she remained what the Edda made her — the most trusted person in the queen's hall, and the proof that in the northern pantheon even abundance has a keeper.
fulla.extendedMeditation: Fulla is the goddess of what is held in trust. Every detail of her portrait is a form of custody: the casket she carries but does not own, the shoes she tends but does not wear, the counsels she shares but does not speak. Even her name works this way — Fullness is not a thing she does but a thing she keeps. The tradition gives her no adventure because her office is the adventure's opposite: Gná rides out with the queen's words; Fulla stays, and what is entrusted to her stays with her. Nanna's ring from Hel is the tradition's own verdict on that office — when the dead send gifts home, they send one to the keeper. In a mythology that ends in fire and betrayal, Fulla is the quiet counterweight: the proof that some things, once entrusted, are simply kept.

fulla.archaeology: Fulla is an entirely textual goddess: no cult site, toponym, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and the runic corpus is silent — unsurprising for a figure the sources place inside the queen's household rather than in the public cult. Her witnesses are manuscripts. The Grímnismál prose, which preserves her one errand, survives in the Codex Regius (c. 1270); her portrait in Gylfaginning 35 and her ring in Gylfaginning 49 come with the Prose Edda codices of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and her name recurs in the þulur, the metrical name-lists appended to Skáldskaparmál. The one continental witness is the Second Merseburg Charm, copied into a theological manuscript at Fulda in the tenth century and now in the Merseburg cathedral library: its Volla, sister of Friia, is the only attestation of the figure outside Iceland and, if the identification holds, the oldest by centuries.

pronunciation.approximation: GAHRM-ur — nearly a single syllable: a hard g, a short open 'ah', the r and m run together, and the final nominative -r sounded as a light syllabic trill, as in Icelandic.
pronunciation.note: Old Norse Garmr names the hound of the underworld and nothing else: Cleasby–Vigfusson record the word only as a mythological proper name, 'the dog of the nether world'. Its etymology is genuinely uncertain — de Vries lists it under the unsolved names — and the standing line connects it with a Germanic root for growling or hoarse crying, whence the traditional gloss 'Howler'. The normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic and no distinctive letter — so the name is Tier-2 by the mechanical rule: nothing is lost in transit, a statement about orthography, never about the hound.
