phonemes.desc: Voiceless sibilant [s] plus short high back vowel [u]; in the Quechua two-syllable word the stress falls on this first syllable.
Bilabial stop [p] plus the diphthong [ai] written -ay; the final glide closes the name the way Quechua orthography writes it.

pronunciation.approximation: SOO-pie — two syllables, stress on the first; the '-ay' is the 'y' of 'fly'.

kin.label: Quechua
kin.form: supay, 'spirit, demon' — the common noun González Holguín glosses as 'diablo' in his 1608 Vocabulario de la lengua general de todo el Perú

kin.label: Aymara
kin.form: supaya, the parallel Aymara word for a spirit of the dead or demon (Bertonio, Vocabulario de la lengua aymará, 1612)

kin.label: Colonial equation
kin.form: Spanish chroniclers equated Supay with the Christian Devil; Polo de Ondegardo (1571) reports the Inca dead descending to uku pacha in the power of the being they called Supay

pronunciation.note: Supay is Tier 2: the Quechua name carries no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII loses; only the capital distinguishes the restored form. Its pre-conquest meaning was 'spirit'; the modern sense 'devil' is a colonial redefinition, not an original one.

domains.title: Supay
domains.subtitle: Underworld
domains.lead: Supay is the lord of uku pacha, the inner world beneath the Andes — the domain of the dead, of cave-dwelling spirits, and of the mineral wealth the earth conceals. No temple bore his name; he was propitiated, not praised. Under Spanish rule the name was reforged: supay became the Quechua word for 'devil', and the lord of the inner world survives today as the miners' Tío.

cards.name: Lord of Uku Pacha
cards.desc: Master of the inner world beneath the earth where the dead dwell and the ore veins run (Polo de Ondegardo 1571; Cobo, Historia 13.10).

cards.name: Master of the Supaykuna
cards.desc: The dangerous spirits — the supaykuna — who send illness and haunt caves and crossroads; offerings kept them from taking the living.

cards.name: The Caves of Tambillos
cards.desc: Caverns near Huarochirí where the people said the supay dwelt; the Huarochirí manuscript records the rites paid there.

cards.name: The Miners' Tío
cards.desc: In the colonial mines, above all Potosí, miners fed the underground lord coca, alcohol, and cigarettes under the alias El Tío.

symbols.name: Cave mouth or mine shaft
symbols.meaning: The visible entrance to uku pacha; every shaft sunk into the earth is a doorway into Supay's jurisdiction

symbols.name: Coca and chicha
symbols.meaning: The standard offerings that made the underground lord generous toward the living who disturbed his realm

symbols.name: Funerary goods
symbols.meaning: Food, tools, and treasure interred with the dead as provision for the journey down to Supay's household

symbols.name: The horned devil figure
symbols.meaning: The post-conquest iconography in which the extirpation campaigns re-imagined Supay as the Christian Devil

mythology.lead: No Inca myth cycle of Supay survives on its own terms. Everything we know comes through colonial chroniclers, Quechua-language manuscripts, and the living memory of Andean communities — the record of a lord of the inner world who was propitiated, feared, demonized, and finally renamed, yet never quite dethroned.

myths.title: Lord of Uku Pacha
myths.text: The earliest European witness is the corregidor Polo de Ondegardo, whose 1571 report De los errores y supersticiones de los indios explains Inca cosmology as three stacked worlds: hanaq pacha, the upper world; kay pacha, this present world; and uku pacha, the inner world within the earth. The dead descended to uku pacha, Polo reports, and there remained in the power of the being they called Supay. Bernabé Cobo repeats the scheme a century later (Historia del Nuevo Mundo 13.10), adding that the dead were furnished with food, tools, and treasure for the journey down. Nowhere in these accounts is Supay a god of a temple or a priesthood: he is the one who holds the dead, and the offerings made at funerals are essentially payments that keep him from reaching further into the world of the living. The Inca underworld was not a place of punishment but of retention, and Supay was its jailer as much as its king. The belief encodes a sober arithmetic: every death adds to his household, so the living must forever feed the boundary between the worlds.

myths.title: The Caves of Tambillos
myths.text: The Quechua-language Huarochirí manuscript, recorded by the extirpator Francisco de Ávila in the first years of the seventeenth century (trans. Salomon & Urioste, 1991), treats supay not as a single lord but as a class of dangerous beings — the supaykuna — who dwell in caves, springs, hills, and crossroads and send illness to those who offend them. The most famous haunt is the cavern of Tambillos, near San Pedro de Huarochirí, where the people made offerings of coca and maize beer so that the spirits of the rock would not take their children. Scholars have long debated whether the chroniclers' single 'Supay, lord of the inner world' is a Spanish simplification of this older, plural spirit-world, or whether the supaykuna were always understood as the lord's subjects. The manuscript itself does not resolve the question; it simply shows communities negotiating, offering, and appeasing. Whatever the hierarchy, the logic is constant: the earth's interior is populated, and it must be paid. Supay's power was never worshipped from a temple — it was managed at the cave mouth, one offering at a time.

myths.title: Supay Becomes the Devil
myths.text: The most consequential chapter of Supay's history was written not by his believers but by his enemies. To convert the Andes, the missionaries needed Satan to have a local name, and they chose Supay's. González Holguín's Quechua Vocabulario (1608) glosses supay plainly as 'devil', and Pablo José de Arriaga's manual for destroying idolatry, the Extirpación de la idolatría (1621), names Supay as the demon who still receives the offerings poured at the Indian shrines. The campaign worked as language policy: within a generation Quechua speakers used supay for the Christian devil, and the pre-conquest meaning — 'spirit' — survived only in scholarly memory. Every colonial confession, sermon, and catechism pressed the word deeper into its new meaning. The transformation is a case study in conversion by redefinition: the church did not first destroy the lord of the inner world; it renamed him, and let the new name do the slow work of displacement. That the word, not the being, was conquered is proven by the mines, where the lord returned under another alias.

myths.title: El Tío of Potosí
myths.text: In the silver mines of the colonial Andes, above all at Potosí, miners developed the cult of El Tío, 'the Uncle': an effigy seated at the deepest level of each mine, fed coca leaves, cane alcohol, and cigarettes on Tuesdays and Fridays, and honored with the ch'alla libation. Michael Taussig's The Devil and Commodity Fetishism in South America (1980) connected the Tío to the older Supay of uku pacha — the lord of the inner world now ruling a new and terrible wealth. The miners said it plainly: the metal belongs to the one below, and he will trade safety for tribute; fatal accidents were read as unpaid debts. Unlike the church's Supay, this underground lord was negotiated with, not merely feared — a business partner who could be generous and could be cheated, at one's peril. The tradition continues today at Cerro Rico and in the Diablada dances of Oruro. Supay's late history shows a power outliving its own demonization: renamed the Devil by the conquerors, he remained — under a new alias — the actual master of the underworld the miners worked in.

supay.syncretism: Supay's entire afterlife is a history of forced translations. The conquering church mapped him onto Satan, and the mapping was so successful that modern Quechua and Aymara use supay as the ordinary word for devil. Yet the older figure survived the translation in the mines, where El Tío — the Uncle — continues the uku pacha lord's contract with those who take wealth from below. Scholars such as Taussig (1980) and Tristan Platt have read this double life as the emblem of colonial capitalism: the indigenous underworld lord re-employed as the owner of the silver that fed Europe. The Diablada dance traditions of Oruro and the miner rites at Potosí keep both identities visible at once — Christian devil masks performing unmistakably pre-Christian obligations.
supay.culturalLegacy: Supay remains embedded in Andean language itself: to this day supay means devil in Quechua and Aymara, a living fossil of the extirpation campaigns. In the mining regions of Bolivia the Tío effigies are still fed and still feared, and the Diablada festivals stage his masked dance before crowds of thousands. For scholarship, Supay is a key witness to how colonialism rewrote indigenous cosmology — studied by Taussig, Platt, and Duviols as the paradigmatic case of a deity demonized, renamed, and secretly retained. The name also circulates in global culture: Andean diaspora communities, museum exhibitions on Inca religion, and contemporary indigenous revival movements all return to the older, pre-Christian meaning of the word — spirit, not devil — as part of recovering what the extirpations tried to erase.
supay.extendedMeditation:
Supay is the lord of the underground who was renamed but never dethroned. Colonial priests thought that calling him 'devil' would finish him; instead the name became a mask, and behind the mask the old contract continued in the dark of the mines. There is a lesson in the economics of belief here: a power that controls what you need — passage for your dead, safety for your labor, metal for your markets — cannot be argued away. It can only be paid.

The restoration of Supay is therefore more than philological courtesy. It returns to the figure his own name, before the extirpators rewrote it, and it asks the reader to hold both histories at once: the lord of uku pacha and the colonial devil, the cave offerings and the Tuesday cigarettes at Cerro Rico. The earth, this name insists, keeps its own accounts, and its oldest creditor is still collecting.
supay.archaeology: No temple of Supay is known — he was propitiated at cave mouths, springs, graves, and mine faces rather than in built sanctuaries. The material record is therefore indirect: the rock shelters and cave shrines of the Huarochirí region, including Tambillos, where colonial extirpation records describe offerings of coca and maize beer; colonial-era dictionaries and confessionals that fixed supay as 'devil' (González Holguín 1608; Bertonio 1612); the Tío effigies and their offerings still maintained at Potosí and Olmillos; and the abundant documentary archive of the extirpation campaigns (Arriaga 1621; Duviols). The evidence honestly shows a cult of place rather than of monuments.

kin.label: Old Russian
kin.form: Сварогъ (Svarogъ), attested in the Svyatoslav Izbornik of 1073 — 'There is a god named Svarog'

kin.form: Dažbog, 'the Giving God' — the Primary Chronicle names him Svarog's son

pronunciation.note: Svarog is single-tier Tier 2: the ASCII form loses no distinctive letter, since the Cyrillic Сварогъ transliterates without diacritics. His name is usually connected to the root svar- 'radiance, bright sky,' though the etymology remains debated (Gieysztor, Mitologia Słowian).

domains.title: Svarog
domains.subtitle: Sky
domains.lead: Svarog is the elusive Slavic god of the sky, fire, and smithing — known almost entirely from a handful of early Russian and Western chronicle notices that name him, compare him to a smith, and make him father of the sun. He is the Slavs' heaven-forge: the god at whose anvil the daylight was made.

cards.name: The Sky-Smith
cards.desc: The Izbornik of 1073 names him beside the forge-god comparison — heaven's smith, working in radiance.

cards.name: Father of Dažbog
cards.desc: The Primary Chronicle makes him father of Dažbog, the Giving God — the sun as the smith's son.

cards.name: Lord of the Fire
cards.desc: As Svarožič he descends to the hearth — the divine fire that must be fed and kept pure.

cards.name: The Named One
cards.desc: Rare among Slavic gods, he is textually attested — a god pagans and preachers both had to name.

symbols.name: The Forge
symbols.meaning: Heaven as smithy — the place where light and daylight were hammered out

symbols.name: The Tongs
symbols.meaning: The smith's tool, emblem of his craft and of handled, controllable fire

symbols.name: The Sun-Disk
symbols.meaning: His finished work — the Primary Chronicle makes Dažbog, the sun, his son

symbols.name: The Anvil-Stone
symbols.meaning: The fixed point of the sky on which the world-shaping blows fall

symbols.name: Sacred Fire
symbols.meaning: The hearth flame addressed as Svarožič — the god scaled to every home

mythology.lead: Svarog has no surviving epic and no surviving cult — his entire dossier is a few chronicle lines, a gloss, and a name. The mythology below is therefore an archaeology of attestations: each 'myth' is a document, read as closely as the evidence allows, with the tradition's silence stated plainly.

myths.title: Named in the Izbornik of 1073
myths.text: The earliest notice of Svarog comes not from a pagan shrine but from a court book. The Svyatoslav Izbornik of 1073 — a miscellany compiled for Prince Svyatoslav of Kiev — pauses over the Slavic gods to say: 'There is a god named Svarog', and in the surrounding passage draws the comparison with the smith-god Hephaestus, whose forge was read as an image of heaven's fire. The compiler's source was probably a South Slavic manual translated for Duke Svyatoslav's court, which would make the notice the fossil of a lost Slavic mythographic handbook. The sentence is three words in Old Russian,The sentence is three words in Old Russian, yet it proves that in eleventh-century Rus', a century and a half after official conversion, learned men still needed to name and explain the old sky-smith. The attestation tells us less what Svarog did than how stubbornly he survived — a god preserved in the margin of a Christian book.

myths.title: Svarog and the Birth of Dažbog
myths.text: The Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let), in its anti-pagan sermon, records the genealogy plainly: 'from him was born Dažbog' — the Giving God, the sun — a line preserved in the Laurentian and Hypatian codices (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor, trans.). Dažbog in turn gave his name to the Rus' themselves in the chronicler's bitter pun — 'Dažbog's grandchildren,' a folk memory the sermon meant to shame into silence. With it comes the whole logicWith it comes the whole logic of the sky-smith: what a smith fathers is a made light, a produced radiance, and Dažbog's very name ('the giver') reads like the boast of a successful forge. Scholars caution that the chronicler's sermon is polemic, not ethnography. Even so, the fragment preserves a genuine Indo-European intuition in Slavic dress: the sun is not a body but a work — hammered out, handed down, and called a gift.

myths.title: Zuarasici among the Slavic Gods
myths.text: Writing around 1172, the German priest Helmold of Bosau lists the gods the Slavs revere — and among them, Zuarasici, the form his Latin ear gave to Svarog (Helmold, Chronica Slavorum I.52). The notice is a single name in a hostile catalogue, yet it matters: it places the god west of Kiev, among the Obodrite Slavs of the Baltic coast, suggesting his name once ranged across the whole Slavic world. The same passage gives him neighbors — a storm-hurling chief god and a god of war — so one hostile paragraph sketches the entire Obodrite pantheon. Helmold's list is our only Western-witness checkHelmold's list is our only Western-witness check on the Russian sources. A name without a story, recorded by an enemy, is fragile evidence — but it is evidence, and for a Slavic god that is rare enough to be precious.

myths.title: Svarožič, Fire of the Hearth
myths.text: In a Novgorod copy of Hilarion's Sermon on Law and Grace, a copyist 'corrected' the text to write Svarožič — 'Little Svarog' — the name scholars take for a fire-god or the domesticated form of the sky-smith (Ivanits, Russian Folk Belief, 1989; Gieysztor, Mitologia Słowian). Later South Slavic and folk materials preserve hearth rites — the fire doused, fed, and addressed with honor — which the scholarship has long connected to this doubled name. South Slavic folklore collected in the nineteenth century still addresses the hearth fire with honorific formulas, and Serbian scholarship has long read in them the memory of a flame that was once a god. The tradition is fragmentary and the reconstruction debated;The tradition is fragmentary and the reconstruction debated; what stands is the shape of the idea: the cosmic smith had a small form that fit inside every house, so that tending the stove was, in origin, tending a god.

svarog.syncretism: Svarog's afterlife is a study in resurrection. After the chronicle notices fell silent, he slept for seven centuries — until the Slavic national revivals of the nineteenth century reforged him. Juliusz Słowacki reached for him in Polish Romantic verse (most famously in Beniowski), and comparative mythologists of the era, seeing the forge-and-sun logic, set him beside Hephaestus and Vulcan. In the twentieth century the identification hardened in schoolbook mythology; in the twenty-first, Rodnovery — the Slavic neopagan movement — restored him to actual worship, with Svarog as smith of heaven and patron of crafts. Every layer must be labeled: attested god in the eleventh century, literary construction in the nineteenth, living deity today. Modern scholarship (Gieysztor; Ivanits) keeps the layers distinct — and notes that a god can be reconstructed honestly, provided the reconstruction admits what it is.
svarog.culturalLegacy: Svarog's modern presence is out of all proportion to his ancient evidence. He is the Slavic god schoolchildren meet first — the smith of the sky in every compendium of Slavic mythology — and his name has become a byword for the lost pre-Christian heritage of Eastern Europe. Rodnover communities keep his festivals; blacksmiths and metalworkers claim his patronage; and in literature from Słowacki onward he stands as the emblem of a Slavic cosmos that conversion only partially erased. The Primary Chronicle line about Dažbog ensured his survival in another way: every retelling of Russian origins must reckon with him. A god of whom three medieval sentences survive now carries a civilization's memory of its own forge — perhaps a fitting tribute to the smith of lights.
svarog.extendedMeditation: Svarog asks what can be known of a god who left almost nothing. The honest answer is: a name, a son, a forge, and a fire. Yet these fragments sketch a complete theology of making. The Slavs looked at daylight and did not call it a lamp or a face — they called it work: something hammered out on an anvil by a craftsman whose son delivers it. In that intuition lies a whole philosophy — that order is manufactured, that radiance is skilled labor, that the sky is a workshop and the sun its product. The hearth-name Svarožič extends the philosophy downward: if the sun is a forge's output, every kitchen fire is a franchise of heaven. A civilization that imagined the cosmos this way honored the smith as its most theologically precise citizen. Svarog survives because the intuition survives: we still speak of 'forging' the future, still feel that making is the most godlike of acts.
svarog.archaeology: There is, strictly speaking, no archaeology of Svarog — no image, temple, amulet, or inscription bearing his name has ever been found, and the famous monumental idols of the Slavs (the Zbruch idol, the Svetovid of Arkona, the Prillwitz figures) belong to other gods. The Slavic smith-god is a documentary phenomenon: three medieval texts and their later copies. This absence is itself instructive. Baltic and Scandinavian pagans left cult objects; the early Slavs, converting earlier and building in wood, left almost none — so the chronicles, compiled by their enemies and converts, are the sole excavation. Every claim about Svarog's worship should be weighed against that silence.

pronunciation.note: Ta'aroa is the Tahitian form of Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa, the name carried across the triangle as Tangaloa, Tangaroa, and Kanaloa. The catalog restoration keeps the older missionary-era spelling used by Henry and Ellis, in which the Tahitian glottal stop is unwritten — a sound DNS cannot carry. Tier 2: no vowel length marks the name; the loss is a display fact, not a judgment of rank.

domains.title: Taaroa
domains.subtitle: Creator
domains.lead: In the old religion of Tahiti, Taaroa is not one god among many but the ground of all divinity — the self-existent one who dwelt alone in the primal darkness, burst the shell of his own being to make sky and earth, and fathered or simply is every other god. The first missionary scholars recorded his cosmogony with respect verging on awe.

cards.name: The Unbegotten
cards.desc: Ta'aroa has no father and no mother: the accounts insist he was never made, because before him there was nothing that could make him.

cards.name: Maker of Sky and Earth
cards.desc: He broke his world-shell: the upper half became the sky, the lower half the earth, and the space between them the living world.

cards.name: Father of the Gods
cards.desc: In the fuller tellings he fashioned the other great gods — Tane, Rono, Tū, 'Oro — and set each over a domain of the world.

cards.name: The Distant One
cards.desc: When creation was finished he withdrew to the highest heaven; every prayer began and ended with his name.

symbols.name: The world-shell
symbols.meaning: The egg-like shell in which Ta'aroa crouched alone in the darkness; when he broke it, sky rose from the upper half and earth spread from the lower (Henry, Ancient Tahiti).

symbols.name: The spiral
symbols.meaning: The ʻōro spiral of growth by which creation proceeds outward from a point — the geometry the priests saw in the unfolding world and in the sacred hair of the gods.

symbols.name: The primal darkness (Te Pō)
symbols.meaning: The night in which Ta'aroa existed alone before anything else; creation is not the defeat of darkness but its self-opening.

symbols.name: The opening invocation
symbols.meaning: Every Tahitian prayer and chant began with Ta'aroa's name and closed with it — the priests named him 'the god of gods' before any other name was spoken (Henry, Ancient Tahiti).

symbols.name: The raised stones of the marae
symbols.meaning: The open-air temple platforms of Tahiti with their carved god-houses (ʻōroʻō); his cult was administered by the highest priesthood of the islands.

mythology.lead: Taaroa's mythology is a cosmogony in the strict sense — an account of how anything at all came to be. The Tahitian priests told it to the first missionaries, and it survives in two nineteenth-century witnesses: the narrative taken down by the missionary John Davies and the longer version preserved by Teuira Henry from the scholars of Papeari.

myths.title: Before There Was Anything
myths.text: The old scholars of Tahiti told the missionary John Davies — and Teuira Henry heard it again two generations later — that before there was sky, sea, land, light, or any other being, Taaroa was. He had no father and no mother, for nothing existed before him that could beget him; his cult name Ta'aroa-'onohi-'ote-na'i-'atu means 'Ta'aroa, the self-existing, the origin of all things.' He dwelt in the primal darkness called Te Pō, wrapped in his own shell like a chick in the egg, calling into the void — and no one answered, because there was no one else to answer. The whole of the world-to-come lay folded inside him, as the tree lies folded in its seed, and the first act of the cosmos was that loneliness outgrew its shell. (Davies' account, preserved in Ellis, Polynesian Researches I; Henry, Ancient Tahiti 336–338.) The myth makes the first moment of existence a soliloquy: creation begins as a being who has no one else to speak to, speaking himself into company.

myths.title: Sky from the Upper Half, Earth from the Lower
myths.text: Weary of confinement, Ta'aroa broke his shell open. The upper half of it he raised high above him and made the sky; the lower half he spread out beneath him and made the earth. From himself he brought forth the sea, the springs, the rocks and sands, the trees and plants, the fish and birds, and the land animals — the whole inventory of the world drawn, item by item, out of his own being, nothing borrowed and nothing left over. In Henry's version he then turned to its government, which is where the third myth begins. (Henry, Ancient Tahiti 336–349; Ellis, Polynesian Researches I.) The image is precise and strange: the cosmos is not built from outside materials but hatched — the world as the broken shell of a god who could no longer bear to be alone.

myths.title: The Maker of Gods and of Men
myths.text: In the fuller tellings, Ta'aroa did not keep the world to himself. He fashioned the other great gods — Tane of the forests and birds, Rono of peace and cultivated food, Tū of war and of humankind, Ta'ata, and the young warrior god 'Oro who would inherit the great national marae — and set each over his portion of creation. He then made men and women to people the earth he had spread. The sources are early and do not always agree on the details — Davies' version, gathered in 1818, is sober where Henry's, drawn from priestly families of Papeari, is expansive — but all agree on the order: gods first, then people, and Ta'aroa before and above both. (Davies in Ellis, Polynesian Researches I; Henry, Ancient Tahiti.) The theology is remarkably austere: a single unbegotten power delegates everything, and rules by having made the rulers.

myths.title: The Distant One Ascends
myths.text: When the work of creation was complete, Ta'aroa did not remain to govern the world day by day. He withdrew to the highest heaven, above the dwelling of Tane and all the other gods, and from that remove he was invoked as 'the god of gods.' Every prayer and every sacrifice on the marae began with his name and ended with his name, whatever lesser deity was being petitioned in between; the priests addressed him as the root from which the other divinities grew, the trunk of which they were branches. It is this withdrawal that his name's traditional gloss — 'the distant one' — is usually taken to mean. (Henry, Ancient Tahiti.) The pattern is the deus otiosus, the resting god familiar from many traditions: having made the world, the creator leaves it running and becomes a direction — the vertical axis toward which all prayer climbs.

taaroa.syncretism: When the London Missionary Society reached Tahiti in 1797, the first catechists did not find a clutter of squabbling idols — they found a supreme god whose creation narrative sounded uncomfortably like Genesis, and they said so in their journals. Tahitian scholars who worked with them, the deacons of the mission schools, readily compared Ta'aroa to Jehovah, a comparison that eased conversion and ultimately doomed the cult: the great marae were abandoned within a generation, the god-houses burned or left to rot. Ta'aroa survived in the cult of his son 'Oro, whose war-god religion absorbed the national priesthood. In the western islands his own name lived on as Tangaloa, creator of Tonga and Samoa; in Aotearoa it had already become Tangaroa, lord of the sea; in Hawai'i, Kanaloa, god of the deep. One god, three more names, many biographies — the comparative method's favorite case.
taaroa.culturalLegacy: Taaroa's direct cult ended in the early nineteenth century, but his name never left Tahiti. It lives in the great marae the Polynesian nations are rebuilding: Taputapuātea on Ra'iatea, dedicated to his son 'Oro, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2017 and re-consecrated by delegations from across the triangle. The cosmogony recorded by Henry remains a foundational text of Polynesian studies, taught wherever the old religion is taken seriously as theology rather than curiosity. Contemporary Tahitian dancers and orators invoke Ta'aroa as the name of origins in the renaissance of ʻōrero and ori Tahiti. And because the creation chant opens every traditional ceremony with his name, 'Ta'aroa' has become the shorthand Polynesians reach for when they want to say: this is where we begin.
taaroa.extendedMeditation:
Most creation stories start with a problem: chaos to be fought, a dragon to be split, a rival to be overthrown. Taaroa's story starts with something rarer — sufficiency. Before there was anything, there was a being who needed nothing: no parents, no materials, no opponent. The world is not a conquest but an overflow, the cracking of a shell that had become too small for the being inside it. And there is a loneliness in this that the myth does not hide: the first thing the god does in the darkness is call out, and no one answers. Creation, on this reading, is not an act of power but of company — the universe as the solution to solitude.

When the work is done, Ta'aroa withdraws to the highest heaven and leaves the world to his children. Power that creates and then steps back is the most difficult kind to imagine, and the Tahitians imagined it — a supreme being whose supremacy consists in having delegated everything and in being, still, the direction of every prayer. That is a theology of confidence: the maker does not need to manage, because the making was perfect. The name Ta'aroa, with its gentle glottal catch like a held breath, is the sound of that confidence.

Ellis, Polynesian Researches I

Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology

taaroa.archaeology: No temple of Ta'aroa survives intact — the LMS converts dismantled the marae — but the stone platforms do: hundreds of paved marae with their upright back slabs (unu) and stepped god-houses (ʻōroʻō) dot the Society Islands, most famously the great complex of Taputapuātea at 'Ōpōa, Ra'iatea (UNESCO World Heritage, 2017). The restored valley marae of 'Ārahurahu in Papeari preserves the setting Henry's informants described. Carved tiki figures attest the anthropomorphic image of the gods: the celebrated figure A'a, from Rurutu in the Austral Islands (British Museum), a deity studded with thirty small figures, is widely read as the creator teeming with the gods and people he brought forth.

pronunciation.note: Tagaloa is single-tier Tier 2: the restoration adds no feature that plain ASCII loses — no diacritic and no distinctive atomic letter — under the mechanical tier rule. The name's dignity is carried by its meaning, 'The Lord,' and by the scholarly consensus behind the restoration (Tregear, Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary; Craig 1989).

domains.title: Tagaloa
domains.subtitle: Creator
domains.lead: Tagaloa is the supreme creator god of the Samoan islands, lord of the layered heavens who looked down on the empty sea and made the land. He is the maker of islands, the father of gods and chiefs, and the dweller in the highest sky — the figure around whom Samoan cosmology turns.

cards.name: Creator of the Isles
cards.desc: He threw down the vine and stone from which the Samoan islands were formed, founding the world itself.

cards.name: Lord of the Heavens
cards.desc: He dwells in Lani-uli, the highest of the layered heavens, above wind, rain, and the soaring birds.

cards.name: Father of Sina
cards.desc: His daughter Sina, mother of chiefs, anchors the island's greatest cycle of stories.

cards.name: Ocean's Lord
cards.desc: Across Polynesia his name is the sea's: Tangaroa in Aotearoa, Ta'aroa in Tahiti, Kanaloa in Hawai'i.

symbols.name: The Vine of the Isles
symbols.meaning: The heavenly vine Tagaloa let down into the sea, whose parts became the islands of Samoa

symbols.name: The Layered Heavens
symbols.meaning: Lani-uli and the descending storeys of the sky, his dwelling above all clouds

symbols.name: The Coconut Palm
symbols.meaning: Born from the body of the eel Tuna in the Sina cycle that belongs to Tagaloa's household

symbols.name: The Star-Path
symbols.meaning: In the wayfinding revival, the ocean road by which his dispersed namesakes are rejoined

mythology.lead: Tagaloa's mythology is cosmogony in the strict sense — stories of how land, people, and rank came to be. It survives not in epic but in creation chants recorded by nineteenth-century missionaries and ethnographers, whose accounts disagree in detail but agree that the world began when the Lord of the Heavens acted upon the sea.

myths.title: The Vine Let Down into the Sea
myths.text: In the beginning Tagaloa dwelt alone in Lani-uli, the highest heaven, and beneath him lay only the boundless sea. He let down into the waters a vine from the sky; where its parts touched the surface, the islands of Samoa rose. On the largest he set the first settlement, and from the sky he watched over it. The fullest form of this creation account was recorded by the missionary J. B. Stair in Old Samoa (1897) and compared with related versions by Augustin Krämer in The Samoa Islands (1902); George Turner had published a shorter form in Nineteen Years in Polynesia (1861). Manu'a, the island group of the myth's first landing, is still styled the 'beginning of Samoa' in formal oratory, and the creation chant remained the deep charter for its paramount titles. The story is the charter of Samoan identity:The story is the charter of Samoan identity: the homeland is not discovered but made — thrown down from heaven and rooted in the sea.

myths.title: Sina and the Eel
myths.text: Tagaloa's daughter Sina came down to the pool of Mata o le Alelo to bathe, where a great eel, Tuna, confessed its love. When the eel was killed at Sina's command, she buried its head, and from it grew the first coconut palm — its two eyes, mouth, and body still showing on the nut. The tale was recorded across Polynesia (Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, 1876; Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology, 1970, §§ on the coconut cycle) and became the most retold of all Samoan stories. In Samoa the cycle carries a chiefly resonance as well: Sina's name became a byword for beauty in proverb, and her bathing pool, Mata o le Alelo, was pointed out to visitors into the twentieth century. The myth answers a child's questionThe myth answers a child's question — why does the coconut look like a face? — and binds the staple tree of island life to the death of an impossible love.

myths.title: The Storeys of the Sky
myths.text: Samoan cosmology stacks the sky into storeys — Lani-uli, Lani-ʻula, and the heavens beneath them — and places Tagaloa at the summit, above the winds that carry rain. Krämer (The Samoa Islands, 1902) recorded prayers addressing the ascending heavens by name, each storey ruled or traversed on the way to the Lord's seat. No text gives a complete, consistent map; the ethnographers themselves note that districts preserved different orders of the heavens. Below the storeys of the sky the same cosmology placed the underworld and the remote ends of the earth, and prayers were imagined to rise through the layers like visitors announced at the thresholds of a great chief's house. Yet the structure is constant:Yet the structure is constant: the sacred is vertical, and the higher the heaven, the nearer the Lord. Cosmology here is not speculation but orientation — the same layering a navigator reads in cloud and star.

myths.title: Tangaroa Driven to the Sea
myths.text: In the Māori version of the same divine name, Tangaroa is a child of Ranginui and Papatūānuku, the sky-father and earth-mother crushed in their parents' tight embrace. When Tāne thrust his parents apart to let in the light, Tangaroa fled to the ocean, and his enmity with Tāne — whose forests silt the sea — endures in myth (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, 1855; Orbell, A Concise Encyclopedia of Māori Myth and Legend, 1998). The Hawaiian Kanaloa and Tahitian Ta'aroa preserve further branches of the same god. Linguists reconstruct the shared ancestral form and read the god's names as a map of settlement itself — each island's dialect keeping its own office for the one Lord. Read across the ocean, the dispersalRead across the ocean, the dispersal of Tagaloa's name is itself the story: wherever Polynesians voyaged, the Lord went with them, changing office — creator in Samoa, sea-god in Aotearoa — but never name.

tagaloa.syncretism: Christian missionaries arriving in Samoa in the 1830s found Tagaloa the principal rival of their God and absorbed rather than destroyed him: his title 'Atua' became the generic word for the Christian deity, and his mythology was pushed into folklore, where it survived. The pan-Polynesian evidence suggests an older unity: Tangaroa of Aotearoa, Ta'aroa of Tahiti, and Kanaloa of Hawai'i are cognate names with divergent portfolios, a pattern linguists explain by the settlement of the Pacific out of the Samoa–Tonga region (Tregear's comparative dictionary; Craig 1989). In Hawai'i, Kanaloa survives as the twin and companion of Kāne, the two wandering the islands together as culture-bringers — a pairing that arguably preserves Tagaloa's original creative role. In the twentieth century the Polynesian Voyaging Society's revival of long-distance navigation deliberately re-enshrined these sea-gods: Hōkūleʻa's ocean road was, in the crews' own framing, Tangaroa's and Kanaloa's road again.
tagaloa.culturalLegacy: Tagaloa's most durable legacy is genealogical. Samoan orators trace chiefly lines (gafa) to divine ancestors of his household, and the sacred honorifics of chiefly oratory still invoke the sky's lordship. His daughter Sina gave her name to one of the most widespread of all Polynesian story-cycles — found from Samoa to Mangaia to Hawaii — and the proverbial Sina remains a figure of beauty and longing in Samoan speech. The god's name lives quietly in the landscape: villages, titles, and the old name Savai'i-region traditions. Since the 1970s the Pacific-wide voyaging renaissance has restored Tagaloa–Tangaroa–Kanaloa to active cultural memory: the canoe is again read as the sea-god's vehicle, and the navigator's art, once missionized into silence, is once more taught as his inheritance.
tagaloa.extendedMeditation: What Tagaloa teaches is that creation can be an act of looking down. His world begins not with a battle or a body but with a lord in the highest heaven and an empty sea — and then a decision: to let something down. Polynesian cosmology is famously oceanic, yet its supreme god is a sky-dweller; the islands are the rope and bridge between the two. This is a theology suited to navigators: the world is made of layers — sky, sea, land, underworld — and authority flows along the vertical axis, from above downward, from the god to the chief to the people. Tagaloa is therefore less a 'god of' any one thing than the source of rank itself: where he acts, land appears; where his daughter descends, chiefs are born. To study him is to see how a non-literate society stored its constitution in cosmology, safe from conquest, until ethnographers wrote it down.
tagaloa.archaeology: No cult image of Tagaloa is known — Samoan religion, like Polynesian religion generally, was essentially aniconic, and its temples were open-air malae and stone platforms rather than statue houses. The material landscape nevertheless preserves his world: Pulemelei mound on Savai'i, the largest prehistoric monument in Polynesia (roughly 60 × 50 m, dated by some researchers to the first millennium CE), served as a ceremonial platform, though which god it served is beyond proof. Scattered stone platforms, star mounds for pigeon-snaring (tia seu lupe), and chiefly burial sites across 'Upolu and Savai'i map the sacred geography the myths describe. The 'archaeology' of Tagaloa himself is documentary: the creation accounts recorded by Turner (1861), Stair (1897), Krämer (1902), and in the Journal of the Polynesian Society remain the primary evidence.

phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar [t] plus pure open [a]; Māori t is unaspirated, with none of the puff English puts on 'top.'
The velar nasal [ŋ] — ng as in 'singer,' never as in 'finger' — one sound, though two letters.
Tapped alveolar [ɾ] plus the diphthong [oa] ('long, extensive'); the diphthong draws the stress to this syllable.

pronunciation.approximation: 'tah-ngah-ROH-ah' — say ng as in 'singer,' tap the r, and let the last two vowels glide together.

kin.label: Tahitian
kin.form: Ta'aroa, the self-existent supreme creator of Tahiti (Henry, Ancient Tahiti)

kin.label: Tongan–Samoan
kin.form: Tangaloa, the supreme creator; his messenger the plover Tuli brought up the sand of the first islands (Craig, Dictionary of Polynesian Mythology)

kin.label: Hawaiian
kin.form: Kanaloa, god of the deep ocean and the underworld, companion of Kāne (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology)

pronunciation.note: Tangaroa is the Māori continuation of Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa — the same name the Tahitians lengthen into Ta'aroa the creator and the Tongans keep as Tangaloa. No vowel length distinguishes the Māori form, so the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII spelling loses: Tier 2, a display fact only. The ng is not two letters but one sound, the velar nasal English lacks.

domains.title: Tangaroa
domains.subtitle: Ocean
domains.lead: Tangaroa is the sea given will: lord of ocean, fish, and all that swims, son of the Sky Father and Earth Mother, and the brother who fled to the deep when his parents were torn apart. Every fish is his child, every canoe his guest, and every storm over the water is family business.

cards.name: Lord of Ocean
cards.desc: He took the sea for his domain when his parents were separated, vowing in the recitations never to return to the land.

cards.name: Father of Fishes
cards.desc: With Hine-moana, the ocean woman, he is ancestor of every finned and swimming creature the nets take.

cards.name: The Exiled Brother
cards.desc: Tāwhirimātea's war drove him from the coast; his grandchildren scattered to sea and shore, splitting into fish and lizard.

cards.name: One Name, Many Islands
cards.desc: Ta'aroa in Tahiti, Tangaloa in Tonga and Samoa, Kanaloa in Hawai'i — one ocean god under four island names.

symbols.name: The fish-hook (matau)
symbols.meaning: The carved hook with which his descendants take his children from the sea — every catch a petition, every offering a repayment.

symbols.name: The whale and the shark
symbols.meaning: His largest and most feared children; the whale (tohorā) and the shark (mangō) carry his mana in bulk.

symbols.name: The canoe (waka)
symbols.meaning: The vessel that crosses his domain; canoes were tapu and addressed as kin, because the sea is a relative who must be asked.

symbols.name: The tide
symbols.meaning: Tangaroa-whakamau-tai, 'Tangaroa who fixes the tides' — one of his names, and the rhythm by which fishermen read him.

symbols.name: The lizard (ngarara)
symbols.meaning: His grandchildren who hid ashore: the lizards, fish that chose the land — kin, yet forever on the wrong side of the beach.

mythology.lead: Tangaroa's stories are the Māori ocean chapter of the great separation cycle — and then the cycle widens: the same name, in other dialects, becomes the supreme creator of the whole Polynesian triangle. The Māori knew what the comparison would later prove.

myths.title: Born Between the Embrace
myths.text: Tangaroa was born into the darkness that lay between Ranginui, the Sky, and Papatūānuku, the Earth, whose embrace left no room and no light for their children. With his brothers Tāne, Tāwhirimātea, Tūmatauenga, Rongo, and Haumia-tiketike he grew to manhood in that cramped twilight, and with them he debated how to escape: Tūmatauenga counseled killing the parents outright, Tāne proposed forcing them apart. When Tāne at last pushed Ranginui into the sky and light flooded the world, Tangaroa looked at the dry land his brother had won and chose the other half of creation: he went down into the ocean, and took it for his own. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1; Smith, The Lore of the Whare-wānanga.) The myth reads the coastline as a family wound: the sea is not the land's opposite but its brother, still angry.

myths.title: The Children Who Split in Two
myths.text: Not all the brothers accepted the separation. Tāwhirimātea, the wind, remained with his father in the sky and made war on the others, and Tangaroa's domain was his first battlefield: the sea boiled under the storm. In the rout, Tangaroa's grandchildren — the children of his son Punga — split forever. Ikatere, father of the fish, fled into the deep and cried 'swim, my children'; Tū-te-wehiwehi, father of the reptiles, scrambled ashore into Tāne's forests and cried 'hide, my children.' Hence the hostility the myth sees everywhere along the tideline: fish devour the lizards cast into the sea, and the sea never forgives the land. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1.) What looks like natural enmity is re-read as a family separated under fire — every fish a refugee, every lizard a deserter's child.

myths.title: Hine-moana, Mother of All That Swim
myths.text: In the traditions recorded by Elsdon Best, Tangaroa's wife is Hine-moana, 'ocean woman' — not a separate power but the sea itself, personified as the mother of the fish tribes. Every species is their child, which is why the fisherman addresses the sea as kin, and why the first fish of a catch was laid back into the water: a family does not eat its greeting. The canoes that crossed Hine-moana to reach Aotearoa were themselves spoken of as her children, and the rituals of launching, fishing, and beaching observed her tapu; even the nets and lines were named and placated. (Best, Māori Religion and Mythology; Best, The Māori as He Was.) The theology is ecological before the word existed: the ocean is not a resource but a marriage, and the catch is a relative arriving for dinner.

myths.title: The Same God in Other Islands
myths.text: Travel west and Tangaroa grows greater. In Tahiti the name becomes Ta'aroa, the self-existent creator from whose body the world was hatched (Henry, Ancient Tahiti). In Tonga and Samoa it is Tangaloa, the supreme god whose messenger, the plover Tuli, dove to the sea-bottom and brought up the sand of the first islands (Craig, Dictionary of Polynesian Mythology). In Hawai'i it is Kanaloa, companion of Kāne in the company of gods who made the first man, and lord of the ocean's dark deep (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology). The Māori sea-god is thus the eastern branch of the oldest divine name in Polynesia — which is why the nineteenth-century comparatists made him their first case study. One proto-god, four biographies: the triangle itself emerges as a single story told in dialects.

tangaroa.syncretism: Tangaroa's syncretic career runs in two directions. Westward, in Tonga and Samoa, his name — Tangaloa — remained the supreme creator's, and Samoan Christians long prayed to a God they still sometimes called Tangaloa, a continuity the missionaries alternately welcomed and fought. Eastward, the Māori had already demoted him: from creator of the cosmos to lord of one domain, a brother among brothers, because the separation cycle re-hierarchized the gods around the family drama. In modern Aotearoa the name rides the cultural renaissance: Tangaroa appears in carving, kapa haka, and marine policy as the person of the moana, the sea that feeds and must be fed. The Treaty of Waitangi fisheries settlements of the 1980s and 90s, and the doctrine of kaitiakitanga over the marine estate, gave him a legal afterlife: his name is now cited wherever the sea is spoken of as an ancestor rather than a commodity.
tangaroa.culturalLegacy: Tangaroa remains the most-seen of the Māori gods — in every coastal marae's imagery, in the school-taught separation cycle, and in the everyday word moana for the sea. Fishermen still speak of him half-jokingly and not entirely jokingly; the Māori fisheries claim and its settlement wrote his descendants' relationship with the sea into law. In Hawai'i, where his form is Kanaloa, the modern voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sails by the same star-compass the old navigators read — the sea-god's ancient craft, relaunched. Across the Pacific the name survives in hundreds of personal names, in ships, in the naming of research vessels, and in the quiet conviction of island peoples that the ocean is not empty water but occupied country.
tangaroa.extendedMeditation:
Tangaroa is the sea as a relative — the most radical idea in the Māori cosmos. A god who is a brother, a domain that is a marriage, a catch that is a visit: the whole grammar of the ocean is familial, and the modern world's grammar of the ocean is exactly the opposite. When Māori negotiators in the 1980s and 90s said the sea is an ancestor, they were not inventing an environmentalism of convenience; they were quoting him. The name Tangaroa carries a complete theory of the deep: that the largest thing on the planet is a person with children, a temper, and a claim on our manners.

There is tragedy folded into the name as well. He is the brother who lost — who left rather than accept the new world, and whose children still flee one another at the water's edge. The tide that has run between brothers for all these generations is the one argument nobody has won: the land says the fish are food, the sea says the fish are family, and every meal from the ocean is a negotiation between the two.

Best, Māori Religion and Mythology
Henry, Ancient Tahiti
Craig, Dictionary of Polynesian Mythology
Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology

tangaroa.archaeology: No temple of Tangaroa survives, and Māori religion built none — but his archaeology is the archaeology of the sea. Coastal middens record the fisheries his priests regulated; the bone and shell of his children, stacked in heaps over centuries, are the oldest testimony to the relationship. Fish-hooks (matau) of bone, stone, and shell, many of superb workmanship, turn up wherever Māori camped on a coast; the great shank-hooks for snapper are functional sculpture. Rock shelters in the South Island preserve fish imagery read as ancestral. The canoe itself — the waka of the great voyages, surviving in fragments, adzes, and drilled hull-plugs — is his true monument: a technology of family visits.

phonemes.desc: Aspirated theta [tʰ] — the breathy consonant that opens the word, like a proclamation clearing its throat.
Short epsilon bearing the acute accent — the pitch peak falls on the first syllable, a high, clear note.
Short iota closed by voiceless sigma — quick and level, the name landing like a verdict.

pronunciation.approximation: 'THAY-miss' — the first syllable rises in pitch like a gavel; both vowels are short and quick.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: θέμις (thémis), 'divine right, that which is established; custom' — a common noun meaning 'ordained order' before it was a goddess's name

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *dʰeh₁- 'to set, place, establish' — the root of Greek τίθημι 'I set, place', Latin facere 'to make, do', and English 'do'

kin.label: Stem
kin.form: θεματ- (themat-), 'that which is laid down' — the family of θέμα, 'theme', 'what is set'

pronunciation.note: Thémis is Tier 2: the Greek Θέμις carries the acute accent on a short initial vowel but no long vowel (η/ω) and no circumflex. The restoration Thémis preserves exactly one feature the ASCII 'Themis' loses — the stress — and so the temple stands at Tier 2.

domains.title: Themis
domains.subtitle: Divine Law
domains.lead: Thémis is divine order — the rightness that exists before anyone legislates it. A Titaness daughter of Ouranos and Gaia, she keeps oracles, mothers the Seasons and the Fates, and counsels Zeus himself. Where her daughters administer what is fated, Thémis personifies what is fitting.

cards.name: Divine Right
cards.desc: Thémis is what is ordained — custom and right older than any written decree; the noun θέμις meant 'established order' before it was a name.

cards.name: The Delphi Succession
cards.desc: Before Apollo, Thémis kept the oracle at Delphi, inheriting it from Gaia and passing it on to Phoebe (Aeschylus, Eumenides 1–8).

cards.name: Mother of the Horae
cards.desc: By Zeus she bore the Seasons — Eunomía (Order), Díkē (Justice), Eirḗnē (Peace) — and the Moirai, the Fates (Hesiod, Theogony 901–906).

cards.name: Counselor of Kings
cards.desc: She warned Zeus against wedding Thetis, foreseeing a son mightier than his father (Pindar, Isthmian 8.26–47).

symbols.name: The scales
symbols.meaning: The balance of what is ordained; in later Greco-Roman art her figure merges with Justitia's, scales in hand.

symbols.name: The tripod
symbols.meaning: Her office at Delphi before Apollo took the oracle — the seat she held between Gaia and Phoebe.

symbols.name: The Horae
symbols.meaning: Her three daughters as her emblem: Order, Justice, and Peace — the visible seasons of a rightly governed life.

symbols.name: The Moirai
symbols.meaning: The Fates, her daughters by Zeus — spinners of the destiny even gods must accept; even Zeus 'gave them the greatest honor'.

symbols.name: The seat of assembly
symbols.meaning: Gods and mortals alike gather 'by Thémis' when they convene lawfully — her name is the Greek word for the lawful convocation itself.

mythology.lead: Thémis's myths are myths of legitimacy — who may hold an oracle, who may marry whom, and what order survives a flood. A Titaness of the first generation, she appears wherever the question is not 'what is powerful?' but 'what is right?' Homer swears by her; Aeschylus seats her at Delphi; Pindar makes her save the cosmos with a single prophecy.

myths.title: The Titaness Who Married Order to Power
myths.text: Hesiod enrolls Thémis among the twelve Titans — a daughter of Ouranos and Gaia born at the very beginning of the ordered cosmos (Theogony 132–136) — and then gives her the most consequential marriage of the succession. Zeus 'lay with Themis, who bore him the Horae: Good Order (Eunomía), Justice (Díkē), and flourishing Peace (Eirḗnē), who watch over the works of mortal men; and the Moirai, to whom wise Zeus gave the greatest honor' (Theogony 901–906). The pairing is the poem's thesis in miniature: the new Olympian king weds not a war prize but Order itself, and their children are the very forces that make civilized life possible. Even the Fates — sternest of powers — are born of this union, as if destiny itself were part of the design. Through Thémis, Zeus's reign is legitimized: he does not merely conquer the cosmos; he marries its law.

myths.title: The Keeper of the Oracle
myths.text: The Pythia opens Aeschylus' Eumenides with a genealogy of her own altar: 'first, in this prayer, I honor Earth, the eldest of the gods, who brought me forth; then Themis, for she, they say, was the next to hold this seat, her daughter as she was; and third, with Themis' good will and none by force, another Titan, Phoebe... gave it as a birthday gift to Phoebus' (1–8). The scene is astonishing in what it omits: no Apollo seizes Delphi — the oracle passes by inheritance and gift, from mother to daughter to sister, until it reaches the god. Athens' most sacred institution is thus traced not to violence but to succession law, and Thémis stands at its center as the first rightful keeper. The trilogy that invents the jury-trial opens, fittingly, with a chain of legitimate title — the oldest property record in Europe is an oracle, and its second owner is Thémis.

myths.title: The Warning about Thetis
myths.text: All mortal life owed its safety to a piece of advice Thémis once gave Zeus. The sea-goddess Thetis was so beautiful that both Zeus and Poseidon desired her — until, Pindar says (Isthmian 8.26–47), Themis revealed the secret: whoever wed Thetis would father a son stronger than his father. The gods instantly withdrew; Thetis was married off to the mortal Peleus, and her child was Achilles — destined to be 'a warrior son, mightier than his father', as the scholiasts spell out what Pindar leaves implied. Aeschylus assigns the same warning to Themis and Gaia (Prometheus Bound 873–900), Apollodorus (3.13.5) to Themis alone — the sources agree on the prophecy, not on its prophet. Either way, the myth's logic is pure Thémis: the law of succession is the oldest law of all, and even Zeus governs by foresight, not force. The Titaness saves the universe with a single well-timed disclosure.

myths.title: Deucalion at Her Oracle
myths.text: When Zeus flooded the world and only Deucalion and Pyrrha survived, the couple drifted to Parnassus and climbed to the oracle of Thémis — in Apollodorus' version (1.7.2) they pray to her by name — and ask how the human race might be restored. The goddess answers in a riddle: leave the temple, veil your heads, loosen your robes, and cast 'the bones of your great mother' behind you. Pyrrha blanches at the impiety — until Deucalion decodes it: the Great Mother is Earth, and her bones are stones. They throw the stones; the hard ones become men, the softer ones women. Ovid (Metamorphoses 1.381–415) retells the scene with Thémis presiding — and adds that the new humanity, born of stone, is a tougher breed than the first. The myth gives law an origin story of its own: after the flood, the first thing humanity rebuilds is not fire or shelter but an oracle — the place where right answers come from.

themis.syncretism: Rome made no translation of Thémis — her name crossed into Latin unchanged, a rarity among the Titans, which tells us how abstractly the Romans took her: not a foreign goddess to be matched but a concept to be quoted. Cicero treats her as personified divine law, and late antique, medieval, and Renaissance art gradually fused her with Justitia, the Roman Justice whose scales and sword became the standard attributes of Lady Justice from the sixteenth century onward. The courthouse allegory of modernity — the robed figure with balanced scales — descends from this merger rather than from any classical cult image of Themis alone. In the Latin West her second life was thus juridical: she became the face the law chose for itself.
themis.culturalLegacy: Every courthouse statue of a robed woman with scales descends from Thémis — filtered through Justitia and the Renaissance, but unmistakably the Titaness who made order divine. Her name passed directly into modern institutions: asteroid 24 Themis (1853), NASA's THEMIS mission (2007), and countless law reviews and legal institutes. In the Greek world her name lived on as a word for lawful right — Homer has mortals and gods act 'by thémis' — and in the modern imagination she stands for the principle that law is not invented but recognized: what is right is discovered, not made. Restoring Thémis restores the name of the oldest idea in law.
themis.extendedMeditation:
Thémis is the most important figure in this lexicon that almost no one remembers. She has no epic adventures, no metamorphoses, no loves. She is simply what is established — the way things are rightly done, before anyone wrote it down. The Greeks could see that custom preceded law, that the unwritten order held where decrees failed, and they gave that order a mother: a Titaness, born before Zeus, honored after him.

There is something quietly radical in making order a goddess rather than a king. Kings die; Thémis remains. When Aeschylus traces the Delphi oracle through her hands, he is tracing legitimacy itself — the idea that authority is valid only when held rightly. In an age that writes new constitutions every decade, Thémis asks a harder question: what do you already know is right, before you vote on it?

themis.archaeology: Pausanias records an altar of Themis among the Elean altars in the Altis at Olympia (5.14), one of the few fixed points of her cult; she was worshipped chiefly in company — with the Horae, at the assembly-seat — rather than alone. Her true monument is theatrical: the opening speech of Aeschylus' Eumenides (458 BCE), performed before the very rock of the Areopagus, makes her the first keeper of Delphi. Vase painters show her occasionally among the assembled gods — at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, in divine councils — recognizable by her modest bearing among the more flamboyant figures. The cult of 'the way things are done' leaves modest remains; which is, perhaps, exactly right.

phonemes.desc: Open back vowel [u] with alveolar tap [ɾ]; the colonial spelling ‘Urca-’ reflects Quechua urqu, ‘mountain; within the earth’.
Voiceless velar stop [k] between open vowels — Quechua k, written c before a in the old orthography.
Labio-velar glide [wa]: colonial gu before a stands for the semivowel w (modern orthography would write wa).
Alveolar tap [ɾ] with close vowel [i]; the final element is related to Quechua quri, ‘gold’.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OOR-kah-wah-ree' — four light syllables; the 'g' is only the glide w and the final y a short 'ee'. Stress placement is not recorded: the initial stress follows modern Quechua habit and is a convention, not a fact.

kin.label: Quechua
kin.form: urqu — ‘mountain; that which is beneath or within the earth’ — the first element of the name (Mannheim, The Language of the Inka since the European Invasion)

kin.label: Quechua
kin.form: quri — ‘gold’ — the second element, the metal of his treasury (colonial dictionaries; Mannheim)

kin.label: Later tradition
kin.form: Hurkaway — the guardian serpent of Uku Pacha, the world within the earth, identified in later Andean tradition with Urcaguary

pronunciation.note: Urcaguary is Tier 2: the restored form carries no diacritic or distinctive letter beyond the capital, and the pre-conquest pronunciation is irrecoverable — even the stress is a modern convention. The catalog's gloss ‘He of the underground’ follows the reading of the name from Quechua urqu and quri; both are ordinary living words, which is why the figure's title and domain are one.

domains.title: Urcaguary
domains.subtitle: Underworld Jewels
domains.lead: Urcaguary is the Inca guardian of what lies beneath the mountains: gold, silver, emeralds and the other precious things sealed in the earth. The figure is known only through the colonial chronicle tradition and later folklore, and the sources are late, brief and partly modern — but they agree on the core: the underground hoard has a watcher, and it is not a vault, it is a god.

cards.name: Guardian of the Hoard
cards.desc: Beneath the mountains Urcaguary keeps the metals and gems of the inner earth; the traditional description hangs gold chains and precious stones from the serpent's tail.

cards.name: The Serpent with a Deer's Head
cards.desc: The figure takes the body of a serpent and the head of a taruka, the Andean deer — wealth that watches and thinks like a mountain animal.

cards.name: He of the Underground
cards.desc: The name reads from Quechua urqu, ‘within the earth’, and quri, ‘gold’: the title is the domain, and the domain is the treasury.

cards.name: The Treasure That Judges
cards.desc: The hoard belongs to the guardian, not the miner: in the moral economy of the Andean mine, gold is taken only as tribute, never as theft.

symbols.name: Gold chains
symbols.meaning: Hung from the serpent's tail in the chroniclers' descriptions — wealth worn as the guardian's own ornament

symbols.name: Emeralds and precious stones
symbols.meaning: The green gems of the Andes stored in the subterranean house the serpent keeps

symbols.name: The taruka (Andean deer) head
symbols.meaning: The alert head he wears: the deer of the high puna, watchful and unreachable

symbols.name: The serpent body
symbols.meaning: The winding form that coils through the veins of ore inside the mountains

symbols.name: The mountain vault
symbols.meaning: Every sealed vein and hidden pocket of ore is a door of his treasury

mythology.lead: Urcaguary has no surviving epic. The sources are late, brief and partly modern, and honesty requires saying so plainly. What the tradition preserves is a portrait rather than a cycle: a serpent-bodied watcher below the mountains, a theology of treasure, and a mining etiquette that is still practiced in the Andes.

myths.title: A God Seen Through Colonial Eyes
myths.text:
Everything securely known about Urcaguary descends from the chroniclers writing after the conquest — above all Martín de Murúa, whose Historia general del Piru (1616) catalogues the gods of the Andes, and Bernabé Cobo, whose Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653) preserves the most orderly account of the Inca huacas. In their pages Urcaguary appears as the deity of metals, jewels and the other precious things hidden underground — a figure who presided over ore-rich mountains and mining shrines, but whose cult left no standing temple and whose myths were never written down in Quechua. The colonial writers worked decades after the religion they described had been outlawed, from informants under missionary pressure, so their catalogues are triage documents as much as testimonies.

Read that way, Urcaguary is half-known by necessity: a god glimpsed through the gap between destroyed shrines and Spanish notebooks. The temple built here is therefore a temple over an archive, not over a ruin.

myths.title: The Serpent in the Veins of Gold
myths.text:
Later tradition gives the figure a body. Urcaguary is pictured as a great serpent with the head of a taruka, the Andean deer, gold chains and precious stones linked along the tail, dwelling beneath the mountains in the uku pacha, the world within the earth. The deer's head is explained as a mark of the guardian's way of thinking — alert, swift, impossible to catch — and in the same layer of folklore the guardian serpent of the depths, Hurkaway, is identified with Urcaguary: the snake that coils through the ore veins is the treasure's own watchman made visible.

The image is exact theology in zoological form. A vault guards wealth with walls; a serpent guards it with intention. The Andes buried their treasure in the most guarded shape the animal world offers.

myths.title: Offering Before the Blast
myths.text:
The etiquette the colonial writers describe at mining shrines still survives in the Andes, where ethnographers from the twentieth century to the present record miners pouring chicha, laying coca leaves and burning cigarettes for the powers of the mine before a single charge is set — the same ritual courtesy, the ch'alla, that crews in Potosí and the central Andes pay to the lord of the mountain and to the Tío, the old one of the deep workings. Urcaguary stands behind this courtesy as its theological ground: the underground metals belong first to the guardian, and gifts earn a share. Mining, in this ethics, is not extraction but tribute.

The rite turns an act of violence into a negotiation, and that is the whole lesson of the god: the earth parts for those who ask and swallows those who only take.

myths.title: The Gold That Cannot Be Stolen
myths.text:
The tradition's moral edge is aimed at thieves: Urcaguary protects the hoard from evil people who dare to steal it. After the conquest, when the ransom of Atahualpa filled a room with gold and the furnaces of Cuzco and Cajamarca melted down the sun god's garden and the huancas of the shrines, Andean storytellers had every reason to sharpen the point — the metal pried from the temples was only surface; the deep treasure has a serpent on watch, and it does not travel. Whether the tale circulated in exactly this form in the sixteenth century cannot now be shown, but the sentiment is old and Andean: gold is not owned, it is kept.

It is the theology of every robbed sanctuary, and it is also simply true: the empire's gold crossed the ocean; the guardian's never left the mountain.

urcaguary.syncretism: Urcaguary's afterlife is a history of translations. Colonial missionaries folded the spirits of the uku pacha into Christian demonology — Supay, lord of the inner world, became the very word for devil in Quechua — while the miners kept the old courtesies under new names. The serpent body invited comparison with the amaru, the sacred Andean serpent of water, earth and the underworld, and in regional folklore the two guardians of the deep merge and separate: sometimes the amaru carries the treasure, sometimes Urcaguary carries the amaru's shape. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century compilations detached the figure from cult context entirely, presenting it as a ‘god of treasure’ in the European fairy-hoard sense, and modern summaries go further still, calling the gender ambiguous — a flattening the chronicles, which say little either way, cannot support. Read through all three layers, Urcaguary is best understood as the Inca theology of subterranean wealth caught mid-translation into European categories.
urcaguary.culturalLegacy: The etiquette Urcaguary presides over is alive: Andean miners still offer coca, alcohol and smoke to the mountain and to the Tío of the workings before blasting, a rite documented ethnographically from Potosí across Bolivia and Peru for over a century. In folklore collections the name circulates as the guardian of hidden treasure — the tesoros ocultos whose gold turns to leaves in the hands of the unworthy, a pan-Andean motif his serpent keeps. In the museums of Cuzco and Lima the legacy is an absence: the gold and silver he hypothetically guarded, described at length by Cobo and Murúa, was melted into ingots within decades of the conquest, and his treasury survives only as chronicle. For Quechua language revival the name's elements remain living words — urqu, the mountain, and quri, gold — so the god's title is still pronounceable as a sentence of modern Quechua.
urcaguary.extendedMeditation: What does it mean that a civilization gave its wealth a god? The Greeks gave Hermes to commerce and the Romans gave Juno Moneta to the mint; the Inca gave Urcaguary to gold that was still in the earth. That choice contains a complete economics. Gold's natural place, the figure says, is inside the mountain, where it is sacred; extraction is not sin but negotiation, and the negotiation never ends, because ownership never begins. The serpent with the deer's head is posted at a boundary the modern world refuses to see — the line between the surface we live on and the interior we dig into. Every blast re-asks his question in dynamite grammar: did you ask, or did you only take? A civilization that must give its minerals a guardian has admitted something the ledger never records.

Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653) — the fullest orderly account of the Inca huacas
Gary Urton, Inca Myths (1999)
Terence N. D'Altroy, The Incas (2002)
