urcaguary.archaeology: No temple, cult statue or offering securely attributable to Urcaguary survives; the figure's archaeology is textual. The chronicles describe the golden effigies and huancas of the Coricancha and of provincial shrines — works seized and melted between 1533 and the 1570s, known today only through Cobo, Murúa and Cieza de León. Mining archaeology supplies the milieu: pre-Hispanic workings at Potosí's Cerro Rico and across the central Andes, stone hammers, ore-processing floors and shaft burials that kept the mountain's dead close to its metal. Andean art gives the iconography of his form without the name — serpents and deer crowd Moche and Inca metalwork and rock art — but no piece can be assigned to this deity with confidence.

phonemes.desc: The canonical restored form Vasubandhu — a Sanskrit compound, not a Greek-accented name; the elements are vasu, 'wealth, good', and bandhu, 'kinsman, friend'.

pronunciation.approximation: Say "vasubandhu" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Vasubandhu".
pronunciation.note: The ASCII form "vasubandhu" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Vasubandhu" preserves the name's scholarly dignity. Sanskrit is not a stress-accent language like Greek; the name is a transparent compound of vasu ('wealth, good') + bandhu ('kinsman, friend') — 'Kinsman of Wealth' — so there is no distinctive accent or long-vowel mark for a restoration to recover, and the lexicon classifies the name Tier 2. What the capitals restore is recognition, not phonology.

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: वसुबन्धु (vasubandhu), 'kinsman of wealth' — vasu 'wealth, good' + bandhu 'kinsman, friend' (Monier-Williams, s.v.)

kin.label: Pāli / Tibetan
kin.form: Vasubandhu in Pāli sources; Tibetan dbyig gnyen, the standard calque translating vasu as 'wealth' (dbyig) and bandhu as 'friend' (gnyen)

kin.label: Family names
kin.form: His mother was named Virañcī; his father Kauśika, a brahmin of Puruṣapura (Peshawar) — his elder half-brother was Asaṅga (Tibetan biographies)

domains.title: Vasubandhu
domains.subtitle: Abhidharma
domains.lead: Vasubandhu is the great systematizer of Buddhist philosophy: author of the Abhidharmakośa, the encyclopedia of Abhidharma that every later school had to answer, and, with his half-brother Asaṅga, co-founder of the Yogācāra, the 'Mind-Only' school that reshaped Mahāyāna thought from India to Japan.

cards.name: The Kośa Verse
cards.desc: Six hundred verses of Abhidharmakośa kārikā summarizing the entire Sarvāstivāda analysis of mind, matter, and liberation.

cards.name: Abhidharma
cards.desc: His auto-commentary made the Kośa the standard curriculum: studied in Nālandā, debated in Tibet, translated in China by Xuanzang.

cards.name: Yogācāra
cards.desc: The Twenty and Thirty Verses argue the world is 'mind-only' — the doctrine his Kośa-era Sautrāntika readers found hardest to accept.

cards.name: The Conversion
cards.desc: Legend says his brother Asaṅga sent him a begging letter: compassion, not argument, turned the Kośa's author toward the Mahāyāna.

symbols.name: The Kośa stanza
symbols.meaning: A verse (kārikā) whose eight-syllable lines hold whole Abhidharma treatises — scholarship compressed into memorable sound

symbols.name: The begging bowl
symbols.meaning: The monk's only equipment; Vasubandhu remained a bhikṣu all his life even while moving courts and schools

symbols.name: The letter from Asaṅga
symbols.meaning: In the Tibetan biographies, the note that converted him — affection and mortality doing what doctrine could not

symbols.name: Treasury (kośa)
symbols.meaning: The storehouse metaphor of the Abhidharmakośa: every dharma catalogued like treasure in a vault, each with its own nature

mythology.lead: Vasubandhu was a historical philosopher, not a mythological figure — a monk of Puruṣapura (Peshawar) who, the early Tibetan biographies say, wrote the Abhidharmakośa as a Sarvāstivādin critic and then embraced the Yogācāra Mahāyāna of his half-brother Asaṅga. His 'myths' are the legends his tradition grew around a real life.

myths.title: Three Years in Seclusion
myths.text: The Tibetan biographies recount that Vasubandhu withdrew into seclusion to master the Abhidharma of the Kashmir Sarvāstivādins, and emerged with the Abhidharmakośa — six hundred verses (kārikā) of flawless eight-syllable metre that summarized the entire system. When the Kashmir masters admired the verses but missed their own subtlety, he added an auto-commentary (bhāṣya) of his own in which, tradition says, he quietly refuted them. The Kośa became what it remains: the one Abhidharma text every later school — Theravāda, Mahāyāna, and the Tibetan lineages — had to study, debate, or answer, translated in its entirety into Chinese by Xuanzang and memorized in fragments by generations of monks from Kashmir to Kyoto. Its author's own allegiance was already drifting as he wrote: the commentary, tradition says, shows the Sautrāntika reservations that would later make his conversion credible. To condense a library into verse, and the verse into a single lifetime, is the legend's whole point: scholarship can be a kind of asceticism.

myths.title: The Begging Letter of Asaṅga
myths.text: Vasubandhu had mocked the Mahāyāna as a corruption of the Buddha's teaching, calling its scriptures fabrications. His elder half-brother Asaṅga, already a great Yogācāra teacher, sent him no rebuttal — only a note reporting that he was dying, and begging Vasubandhu to recite the Mahāyāna sūtras for him. Struck by the affection of the request, Vasubandhu read them, found them profound, and entered the Mahāyāna himself. The story is hagiography — no Indian source records it independently — yet it encodes the tradition's own account of its greatest conversion: Vasubandhu did not abandon analysis for devotion. He turned the same razor-sharp mind to the 'mind-only' philosophy, composing the Twenty Verses (Viṁśikā) and the Thirty Verses (Triṁśikā) that define the Yogācāra, and the two halves of his career became one continuous argument about how carefully the world must be taken apart before it can be seen whole.

myths.title: The Victory over Vasurāta
myths.text: The biographies carry Vasubandhu to the courts of northern India, where the grammarian-philosopher Vasurāta, champion of an opposing school, had humiliated all comers. Vasubandhu entered the contest — the tradition describes a great assembly of rival teachers and lay patrons gathered to watch — and his opponent was worsted. After the debate he was offered a great patron's gold — and the legends insist that, as a monk, he spent the wealth on works of benefit to the saṅgha and on gifts to the poor. The story matters less as history than as the template it sets: the philosopher's victory is measured not in refutation but in what the victor refuses to keep. Every medieval debate culture of the Buddhist world — Nālandā's, Tibet's, Japan's — repeated this scene with Vasubandhu's name in it, and his reputation as the undefeated champion of two successive orthodoxies made the later conversion legend necessary: only love, the tradition decided, could have beaten him.

myths.title: One Vasubandhu or Two?
myths.text: Modern scholarship has had to ask whether one man could have written both the Kośa's analytical Abhidharma and the Yogācāra's visionary metaphysics. Erich Frauwallner (1951) argued the dates fit a single long life; others have proposed two Vasubandhus — the Yogācāra co-founder and a later Kośa author — and the question is still argued in the journals. The tradition itself never doubted: one Vasubandhu, brother of Asaṅga, whose conversion joined the two oeuvres into a single career — and the hagiographies even extend that life into legend, saying he ended it in the Pure Land of Amitābha, or in Nepal, depending on which strand one follows. The modern debate is itself a tribute: few ancient authors are so prolific and so consistent in brilliance that posterity must ask whether they were two people.

vasubandhu.syncretism: Vasubandhu's legacy is the creation of a pan-Asian scholastic commons. In China, Xuanzang's pilgrimage was undertaken substantially to resolve disputes over the Kośa, and his massive translation of 649–660 CE made Vasubandhu the doctrinal backbone of the Faxiang (Consciousness-Only) school. In Japan the Hossō school of Nara claimed him as its patriarch, while the Kyoto lineages of the future would read his Viṁśikā as the foundation of 'mind-only' meditations. In Tibet every monastery curriculum begins with the Kośa. Modern comparative philosophy — from Thich Nhat Hanh's engaged Buddhism to analytic treatments of idealism — still frames its questions in his vocabulary. He is perhaps the only ancient philosopher whose works are simultaneously a living liturgy, a graduate textbook, and a modern research programme.
vasubandhu.culturalLegacy: The Abhidharmakośa never went out of use: it has been memorized, commented, and debated continuously for some fifteen centuries, from Nālandā to the great Tibetan commentarial traditions (Prajñākaramati's and Yaśomitra's subcommentaries in Sanskrit; Sthiramati's in the mind-only line). Its author is honored as a patriarch in China and Japan, and Tibetan debate courtyards still open with his verses. In the modern academy Vasubandhu anchors the study of Buddhist philosophy — his Viṁśikā is a standard text in courses on philosophy of mind, cited in debates about idealism and representation. A brahmin-born monk of Gandhāra thus became one of the most-read authors in human history, his name a byword for the possibility that analysis itself can be a path to compassion.
vasubandhu.extendedMeditation: Vasubandhu is the scholar as religious figure — proof that in the Buddhist world, thinking carefully was itself a sacred practice. His two careers look like a contradiction: the great classifier of the mind's parts, then the teacher who said the parts and the world they compose are 'mind-only'. Read together, they form one argument: you must take the world apart completely before you can see what holds it together. His legend conversion turns not on a vision but on a letter from a dying brother — intellect bending at last to love. Modern philosophy of mind still returns to his Viṁśikā, where a dream, a reflection, and the waking world are made to trade places in a few pages. Few ancient authors remain so contemporary: the question of what the world is made of, and whether mind is on the list, is still his question.

sources.name: Frauwallner, Erich, 'On the Date of the Buddhist Master of the Law Vasubandhu', Serie Orientale Roma 3 (1951)

Buswell, Robert E., and Donald S. Lopez Jr., The Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism (2014), s.v. Vasubandhu
Williams, Paul, Mahāyāna Buddhism: The Doctrinal Foundations, 2nd ed. (Routledge, 2009)

vasubandhu.archaeology: Vasubandhu left no shrine — his witnesses are manuscripts. Fragments of the Abhidharmakośa survive in Central Asian Sanskrit finds, and the complete tradition rides on Xuanzang's Chinese translation (Taishō 1558) and the later Tibetan canon (Toh. 4089–90). Gandhāra, his homeland, is one of the richest archaeological regions of the Buddhist world: the monastery and stupa complexes around Peshawar — where the biographies place his birth — have yielded the oldest datable Buddha images (c. 1st–3rd c. CE). At Nālandā, the university whose ruins still stand in Bihar, his Kośa was a founding text; the debate-court culture his legend describes is the same institution archaeology reveals. The colophons of the Dunhuang and Gilgit manuscript finds carry his name as authority across the Silk Road.

phonemes.desc: Voiced labiodental fricative [v], as in English 'vine'.
Short open-mid front [ɛ], the reduced vowel of the first syllable.
Voiced lateral l, short [ɛ], voiceless s; the name's deeper etymology is one of the open problems of Slavic philology.

pronunciation.approximation: 'VEH-les', two quick syllables; the stress falls forward, as in the modern South Slavic reflexes of the name.

kin.label: Baltic
kin.form: Lithuanian velnias 'devil; spirit of the dead', Latvian velns, Lithuanian vėlės 'the host of the dead' — the closest cognate family

kin.label: Proposed
kin.form: Toporov's comparison with Vedic Varuna, sovereign of oaths and of the waters' depths — influential, but a hypothesis, not a proof

kin.label: East Slavic
kin.form: Volos, the form of the name in the chronicle oath-texts and in Novgorod's Volosova ulica

pronunciation.note: Tier 2. The restored form Veles preserves no feature the plain ASCII form loses — no diacritic, no distinctive non-ASCII letter — so the temple stands at Tier 2 by the mechanical rule.

domains.title: Veles
domains.subtitle: Cattle
domains.lead: Veles — Volos to the East Slavs — is the god of cattle and wealth, of the underworld's moist depths, and, in the great reconstruction of Ivanov and Toporov, of poetry and magic. Where Perun strikes from above, Veles moves below: through herds, graves, bargains, and song.

cards.name: Lord of Cattle
cards.desc: The chronicles gloss him explicitly: Volos, 'the cattle god' — herders swore their oaths by him alone.

cards.name: The Underworld River
cards.desc: He rules the wet, root-filled depths beneath the world-tree: the realm of the dead and of hidden treasure.

cards.name: God of Poetry
cards.desc: In the reconstructed mythology he is patron of singers and sorcerers; the wandering volkhvy acted in his name.

cards.name: Adversary of Perun
cards.desc: The eternal enemy in the myth-cycle: thief of cattle, storm of wealth, struck down each spring by the thunderer's bolt.

symbols.name: Cattle horns
symbols.meaning: The herds that were his treasure and the sign under which herders and merchants swore

symbols.name: The serpent
symbols.meaning: His disguise in the myth-cycle: low, wet, and close to the earth — the eternal adversary of the eagle

symbols.name: The bear
symbols.meaning: His chthonic animal in the alternating lore of the Slavic year — master of the wilderness beyond the fence

symbols.name: Gusli (harp)
symbols.meaning: The instrument of the singer he protects; in folklore the magic fiddle makes even the forest dance

symbols.name: Wet earth and roots
symbols.meaning: The moist underworld into which he withdraws and from which wealth returns

mythology.lead: Veles has no surviving epic. His dossier is a chronicle oath here, a famine there, and — towering over the fragments — the modern reconstruction by Ivanov and Toporov of the myth-cycle in which he is the thunderer's eternal adversary. Read together, the fragments describe a god of everything that grows, burrows, and accrues out of sight.

myths.title: Sworn by Volos
myths.text: The Rus'-Byzantine treaty of 944, copied into the Primary Chronicle, has left the only verbatim ritual text of pre-Christian Rus'. For the clauses of war the envoys swear by Perun; for everything touching livestock — sale, theft, compensation — they swear by Volos alone, and the curse on the perjurer is total: 'may we be cursed by the god in whom we believe, by Perun and Volos, the furred one... may we not be protected by our shields, may we be slain by our own swords, may we be shot by our own arrows.' A later copyist glossed the unfamiliar name for his readers: 'Volos — that is, the cattle god.' The division of labor is the myth in miniature: the sky-god witnesses between warriors, while the god of herds and wealth underwrites the peasant's entire fortune, animal by animal. Where your property lives, there your god is invoked.

myths.title: The Angry God of Suzdal
myths.text: In the terrible famine year of 1024, the Primary Chronicle (s.a. 6532) tells how wandering sorcerers came to Suzdal' and announced the cause of the people's misery: 'It is the god Veles who is angry.' The volkhvy demanded the sacrifice of a youth — a red-haired one, they specified, from a particular kin — and when the killing was done, they ate the body. The bishop of Rostov rode in, arrested the sorcerers, and drowned them in the Volga. The tale is told by Christian enemies, and its details are horrific precisely in order to damn the old religion; yet its center is precious evidence. A generation after the baptism, when the official gods were Perun's rivals long drowned, it was still Veles whose name a prophet reached for when the earth would not feed her children. The underworld god was the one who explained hunger.

myths.title: The Theft of the Cattle
myths.text: In the reconstruction of Ivanov and Toporov, Slavic mythology's central cycle runs like this: Veles, dwelling in the underworld beneath the world-tree, commits a crime against the sky — he steals Perun's cattle, his treasure, sometimes his bride. Perun descends in pursuit, hurling his bolts; Veles transforms and wriggles — serpent, catfish, black eel — and each spring the thunderer strikes him down, and the rain returns to the herds. No East Slavic manuscript tells this story; it survives in the pairing of the gods in the treaty oaths, in wedding laments where the bride weeps for a brother struck or drowned, in South Slavic spring songs, and in the universal Indo-European pattern of the storm-god and the serpent. The scholars who built it were explicit that they were reconstructing — and the pieces fit with a stubbornness no rival hypothesis has matched.

myths.title: Volos's Street
myths.text: Novgorod kept Veles in its very street plan. Birchbark letters of the eleventh and twelfth centuries — mundane shopping lists and debt notes scratched by ordinary citizens — give addresses on Volosova ulica, 'Volos's street', the commercial quarter by the market. No chronicle mentions it; the god's presence in the townscape was simply assumed, a neighborhood named for him the way others were named for craftsmen. When we read a debtor promise to pay on Volos's street, we watch the cult outliving the conversion in the least sacred of registers: commerce. Perun got treaties, curses, and weeping crowds; Veles got the marketplace — which may be the more honest monument, since people swore by the thunderer but they lived by the herder. A street, unlike a statue, has to be used to survive — and Volosova ulica was used every market day for a hundred years after the gods went under.

veles.syncretism: Veles's Christian afterlife ran through the saints of the herd. In the Balkans he survives in Sveti Vlaho — Saint Blaise — the Dalmatian patron of cattle whose feast ends with animals blessed in his name; in Russia the same role fell to Saint Vlasiy, whose name is simply Veles re-clothed. The divine adversary was absorbed too: the serpent of the myth-cycle slithered into dragon-slayer legends, and Perun's spring victory was reassigned to Saint George and Elijah. Byzantine-educated writers performed interpretatio on the pantheon as a whole, while comparative scholarship drew bolder lines — Toporov's Veles–Varuna, the Norse Óðinn of poetry and the dead, Hermes as god of herds and boundary-crossings — each a hypothesis about what sort of god this was: sovereign of everything the sky does not see. Demonized in the languages (Czech veles gave way to čert for 'devil'), he remained the underworld's landlord in folklore down to the modern era.
veles.culturalLegacy: Veles endures most durably in words: toponyms like Volosovo across the Russian north, the Dalmatian cult of Sveti Vlaho, the devil-haunted velnias of Lithuanian folklore, and the root itself in Slavic speech. Folklore kept his portfolio — treasure guarded by a chthonic serpent, the magic fiddle of the singer who bargains below, oaths sworn over a herd at market. The nineteenth and twentieth centuries were less kind: the so-called Book of Veles, publicized in the 1950s, purports to be a pre-Christian epic of his people and is now universally judged a modern forgery — a tribute, of a crooked kind, to how badly moderns wanted the lost god back. Rodnover communities today honor Veles as lord of wisdom, wealth, and the written word, and his serpent still guards vaults in banks' logos and fantasy novels alike.
veles.extendedMeditation: Veles is the god of the other economy. Perun owns everything visible — the strike, the oath, the battle won — but Veles owns what accumulates quietly: calves, coins, verses, graves. He is the patron of everyone who works below the threshold of glory: the herder, the merchant, the poet, the sorcerer, the dead. His mythology, reconstructed stitch by stitch by modern scholars, tells of a being who is defeated every spring and never finally destroyed — which is exactly the biography of wealth, and of life itself returning from underground. There is something subversive in his survival. The chronicles drown his sorcerers in the Volga, demonize his name, and reassign his cattle to Saint Blaise; and meanwhile ordinary Novgorodians keep doing business on his street, in writing, for centuries. Veles teaches that the underworld is not the opposite of prosperity but its storehouse: everything valuable is buried for a season, and the god of the deep is the one who remembers where.
veles.archaeology: No temple of Veles has been identified, and his material dossier is thin — fitting for a god of hidden things. The anchor is textual-archaeological: birchbark letters from eleventh–twelfth-century Novgorod address creditors and debtors on Volosova ulica, 'Volos's street', the market quarter — proof that the cult left footprints in urban topography even where no shrine survives. Riverside hoards and water-logged deposits are sometimes laid at the door of the underworld god, but the attribution is unprovable, and no figurine or amulet bears his name. The honest summary is that Veles's archaeology is his absence: the god of concealment kept himself concealed, and the street sign is the whole monument.

pronunciation.approximation: Say "viracocha" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Wiraqucha".

kin.label: Quechua
kin.form: wira 'fat, grease, foam' + qucha 'lake, sea' — the gloss 'lake of fat' is the chroniclers' own (Murúa, Historia general del Piru)

kin.label: Aymara
kin.form: Wilaquta, 'red lake' — the Aymara form of the name, still spoken around Lake Titicaca

kin.label: Epithets
kin.form: Ticci, 'foundation, beginning,' and Pachayachachic, 'creator of the world' (Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica)

pronunciation.note: Wiraqucha is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the restored form is plain ASCII, with no distinctive feature the ASCII alphabet loses. The name compounds Quechua wira, 'fat, grease, foam,' and qucha, 'lake, sea' — Father Murúa glossed it 'lake of fat,' more evocatively 'foam of the sea.' The restoration follows modern Quechua orthography rather than the colonial Spanish spelling Viracocha.

domains.title: Wiraqucha
domains.subtitle: Creator
domains.lead: Wiraqucha is the maker of the Inca cosmos: sky father, creator of sun and moon, and the weeping wanderer who once walked the length of the Andes and was never seen again. The chroniclers knew him as the invisible god who made the world and then withdrew from it — and his name still survives in the politest word an Andean elder can offer a stranger: wiraqucha, sir, gentleman, lord.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The name compounds Quechua wira, 'fat, foam,' and qucha, 'lake, sea'; the chroniclers glossed it 'lake of fat,' more evocatively 'foam of the sea.'

cards.name: Creator
cards.desc: Maker of the sun, moon, and stars and of every nation; to the Andes he is Pachayachachic, 'creator of the world.'

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: Honored at Titicaca, Tiwanaku, and Cusco; his cult outlived the empire and endures in solstice pilgrimage, shrine, and everyday address.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple; the scholarly restoration Wiraqucha replaces the colonial spelling Viracocha with modern Quechua orthography.

symbols.name: Sea foam of the lake
symbols.meaning: The etymon wira-qucha, 'foam (or fat) of the lake' — the foam from which the name, and the god, emerged

symbols.name: The staff and traveler's bundle
symbols.meaning: He crossed the Andes as a staff-carrying beggar, weeping at springs and prophesying — the god as itinerant stranger

symbols.name: The reed float
symbols.meaning: The totora-reed float that bore the two survivors of the flood — the seed of the remade world

symbols.name: The stone models of Tiwanaku
symbols.meaning: The sculpted prototypes of every nation, from which Wiraqucha shaped humankind at his workshop

symbols.name: The golden image of Cusco
symbols.meaning: The solid-gold statue in the Coricancha, described by Cobo and Murúa and melted down within years of the conquest

mythology.lead: Wiraqucha's mythology reaches us only through the reports of conquered lords to Spanish chroniclers — Betanzos, Cobo, Sarmiento — yet it holds together a coherent cosmic biography: the making of the world, the flood that erased its first people, the shaping of the nations at Tiwanaku, and a final journey westward that ended in disappearance.

myths.title: The Flood of Unu Pachakuti
myths.text: Juan de Betanzos, whose Suma y Narración de los Incas (1551) is the fullest early account, tells that Wiraqucha made the first people at Tiwanaku and gave them the world to keep; but they grew proud and lived without worship, so he resolved to undo them. He sent a great flood — unu pachakuti, a watery overturning of the world — that drowned the first race, the wari, while he himself rose into the sky above Titicaca. Yet he spared two, a man and a woman, calling them from the waters onto a float of totora reeds near the island, and commissioning them as the ancestors of a new humanity. The myth fixes the shape of Andean time: catastrophe and renewal in cycles, a world unmade and remade, with the creator always watching from above. It is also a charter for the lake itself — Titicaca is not scenery but the hinge where the first world ended and the second began.

myths.title: The Making of Nations at Tiwanaku
myths.text: Father Bernabé Cobo's Historia del Nuevo Mundo (Book 13) preserves the imperial version: after the flood, Wiraqucha set to work at Tiwanaku, where he sculpted the forms of all the nations to come — each with its own face, dress, language, songs, and seeds — and brought them to life. When the work was done he dispatched them, calling them out of caves, springs, and rivers to find their homelands: one nation he sent by way of a cave, another along a river's course, and to the Inca ancestors he gave the special charge that would lead them at last to Cusco. Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa's Historia Indica (ch. 6–7) gives the same program and adds the full titulature: Ticci Uiracocha Pachayachachic, 'ancient foundation, creator of the world.' The myth is a map of the Andes read backward — every people is the deliberate work of the same hand, and the Inca are simply the nation that remembered best who made them.

myths.title: The Sun, Moon, and Stars
myths.text: The same accounts make Wiraqucha the maker of the sky. On the island of Titicaca in the great lake he fashioned the Sun — Inti — and the Moon, and set the stars in their courses, appointing the Sun the most honored of all, 'like a rich ornament' among the rest (Sarmiento de Gamboa, ch. 7; Cobo 13.3). In imperial theology Inti then became the visible ancestor of the Inca dynasties, while Wiraqucha remained the invisible maker behind the visible god — a two-tier heaven in which the sun was, as it were, the son, and the emperor the sun's line. The pairing let Cusco worship a present, national god without ever forgetting the older, unbounded one above and behind him. It is one of the few world mythologies in which the supreme creator deliberately steps back from the machinery of daily rule, delegating the visible sky to his own workmanship and reserving for himself only the authorship of everything.

myths.title: The Weeping Stranger
myths.text: Betanzos closes the biography with Wiraqucha's departure. The maker walked the length of the Andes in the dress of a poor traveler, staff in hand, teaching as he went and weeping at springs; in the province of the Canchis he wept, foretelling that men dressed exactly as he was — bearded strangers from across the sea — would one day come and overturn the land. He came as far as the region of Manta on the coast and then, Betanzos says, passed into the sea and was gone. The detail is breathtaking in hindsight: a colonial-era text, written within twenty years of Pizarro, preserving a native prophecy that fits the conquest like a glove — and whatever its origin, the story made Wiraqucha the god who knew the strangers before they arrived. A maker who weeps over the future of his own work is a rare figure in any pantheon; the Andes kept him.

viracocha.syncretism: Spanish missionaries moved quickly to identify Wiraqucha with the Christian God: Father Bernabé Cobo reports Andean lords hearing the gospel and concluding that this Dios must be their own Pachayachachic, finally named. The identification stuck — in Andean parishes 'Dios Pachayachachic' is still a natural sentence — and it let the old shrine centers be absorbed rather than erased, most completely at Copacabana on Titicaca's shore, where the basilica of the Virgin stands where pilgrims once took ship for the island shrines. More remarkably, the god's name became a title for the conquerors themselves: from the earliest chronicles onward, viracocha meant a Spaniard, a gentleman, a lord — the word a conquered people used for strangers who arrived dressed, as Betanzos' prophecy said, exactly like their departing god. Even Tiwanaku's sculpted Gateway of the Sun is popularly read as his image, though that identification is a modern antiquarian conjecture — the gate predates the name by centuries.
viracocha.culturalLegacy: Wiraqucha never lost his mountain. Pilgrims still cross to the Island of the Sun and Moon on Titicaca, and each June solstice thousands gather at Tiwanaku to watch the sun rise through the Gate of the Sun — a rite older than any written version of the myth it now frames. In modern Quechua and Aymara, wiraqucha remains an honorific — sir, elder, gentleman — a fragment of the god carried in everyday address. The modern Inti Raymi festival at Sacsayhuamán keeps the creator in public view, and the story of the weeping god who foresaw the bearded strangers is still told as the Andes' own prophecy of the conquest. The empire that carried his name fell in a generation; the name outlived the empire by five centuries and is still a polite word for a stranger on a mountain road.
viracocha.extendedMeditation:
Wiraqucha is the absent creator — the maker who finished his work, wept once over what was coming, and left. Andean theology has no jealous guardian and no returning savior: the world was handed over, and what happens in it is, up to a point, the world's own business. That withdrawal is the deepest note in his mythology. Where other high gods demand attention, Wiraqucha demands only remembrance — his name spoken in honorifics, his lake crossed at the solstice, his ruined workshop kept as pilgrimage ground.

And the weeping is the detail that keeps scholars returning. A god who cries at a spring, foretelling bearded men in his own dress, is a god who has read the ending of the story he began. The chronicles that preserve the scene were written under colonial rule, which should make us careful — but even as colonial construction it is extraordinary: a conquered people explaining the conquest in the voice of their own god, who saw it coming and left before it arrived. Absence, prophecy, grief: the maker's last gifts were the ones no one could take.

Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Book 13, chapter 3 (creation and Titicaca)
Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica, chapters 6–7 (the 1572 inquiry of Cusco)

viracocha.archaeology: Wiraqucha's archaeology is the archaeology of his stage. Tiwanaku, the great center of the altiplano (c. 500–1000 CE), holds the Kalasasaya platform, the monumental Gateway of the Sun, and the precision-cut blocks of Puma Punku — the ruins later tradition named as his workshop, where the myth says he modeled the nations in stone. On the Island of the Sun and Island of the Moon in Lake Titicaca, Inca pilgrims' shrines — the Chincana labyrinths, the sacred rock, the sanctuary terraces — mark the myth's exact geography, and Copacabana's basilica stands on the shore where the ritual boats once left. In Cusco, the chroniclers describe a solid-gold image of the god in the Coricancha (Cobo; Murúa), melted down within years of 1532. No pre-Columbian inscription names him: the ruins give the stage, and the chronicles give the script.

Voiced bilabial nasal [m] plus open [a], the first syllable of 'mind'.
[n] plus [a] plus a soft final [h] — manah, 'mind, thought', from the root *men- 'to think'.

domains.title: VohuManah
domains.subtitle: Good Mind
domains.lead: VohuManah — Good Mind, Good Purpose — is the first of the six Amesha Spentas, the Holy Immortals who surround Ahura Mazdā. He is the thought that chooses truth before word and deed, the guardian of cattle and patient prosperity, and the divine visitor who appeared to Zarathuštra on the river Dāitya to open the way to revelation.

cards.name: The First Immortal
cards.desc: First of the Amesha Spentas invoked in every Yasna — the thought that chooses Aša before word and deed (Yasna 1.12).

cards.name: Guardian of Cattle
cards.desc: Charged with the soul of the bull and the herds — the slow, patient goods of a well-kept world (Yasna 29).

cards.name: The Two Minds
cards.desc: Opposed at creation by Aka Manah, Bad Mind — the twin and shadow he has fought ever since (Yasna 30.4–6).

cards.name: Bahman, the Eleventh Month
cards.desc: His Middle Persian name Vahman lives in the calendar: the month Bahman, its day dedications, and the feast Bahmanagān.

symbols.name: The bull
symbols.meaning: The soul of the ox whose complaint opens the Gāthās' ethics; cattle are his charge (Yasna 29)

symbols.name: The good word
symbols.meaning: Thought made speech: the middle term of the triad good thought, good word, good deed

symbols.name: The garment of light
symbols.meaning: In Zarathuštra's vision Vahman appears as a figure of light on the river Dāitya (Dēnkard, Book 7)

symbols.name: Bahman, the eleventh month
symbols.meaning: His Middle Persian name as a living calendar dedication and the feast Bahmanagān

mythology.lead: Vohu Manah's mythology runs through the Gāthās' deepest scenes: the complaint of the bull, the choice of the two spirits, the vision on the river Dāitya, and the dark roster of demons set against each Immortal. He is less a hero than the condition of heroism — the good mind without which no right choice is made.

myths.title: The Soul of the Bull
myths.text: The Gāthās' strangest litigant is cattle. 'The soul of the bull came to you, O Wise One, lamenting' — the lament asks for whom the herds were shaped and who will protect them from violence and ill care (Yasna 29.1, 9). Against the raider and the careless master, the soul of the ox — emblem of every creature that feeds and works for us — demands an advocate, and the divine council deliberates with the Good Mind, promising a prophet who will teach protection through Vohu Manah (Yasna 29.7–10). Later tradition assigns him the guardianship of cattle explicitly, and the bull becomes his living emblem. The lawsuit never closes: the herd's welfare remains the standing test of every settlement. Zoroastrian ethics begins with the weakest plaintiff — a voiceless animal — and its first commandment is husbandry: the good mind is the mind that keeps the herd alive.

myths.title: The Two Minds
myths.text: 'Now the two spirits, in the beginning the twins, renowned to be in conflict' (Yasna 30.3). One, the Bounteous, chose truth as the wise masters do; but the other refused, and through the fury of violence the worst mind, akəm manō, rushed upon mortals (Yasna 30.4–6). Thus Aka Manah — Bad Mind — is born as Vohu Manah's twin and shadow, and every human skull becomes the battlefield where the two contend for attention. The myth reads like psychology before the word existed: the origin of evil is located not in matter, not in fate, but in mentality — a choice of orientation made at the beginning and repeated in every waking hour. Evil is not an invading army but a way of thinking, and goodness likewise — moral life begins as a mental choice repeated daily.

myths.title: The Vision on the River Dāitya
myths.text: The Pahlavi Dēnkard (Book 7) preserves the great theophany. Zarathuštra, mocked by the sacrificial guilds, withdraws to the ford of the river Dāitya — and there Vohu Manah appears to him in a form of light, come to open the way: bring your questions before the Creator, he says, and the dialogue that becomes the Gāthās begins. The vision sets the pattern of Zoroastrian revelation: the Good Mind is the doorkeeper of wisdom; prayer must be intelligent before it is fervent, and the seeker's disposition is part of the revelation's equipment. Later tradition made Vahman the first of the four Amahraspands set around Ohrmazd and the guardian of the first watch of day. The pattern became doctrine: in the daily round, Vahman's hour is the first watch of morning, and prayer begins where he appeared. Before any angel appears, the seeker must be mentally prepared — theophany rewards the disciplined mind.

myths.title: Aka Manah at the Front
myths.text: The pairing of the minds is a war with fronts. In the demonology of the younger Avesta each Holy Immortal has an appointed destroyer, and the lists are consistent: against Vohu Manah stands Aka Manah; against Ašavahišta the daevas Indra and Saurva; against Haurvatāt and Amərətāt the she-demons Taurvi and Zairi (Vendidad 10.9; Yašt 1). The tradition warns that when Aka Manah advances, herds sicken and counsels divide; when Vohu Manah holds, the herd thrives and deliberation converges. Household, kingdom, and character all run the same circuit: thought first, then word, then the shape of the world. Priests memorized the roster in training; it doubles as a diagnostic chart of social ills. The ruin of households and kingdoms is traced upstream to a corrupted mind — moral infrastructure is mental infrastructure.

vohumanah.syncretism: Vohu Manah passed into Middle Persian as Vahman — and into every Iranian calendar as Bahman, the eleventh month, with its second day also his; Bahmanagān, his autumn feast, is still kept. In the Shahnameh, Bahman is the very name of Esfandiyār's son — epic memory of the old divine name in royal flesh. Pahlavi theology ranked him first among the Amahraspands set around Ohrmazd, and in medieval Zoroastrian speculation Vahman became the guardian of the first watch of day and the patron of the good disposition. His adversary Aka Manah, by contrast, survives only as a concept — Bad Mind — proof that in this tradition the better twin writes the history.
vohumanah.culturalLegacy: The good thought is the first bead of Zoroastrianism's triad — good thoughts, good words, good deeds — and Vohu Manah is that bead incarnate. His name is a calendar name (Bahman), a feast (Bahmanagān), and one of the most common male names in Iran. In Zoroastrian ethics the sequence matters: the deed is downstream of the word, the word downstream of the thought, so the tradition locates moral reform exactly where modern psychology does — upstream, in attention and habit. Few gods survive so usefully: a monthly reminder that the mind is the first battlefield and the first garden.
vohumanah.extendedMeditation: Cattle are the clue. Vohu Manah's charge is not intellect but the slow, warm, patient goods: herds, harvests, the long prosperity of a well-kept household. The Good Mind is the mindset of the good shepherd — unhurried, watchful, kind to what feeds us. Against it stands Aka Manah, the mind that is clever, quick, and ruinous. The pair maps uncomfortably well onto our own economy of attention: the feed engineered to be bad for us is a cattle-drive run by Aka Manah. Zarathuštra's question — whose mind are you thinking with? — is four millennia old and still the diagnostic question of a life.

Avesta, Yasna 30 (the two spirits)
Avesta, Yašt 1; Vendidad 10.9 (the opposing daevas)
Dēnkard, Book 7 (Zarathuštra's vision by the Dāitya)
Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (Bahman, the Middle Persian form of the name)
Boyce, Zoroastrians: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices
Skjærvø, The Spirit of Zoroastrianism
vohumanah.archaeology: An abstract Immortal leaves few images: Vohu Manah's 'archaeology' is calendrical and liturgical rather than sculptural. The Sasanian and later Zoroastrian calendars preserve his dedications — the month Bahman and the second day of every month — in colophons, ephemerides, and festival lists transmitted from Iran to India. Avestan manuscripts carrying the twenty-ninth Yasna and the invocation lists of Yasna 1 document his cult in continuous use, and the modern celebration of Bahmanagān in Iran and the diaspora is the dedication's living form.

Bilabial nasal [m] resting between two open vowels; the middle syllable carries the weight.
Alveolar [n] plus close, unreduced [i]; the name closes bright, like the sky it names.

pronunciation.approximation: wa-MA-ni — three even syllables, the middle one weighted; every vowel pure and Spanish-like.

kin.label: Quechua

kin.label: Related office
kin.form: apu, 'lord' — the living title of the great sacred mountains of the Andes

pronunciation.note: Tier 2: the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter — the distinction lies in scholarship and meaning, not orthography. The chronicles and modern Quechua sources agree on the mountain-sense; the older gloss 'falcon' (waman) survives in place-names and surnames.

domains.title: Wamani
domains.subtitle: Sacred Mountain
domains.lead: Wamani is the Andean sacred mountain made person: the tutelary peak of a province, ancestor of its people, and keeper of the springs that descend from its snowfields. In the Inca world every region had its wamani, and the covenant between community and mountain — offerings for water, harvest, and protection — remains alive in Andean religion today.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The name joins Quechua waman, 'falcon,' to the mountain-sense recorded by the chroniclers — the falcon that watches from the peak.

cards.name: Sacred Mountain
cards.desc: The apu of a province: snowfield, spring, and ancestor in one body — the vertical axis of Andean religion.

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: Qoyllur Rit'i pilgrims still dance before the glacier of Sinakara each June; the covenant with the mountain has never lapsed.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Kept at the registrable form while the temple explains the restoration and the falcon-meaning the plain form conceals.

symbols.name: Snowfield and spring
symbols.meaning: The glacial melt that feeds the terraces below — water is the wamani's first gift and the reason for his cult

symbols.name: The falcon (waman)
symbols.meaning: The older sense of the name: the raptor that quarters the peaks — from it come Wamanga (Ayacucho) and Guamán Poma

symbols.name: Coca and chicha
symbols.meaning: The covenant's currency: coca leaves and maize beer laid on the stone platforms for the mountain's favor

symbols.name: The paqarina
symbols.meaning: The emergence-place where ancestors rose from the earth; each wamani is someone's birthplace in the genealogies

symbols.name: The ukuku
symbols.meaning: The bear-dancer of Qoyllur Rit'i who climbs the glacier and carries the star-snow down to bless the fields

mythology.lead: Wamani has no epic cycle: Andean mountain religion lives in ritual, pilgrimage, and origin story rather than narrative text. What survives — from the colonial chronicles, the temple origin legends, and a living cult at Qoyllur Rit'i — reads as one long covenant between people and peak; the four 'myths' below are its chapters.

myths.title: The Mountain that Gives Birth
myths.text: Every Andean community once knew which mountain it came from. The colonial chronicles — Cobo's Historia del Nuevo Mundo (Book 13), Sarmiento de Gamboa's Historia Indica, and the now-lost Cusco paintings they copied — record a landscape dense with paqarina, 'emergence places,' from which founding ancestors rose to establish the ayllu. The Inca told the type-tale at the greatest scale: their own forebears, the four Ayar siblings, emerged from the cave of Pacaritambo and traveled ridge by ridge until the golden rod sank at Huanacauri, the hill that chose Cusco. A wamani is this story in the singular: one peak, one people, one bloodline running from snowfield to village. The mountain is not scenery behind the genealogy; it is the first ancestor and the final grave, and the covenant — people tend the mountain, the mountain feeds the people — is the oldest contract in the Andes.

myths.title: Water for Offerings
myths.text: The wamani's side of the covenant is water: from the snowfields the apu sends the springs that fill the terraces, and the people's side is the offering — coca leaves and maize beer poured on stone platforms, llamas driven to high pasture, prayers spoken to the peak by name. Cobo watched the rites; modern ethnography (Flores Ochoa) records their grammar: an offering is not a purchase but a greeting, the same exchange of coca and goodwill with which one honors an elder. Neglect brings drought, hail, and sickness — the mountain, like any elder, is patient but not forever. Brian Bauer (The Sacred Landscape of the Inca) calls this reciprocity the operating system of the Inca state. The covenant makes hydrology a religion: the aquifer has a face, the watershed a will, and the annual offering the family's standing appointment with both.

myths.title: The Star Snow of Sinakara
myths.text: Each June, tens of thousands of pilgrims climb from the Quechua-speaking nations to the glacier of Qoyllur Rit'i — 'Star Snow' — in the Cordillera Vilcanota, below the peak of Sinakara, and dance for five nights at the edge of the ice. The rite is old enough to have watched the Pleiades: Quechua farmers once timed sowing and harvest to tianquiztli's disappearance and return (Urton, At the Crossroads of the Earth and the Sky), and the shrine stands exactly where sky-calendar and snow-melt meet. The ukukus — dancers costumed as bears — climb the glacier itself and carry down blocks of star-snow to bless the fields; in 2004 Peru declared the pilgrimage national patrimony. Here the wamani's myth is not told but enacted, annually, at 4,800 metres — the rare deity whose scripture is a dance and whose cathedral melts a little every year.

myths.title: Children of the Summit
myths.text: When the Inca state faced crisis — an eclipse, an epidemic, an emperor's death — its answer was the capacocha: a procession to the high peaks bearing what was most precious. The chosen children were dressed as miniature lords, feasted in Cusco, given coca and maize beer, and walked with gold and silver figurines to shrines at five and six thousand metres, where they were left in the cold that would not let them decay. In 1999 Johan Reinhard's expedition on Llullaillaco found three such children — a girl of about fifteen and two younger companions — frozen, intact, wrapped in fine textiles with llama statuettes and shells; they rest today in Salta's Museum of High-Altitude Archaeology. The mountain received what the empire valued most — its children and its gold — a covenant written at an altitude where nothing human stays, and everything sacred does.

wamani.syncretism: The extirpators did their worst. From 1610 the colonial Church ran campaigns — Diego de Arriaga's manual of 1621 prescribed them — to unmask and destroy huacas, and the wamanis of the rites were beaten, burned, and forcibly 'baptized.' What survived, survived by translation: the mountain became a saint's hill, the cave-shrine a Virgin's chapel, and at Qoyllur Rit'i the glacier apu of Sinakara now shares his sanctuary with a rock painted as the crucified Christ. Scholars of the pilgrimage (Sallnow, Pilgrims of the Andes; Flores Ochoa) warn against calling this a disguise: the rites' logic — reciprocity with the living landscape — is pre-Columbian, and the Catholic overlay functions less as mask than as a second language the mountain was given, and never asked for.
wamani.culturalLegacy: The covenant still runs. Qoyllur Rit'i draws tens of thousands of pilgrims every June; coca is still offered to the apus before planting; and in modern Quechua wamani itself has widened from one mountain to a whole people or nation — Peru wamani, 'the land of Peru.' The mountain-deities entered the colonial church as saints and virgins and came out the other side still mountains. And in the Andean diaspora — miners, market vendors, students abroad — the first libation still goes to the Pachamama and the apu of wherever you happen to be standing: the wamani's greatest miracle is portability, a god who moves with his people.
wamani.extendedMeditation: The wamani corrects a flatland habit of mind. Lowland cosmologies spread horizontally — a tree, a river, a road; the Andes think vertically, in the thousand metres between maize and snow, and the mountain concentrates the whole journey in one body: spring at its foot, pasture above, ice at the crown, ancestors in its caves. To say 'the mountain is my grandfather' is not metaphor but hydrology with a face: the meltwater that feeds the terrace is his care, the drought his displeasure, and the offering the courtesy owed an elder. The modern world is relearning this grammar late — that a watershed is a relationship, that aquifers and glaciers keep accounts — and the wamani, whose covenant has been running since before Cusco, waits with the patience of stone for the lesson to land.
wamani.archaeology: The wamani's evidence is the mountain itself. The great capacocha shrines have yielded the most spectacular finds in Andean archaeology: the three Llullaillaco children (excavated 1999 by Reinhard and Ceruti; Museum of High-Altitude Archaeology, Salta), the Ampato mummy ('Juanita,' found 1995), and more than a hundred high-altitude sites from Argentina to Ecuador. At Cusco, the Inca capital's ritual landscape — documented building by building in Bernabé Cobo's Book 13 before the colonial city erased it — was a mapped constellation of apus, anchored by the Coricancha's golden garden and the intihuatana stone. Machu Picchu's planners sited its sacred district by the same rule: the city is a wamani-cult in masonry, every window and altar answering a named peak.

Rolled r followed by a short open o.

kin.form: Hiro, a Tahitian atua of the underworld — a plausible eastern cognate (Tregear, Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary; treated cautiously by Craig)

pronunciation.note: Whiro is single-tier Tier 2: ASCII preserves everything the Māori name requires; the digraph wh already encodes the f-sound to those who know Māori orthography. His epithet -te-tipua marks him as a tipua, a goblin-like being — a class, not a compliment.

domains.title: Whiro
domains.subtitle: Darkness
domains.lead: Whiro is the Māori personification of darkness, evil, and death — the adversary of Tāne and the lord of the night-world. He sends sickness, commands the reptiles of the night, and, in the oldest accounts, wars against every ascent toward light, knowledge, and life.

cards.name: Lord of Darkness
cards.desc: He rules the Pō, the realm of night and the dead that lies beneath and behind the world of light.

cards.name: Enemy of Tāne
cards.desc: He battles Tāne at every ascent — the cosmic rival who must be defeated for knowledge to come down.

cards.name: Sender of Sickness
cards.desc: Disease is his assault; the tohunga's art was, in origin, the war against his influences.

cards.name: Father of the Lizards
cards.desc: He is styled ancestor of the ngarara, the reptiles — the creatures Māori tradition reads as his embodied kin.

symbols.name: The Lizard (Moko/Ngarara)
symbols.meaning: His embodied kin — reptiles were feared as carriers of his malign influence (hence 'the lizard of death')

symbols.name: The Night (Pō)
symbols.meaning: His domain — the darkness that preceded light and that receives the dead

symbols.name: The War-Party of Spirits
symbols.meaning: The host of atua he leads against the worlds of light, named in accounts of Tāne's battles

symbols.name: Sickness (Mate)
symbols.meaning: The weapon he hurls — illness conceived as an invading atua to be fought and expelled

symbols.name: The Underworld Path
symbols.meaning: The descent to Rarohenga over which, in some traditions, he holds final power

mythology.lead: Whiro's mythology is an antagonist's dossier — he exists in the Māori corpus chiefly as the power Tāne and the tohunga must overcome. The sources are nineteenth-century records of oral tradition (Grey 1855; White 1887–90; Best 1925), and they agree on his office while differing on his genealogy and extent.

myths.title: The War Over the Baskets of Knowledge
myths.text: In the great myth preserved by George Grey (Polynesian Mythology, 1855; Nga Mahi a nga Tupuna), Tāne ascends through the layered heavens to obtain the three baskets of knowledge (ngā kete o te wānanga) for humankind. Whiro — Whiro-te-tipua — marshals the powers of darkness against the ascent, and the myth is explicitly a war: each heaven is contested, and Tāne prevails only with the aid of the winds and ancestor-gods above. Grey's text, dictated by Māori experts in the 1850s, is our fullest witness; the Tūhoe versions add that the battle-lines were drawn anew in each heaven as Tāne climbed. The variant accounts collected by Elsdon BestThe variant accounts collected by Elsdon Best (Tūhoe, 1925) and John White (Ancient History of the Maori) fill in different battle-lines. Whatever the version, the structure is fixed: knowledge descends only through victory over darkness, and darkness is a person who resents the delivery.

myths.title: Whiro and the Descent to Pō
myths.text: Māori eschatology sends the dead (ngā mate) to the underworld of Rarohenga, in the keeping of the goddess Hine-nui-te-pō. Within that realm the sources assign Whiro a dreadful office: Best (Tūhoe, 1925) records that Whiro consumes the dead — the final extinction that awaits those who pass fully into his night — while other authorities make the underworld a guarded, not devoured, existence. Best records how carefully the dying were guarded: kin kept vigil so the soul's journey began rightly, for a misstep on the path meant falling among the powers that answered to Whiro rather than to the ancestors. The disagreement is itself instructive:The disagreement is itself instructive: Māori tradition was not systematic about its dark gods. What holds across the accounts is the direction of dread: after death lies a jurisdiction Whiro administers, and his administration is nothing to hope for.

myths.title: The Ngarara His Children
myths.text: Whiro's epithet 'the lizard of death' is not metaphor alone: Māori genealogical chant makes him ancestor of the ngarara — the lizards, tuatara, and reptiles — whose cold eye and sudden movement marked them as his embodied kin (Best, Tūhoe; Orbell, A Concise Encyclopedia of Māori Myth and Legend, 1998). A lizard in the house could be an omen or an emissary; killing one carelessly was dangerous. The tuatara — a living fossil, stranger than any creature the Māori had names for — was the most charged of all his children, and some traditions set it as guardian at the very threshold of Hine-nui-te-pō. The genealogy does ecological work:The genealogy does ecological work: it assigns the island's most alien-seeming creatures to the one god who is himself alien to the world of light. The reptiles are Whiro's diaspora — small darknesses walking in the daylight world.

myths.title: Illness as His Assault
myths.text: In Māori medical tradition, sickness (mate) was the work of hostile atua, and Whiro stood behind the host: Best's ethnography (Tūhoe; 'Maori Medical Lore') describes the tohunga diagnosing which atua had 'shot' the patient and performing rites to drive the invader out. The rite was theater as much as medicine: the tohunga named the invading atua aloud, drove it toward the sea with the village's shouting, and bound the patient with cords — law, drama, and therapy in one operation. The afflictions attributed to Whiro's sideThe afflictions attributed to Whiro's side of the spirit world were grave and creeping — the wasting illnesses, the illnesses that came at night. The practical corollary was a therapy of confrontation: healing was a battle with Whiro's agents, fought with chant, gesture, and the authority of ancestors who had beaten him before. Illness had an enemy, and therefore a remedy.

whiro.syncretism: The missionaries who translated Māori cosmology reached immediately for their own devil — and George Grey's English Polynesian Mythology (1855) already frames Whiro as a 'personification of evil' in Victorian moral vocabulary, a reading modern scholarship (Orbell; Craig) treats as an over-Christianization of a more ambivalent figure. Whiro is darkness and death, but Māori tradition also treats night as generative — the Pō is where spirits dwell and from which thought ascends — so his 'evil' is an office in a balanced cosmos, not a fallen angel's rebellion. In the modern renaissance, Whiro has been reclaimed as exactly that: a necessary power, appearing as an antagonist in Māori-language fiction, film, and graphic narrative where a culture works out its relationship to sickness, night, and fear on its own terms rather than Christianity's.
whiro.culturalLegacy: Whiro was never worshiped — he had no marae, no priesthood, no offering; his 'cult' is a vocabulary of avoidance and exorcism. His legacy runs through language and practice instead: the fear of lizards as omens, the ritual cautions of the night, and the entire therapeutic tradition of the tohunga, whose first question — which atua did this? — assumes his world. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries Whiro has become a figure of the Māori cultural renaissance: a dignified, fully Māori face for the dark side of existence, used in health frameworks that treat illness within a Māori cosmology (te ao Māori models of wellbeing explicitly name and counter the atua of affliction). A god nobody prayed to thus shapes how a people still prays for health — his lasting temple is the rite that casts him out.
whiro.extendedMeditation: Whiro is a lesson in how a culture personifies what it fears without worshiping it. The Greeks had Éris; the Māori have Whiro — a being defined entirely by opposition, known through the myths of his defeats. Yet the Māori construction is subtler than a devil: Whiro is not fallen but resident — darkness is part of the building, the Pō beneath the Ao, and a cosmos without him would be a day without night, unthinkable and infertile. His myths are therefore really about the other side: Tāne's knowledge matters because Whiro contested it; the tohunga's cure works because Whiro sent the sickness. To study Whiro is to study a people's map of dread — lizards, wasting illness, the path of the dead — drawn with such precision that the map became the means of rescue. Fear, given a genealogy, can be argued with.
whiro.archaeology: As with most Māori atua, there is no material representation of Whiro: Māori religion was aniconic, and no carving, amulet, or structure is identified with him — the dread of his likeness would itself have been a contradiction. The relevant archaeology is contextual: the carved meeting houses whose pou (posts) embody ancestors of light, set against the prohibitions and ritual zones around burial caves and urupā, where his jurisdiction was strongest. Traditional Māori rock art and tattoo (tā moko) employ curvilinear forms sometimes read as reptilian, but attributing them to Whiro exceeds the evidence. The 'sites' of Whiro are instead the documented places of night practice — the sickbed, the burial ground, the lizard-haunted gully — mapped for us by Best's ethnography rather than by excavation.

pronunciation.note: Xipe is Tier 2: the Classical Nahuatl x stands for [ʃ], but the ASCII string 'xipe' already encodes that phoneme, and the restoration 'Xipe' adds only capitalization — no distinctive letter that ASCII loses. The name means 'the flayed one', from xipehua.

domains.title: Xipe
domains.subtitle: Spring
domains.lead: Xipe — Xipe Tōtec, 'Our Lord the Flayed One' — is the Mexica god of spring, agriculture, and renewal whose priests wore the flayed skins of sacrificial captives for twenty days. Beneath the terror lay a farming theology: as the maize seed sheds its husk to sprout, so the god sheds his skin to feed the world. He was also patron of goldsmiths and lord of the west.

cards.name: The Flayed Lord
cards.desc: Xipe Tōtec, 'Our Lord the Flayed One': the deity who wears a second skin, honored from the shaft tombs of West Mexico to the Great Temple of Tenochtitlan.

cards.name: Spring
cards.desc: Patron of the planting season; his festival Tlacaxipehualiztli opened the agricultural year, when the maize sheds its husk (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 2).

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: For twenty days his priests, dressed in flayed skins, walked from house to house — the renewal of the earth enacted in the streets.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form; the restoration returns the god's name to scholarly recognition.

symbols.name: Flayed human skin
symbols.meaning: His defining attribute — a second skin knotted at the wrists and ankles, the visible claim that the old covering must die for new life to emerge.

symbols.name: Maize husk
symbols.meaning: The theological key to his cult: the seed cannot germinate until it sheds its sheath, as the god shed his skin to feed humanity.

symbols.name: Temalacatl
symbols.meaning: The round gladiator stone on which captive warriors fought bound during Tlacaxipehualiztli before being sacrificed in his honor.

symbols.name: Pointed cap (copilli)
symbols.meaning: The conical headgear of his image, marking lordship and linking him to the solar-warrior complex of the western sky.

symbols.name: Chicahuaztli
symbols.meaning: The rattle staff he carries in codex imagery, an instrument of fertility whose sound accompanies the ancestral dances.

symbols.name: Knots at the back
symbols.meaning: In sculpture the god's own skin shows beneath the tied cords of the borrowed skin at his back — death worn as a garment.

mythology.lead: Xipe's mythology survives only in fragments: one late creation story, the great festival book of the Florentine Codex, and the uneasy testimony of Spanish friars. Pieced together, they reveal a god whose apparent cruelty is an agricultural theology — the flayed skin is the seed coat, and the death of the husk is the birth of the maize.

myths.title: The Lord Who Fed the World
myths.text: One late account, preserved in the colonial Histoyre du Mechique, tells that after the great flood the earth gave humanity nothing to eat, and the god Xipe Tōtec flayed himself so that people might be fed; for this reason his images are always shown wearing a human skin. Diego de Durán, who watched the rite's last performances in sixteenth-century Mexico, recorded the same conviction: the god had given his own covering for the world's sustenance. The friars were witnessing an agricultural allegory they only half understood. A maize seed cannot sprout until it splits and sheds its husk; the Mexica made that everyday miracle into a deity who wears the shed skin of a man. The myth teaches that feeding others is never costless: the renewal of the world is paid for with a skin.

myths.title: The Festival of the Flaying
myths.text: The Florentine Codex (Book 2) and Durán describe the great feast of the second veintena, roughly February–March: captives taken in war were dedicated at Yopico, the flayed lord's shrine in the Templo Mayor precinct; bound to the round temalacatl stone, they fought gladiatorial combats against seasoned warriors, then were stretched across the sacrificial stone. The priests then flayed the victims and wore their skins for twenty days, knotted at the wrists and ankles, visiting houses and receiving offerings as living images of the god, until the dried skins were laid away. Sahagún's informants named them tototectin, 'the flayed ones.' The rite horrified the friars and obsesses modern readers, but its logic was exact: at the start of the farming year the city reenacted the first flaying, so that what was done to the god might be done to the seed. Shed skin, shed husk, new season.

myths.title: The Red Lord of the West
myths.text: In the theological geography recorded from Sahagún's informants, Xipe Tōtec was also Tlatlauhqui, 'the red one' — the Red Tezcatlipoca, lord of the west, the quarter of the setting sun and of the earth's buried treasures. During Tlacaxipehualiztli the goldsmiths held their own feast, for Xipe was patron of their craft: gold, the Nahuatl-speakers called teocuitlatl, 'divine excrement', the sun's deposit in the earth's gut. The same festival that flayed a man to renew the fields also honored the men who pulled shining metal from the ground. Modern scholarship (Miller & Taube) has long noted the coherence: metal and maize are both riches that must be stripped out of a dead covering — ore from rock, grain from husk, flesh from skin. The red lord of the west governs them all.

myths.title: The God Made Flesh
myths.text: Central Mexicans did not think their gods watched the rite from afar. For the duration of the feast the chosen captive became an ixiptla — a 'representation', a living image of Xipe Tōtec — dressed, honored, and addressed as the god himself before he was killed and his skin assumed by the priests. Bernardino de Sahagún and Diego de Durán both describe how the impersonator was adorned and escorted through the city as though the deity had come down to walk among his people. The institution startled the friars into comparisons with the Christian God made man, and modern scholars such as Inga Clendinnen have made the ixiptla the key to understanding Mexica religion: a god who must enter a human body to renew the world, and leave it as a skin.

xipe.syncretism: The Dominican Diego de Durán, watching Tlacaxipehualiztli in the decades after the Conquest, was struck that the feast fell near Holy Week — the god who wore a flayed skin commemorated at the season when Christians mourned a god who wore a body and lost it. The friars suppressed the rite, yet its imagery proved durable: in the Puebla and Guerrero regions, masked and costumed dance confraternities — ancestors of today's concheros and Danza Azteca — carried the flayed lord's memory in transformed dress. Twentieth-century revival movements such as the Mexicayotl circle reclaimed Xipe Tōtec as a figure of indigenous identity and renewal rather than barbarism. Comparative religion places him among the world's 'dying vegetation' gods, but the Mexica theology was stranger and more precise: not a god who dies like a plant, but a god who peels like a seed.
xipe.culturalLegacy: Xipe Tōtec stands at the center of the modern debate over Aztec sacrifice — read by some as the theological heart of a sophisticated agricultural civilization, by others as evidence of state terror (Clendinnen, Townsend). His images anchor museum collections: the monolithic Xipe of the Templo Mayor Museum, wearing his knotted second skin, is among the most reproduced Aztec sculptures. Nahuatl lexicography (Karttunen, Lockhart) keeps his name etymologically alive, and Danza Azteca troupes across Mexico and the United States still perform in the spring season his festival once owned. For better and worse, the Flayed One is now the world's most recognizable emblem of Mexica religion.
xipe.extendedMeditation:
Xipe Tōtec asks the question every farmer knows and every city forgets: what must die for something else to live? His answer is a skin. The maize seed does not negotiate with its husk; it splits it. The god does not sympathize with the covering; he wears it. In a culture that now separates death from dinner by an almost perfectly opaque supply chain, the Flayed One insists on the connection: your bread was once a seed's corpse, your gold was once a stone's wound.

To meditate on Xipe is to meditate on the cost of renewal. He is not a god of resurrection — nothing in the rite promises the flayed man his life back. He is a god of transfer: life moves, and something is always left behind. The friars saw only cruelty; the Mexica saw the farming year. Both were reading the same skin.
xipe.archaeology: The earliest material witness to the flayed-skin complex comes from the shaft tombs of West Mexico (Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit, c. 200 BCE–500 CE), whose ceramic figures wear the flayed skins of other men — proof the imagery predates the Aztec state by centuries. At Tenochtitlan, the INAH excavations of the Templo Mayor precinct (from 1978) located Xipe's shrine, Yopico, and its caches; the Templo Mayor Museum preserves a monolithic Xipe Tōtec whose back shows the wearer's own skin beneath the knotted cords of the second skin. The cult's heartland lay among the Yope of the Guerrero coast and in the Puebla region, and the screenfold Codex Borgia (c. 1500) gives the god's fullest painted dossier.

domains.title: Yongwang, the Dragon King
domains.subtitle: sovereign of the seas, storms, and waters
domains.lead: Yongwang — 龍王, “dragon king” — is the sovereign of the Korean seas: master of storms, rain, and the shoals of fish on which coastal villages live. Reached through Buddhist liturgy, shamanic gut ritual, and village folktale alike, he rewards respect with calm water and punishes neglect with empty nets and sudden gale.

cards.name: Dragon King
cards.desc: The royal dragon enthroned in the underwater palace Yeonggung, sovereign of the four seas of the compass.

cards.name: Ruler of Seas
cards.desc: He governs tides, currents, and the creatures of the deep — the shoals are his armies, the turtles his couriers.

cards.name: Rain and Storms
cards.desc: From his palace he releases the rains that fill the paddies and the typhoons that empty the harbours.

cards.name: Fisherfolk Protector
cards.desc: The south-coast villages honour him with the Yongwang-gut, the annual rite that secures safe voyages and abundant catch.

symbols.name: Dragon
symbols.meaning: The serpent perfected — after a thousand years guarding the yeouiju jewel, the imugi ascends as a true dragon.

symbols.name: Waves
symbols.meaning: The visible form of Yongwang’s domain; the sea’s temper is read as the king’s mood.

symbols.name: Pearl (yeouiju)
symbols.meaning: The wish-granting jewel of the underwater palace — the treasure for which a python waits a thousand years.

symbols.name: Turtle
symbols.meaning: A messenger and attendant of the dragon king, ferrying petitions and souls between land and sea.

mythology.lead: Yongwang is the Dragon King of the Korean seas — sovereign of storms, rain, and the shoals of fish on which coastal life depends. Buddhist scripture, shamanic gut ritual, and village folktale each give him a different throne: a guardian of the dharma, a king placated with offerings set afloat, and a grateful serpent who repays a kindness. His mythology is the story of how Korea learned to live beside a beautiful, dangerous sea.

myths.title: The Python and the Wish-Jewel
myths.text: The Samguk Yusa, “Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms” (13th century), tells of a poor but kind-hearted man who gave shelter to a strange traveller caught by night and rain. The stranger revealed himself as an imugi — a python that had waited a thousand years for the yeouiju, the wish-granting jewel that alone can raise a serpent to dragonhood. Entrusting the jewel to his host, the imugi attempted the ascent to heaven; when it slipped, the man caught it and set it upon the serpent’s head, and the imugi became a true dragon and rose into the sky. In gratitude the dragon left a bright band of his own body coiled around the man’s house as a blessing, and the Samguk Yusa says this is why Koreans paint banded, rainbow colours along the eaves of their houses to this day. The tale teaches that the sea’s greatest power answers to ordinary human kindness — and that even a dragon’s fortune once depended on a stranger’s open door.

myths.title: The King Who Became a Dragon
myths.text: The Samguk Sagi and Samguk Yusa record that King Munmu of Silla (r. 661–681), dying, commanded that his body be cremated and the ashes cast into the East Sea. “I will become a dragon,” he said, “and protect this kingdom from the pirates of the east.” His queen and son fulfilled the vow; the ashes were committed to the sea off the coast near Gampo, and his son King Sinmun raised above the shore the temple Gameunsa — “the temple that appeases the sea” — whose pagodas still stand at Gyeongju. The episode makes explicit what coastal religion had long implied: that the Dragon King and the dead king could share one body, and that the sea’s protection was a royal responsibility, paid for in flesh. Korean Buddhists still honour Munmu as the dragon of the East Sea; the tale binds kingship, Buddhism, and the sea into a single sacred geography.

myths.title: The Yongwang-gut of the Fishing Villages
myths.text: In the fishing villages of Korea’s south coast — Chaeseon in Tongyeong, Suyeong in Busan — shamans performed the Yongwang-gut, the rite of the Dragon King, to open the fishing season and beg calm seas. The folklorist Im Seok-jae recorded these rites in the twentieth century, when they were already old: the shaman invokes the dragon kings of the four seas in turn, receives their possessing presence, and sends a paper dragon-boat laden with rice, fruit, cloth, and coins out onto the water, the offering itself sailing to the palace beneath the waves. If the season proves good, the debt is remembered; if storms come, the rite is repeated with greater care. Here mythology is not a story but a contract renewed each year — a working relationship between a fishing people and the sovereign of the deep, maintained with drum, cymbal, and a boat far too small for its cargo of gratitude.

myths.title: The Monk and the Sea God’s Dream
myths.text: The temple of Haedong Yonggung at Busan, founded in 1376 by the Goryeo monk Naong Hyegeun, stands where cliffs meet the open sea — a rare orientation for a Korean monastery, whose temples customarily turn their backs on the water. Its foundation legend, preserved in the temple’s own tradition, tells that Naong dreamed the Dragon King of the East Sea rose from the waves and showed him a stretch of coast where, if a temple were built, prayers would surely be answered; waking, the dream-site proved to be a rugged shore east of the walled city. He built there, and the fishermen came. The tale reflects the late Goryeo world in which Buddhist and shamanic readings of the sea overlapped completely: the same Dragon King who received paper boats from shamans appeared in the dream of a great Seon master. Visitors still descend the temple’s 108 stairs to the seaside shrine of the dragon king — one of the few places where the old sea cult can be visited, not merely read about.

etymology.derivation: The name combines 龍 (yong, "dragon") and 王 (wang, "king"). Read 용왕 in Korean, it denotes the royal dragon sovereign of the waters, a figure shared across East Asian religions.

nameVariations.note: Standard romanisation of 龍王.
Alternate term for dragon spirit, especially in shamanic contexts.
Hangul form.

yongwang.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Yongwang, the Hangul form is 용왕 and the Hanja form is 龍王. Hangul ‘용왕’ and Hanja ‘龍王’; the figure is shared with East Asian dragon-king traditions but has distinct Korean cultic forms. The ASCII form yongwang is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Yongwang is the scholarly citation form.
yongwang.syncretism: Yongwang is part of a broader East Asian dragon-king tradition, with close parallels in Chinese, Japanese, and Vietnamese religion; the Sino-Korean name itself, 龍王, is borrowed directly. In Korea the figure was absorbed into both Buddhism and shamanism: he appears as a deva-like guardian and rain-maker in Buddhist temples, and as a sovereign spirit who must be formally petitioned in gut rituals. The Chinese cult of the Four Dragon Kings and Daoist rain-making liturgy supplied much of his ceremonial vocabulary. Despite these borrowings, the Korean Yongwang has a distinctive local colouring tied to fishing villages, the south coast, and the hazards of the Korea Strait.
yongwang.culturalLegacy: Yongwang remains a vivid figure in Korean coastal culture, appearing in temple art, village rituals, seafood markets, and popular media. Dragon king imagery decorates boats, restaurants, and festivals, and prayers for safe fishing continue in many communities. Temples by the sea — Haedong Yonggung above all — keep his cult publicly visible, and the figure also influences Korean environmental thought, serving as a symbol of the sea’s power and the need for respectful relations with marine ecosystems. In games and animation, Yongwang often appears as a majestic dragon lord.
yongwang.extendedMeditation: Yongwang embodies the oldest human bargain with the sea: reverence in exchange for survival. The ocean that feeds Korea can erase it in a night, and the Dragon King gives that double truth a face, a palace, and a name. He is what a fishing people build when they cannot control the water but cannot leave it either — a sovereign to whom gratitude, offerings, and good behaviour can be addressed. In him the natural and the political also fuse: a king of Silla becomes a dragon to guard the coast, because protecting the realm at sea was understood as the same office as protecting it on land. To study Yongwang is to study how religion works at its most practical: not to explain the storm, but to negotiate with it — year after year, in the only coin a dragon accepts, ceremony.

yongwang.archaeology: The dragon king left few monumental traces, but his cult surfaces across the peninsula’s material culture. Goryeo and Joseon temple paintings place dragon kings and the underwater palace among the assembly of guardian deities, and the seaside temple of Haedong Yonggung (founded 1376 near Busan) preserves its founder Naong’s dream of the East Sea dragon king as a living foundation charter. The coastal shrine communities of the south sea — Chaeseon and Suyeong among them — anchor the Yongwang-gut traditions recorded by the folklorist Im Seok-jae in the twentieth century. Most strikingly literal is the royal evidence: the underwater tomb of King Munmu’s ashes off Gampo and the twin pagodas of Gameunsa (682 CE) at Gyeongju mark the dynasty’s fusion of kingship with the sea-dragon cult.

phonemes.desc: Voiced alveolar [z] plus palatalized m [mʲ] and a diphthong [ej] — 'zm-YAY', the hissing onset of the serpent-word zmei.
Unstressed [ɡɐ] — the back of the name, the mountain lying low before the storm.
Stressed [ˈrɨnɨtɕ] with the rolled r and soft final [tɕ] — 'RY-nich', the syllable where the fire lands.
